Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 31, verses 1–2:

Surat Luqman

Ibn al-Durays, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Dala'il* related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he said: "Surat Luqman was revealed in Makkah, and there is no exception in this report." In the report of al-Nahhas in his *Tarikh*, from him, there is an exception of three verses from it, namely: ﴿And if whatever trees on the earth were pens﴾ [Luqman: 27], up to the end of the three verses, for they were revealed in Madinah. This is because "when the Prophet (ﷺ) migrated, the rabbis of the Jews said to him: 'We have been informed that you say: ﴿And you have not been given of knowledge except a little﴾ [al-Isra: 85]. Do you mean us or your people?' He said: 'Not at all, I mean you.' They said: 'You know that we have been given the Torah, and in it is the explanation of everything.' The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'That is, in the knowledge of Allah, little.' So He revealed the verses."

Al-Dani related from Ata', and Abu Hayyan from Qatada, that they both said: "It is Makkan except for two verses, which are ﴿And if whatever trees on the earth were pens﴾ up to the end of the two verses." It has also been said: "It is Makkan, except for one verse, which is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those who establish prayer and give zakah﴾ [Luqman: 4], for their obligation was in Madinah." But you know that prayer was made obligatory in Makkah on the night of the Isra' (Night Journey), as in Sahih al-Bukhari and others. Therefore what was mentioned, that its obligation was in Madinah, is not accepted. And even if it were accepted, it is sufficient that they were commanded to it in Makkah, even if as a recommendation, so the argument does not hold in it. Yes, the well-known view is that the obligation of zakah was in Madinah, so perhaps that speaker meant that the obligation of both together was established in Madinah, not that the obligation of each of them was established there. Nor does it harm this that the obligation of prayer was in Makkah. It has also been said: the obligation of zakah was in Makkah just like prayer, and the specifying of the shares (of zakah) was what was in Madinah, and according to this there is no argument in either.

Its verses are thirty-three in the Makkan and Madani count, and thirty-four in the count of the rest.

[p. 65]

The cause of its revelation, according to what is in *al-Bahr* (Tafsir al-Bahr al-Muhit): Quraysh asked about the story of Luqman with his son and about his kindness to his parents, and so it was revealed. The relation of its connection to what precedes it, according to what is also in it, is that He, exalted is He, said before: ﴿And We have certainly presented for the people in this Qur'an from every example﴾ [al-Rum: 58], and He alluded to that at the beginning of this surah. And at the end of what precedes it is ﴿And if you brought them a sign﴾ [al-Rum: 58], and in it (this surah) is: ﴿And when Our verses are recited to him, he turns away arrogant﴾ [Luqman: 7]. Al-Jalal al-Suyuti said: It has appeared to me, in its connection with what precedes it, along with the pairing in the opening with (Alif Lam Mim), that His saying, exalted is He: ﴿a guidance and mercy for the doers of good, those who establish prayer and give zakah, and they, of the Hereafter, are certain﴾ [Luqman: 3–4] is related to His saying before: ﴿And those who were given knowledge and faith will say: "You have remained within the Book of Allah until the Day of Resurrection"﴾ [al-Rum: 56], the verse. This is precisely their certainty about the Hereafter, and they are the doers of good described by what was mentioned. Also, in both surahs there is a group of verses about the beginning of creation.

He mentioned in the previous surah: ﴿in a meadow they will be delighted﴾ [al-Rum: 15], which was explained as meaning listening (to music). Here He mentioned: ﴿And among the people is one who purchases idle speech﴾ [Luqman: 6], which was explained as singing and musical instruments. End of quote. What is to come, if Allah wills, of the discussion of that. And I say, regarding the connection as well: it has been mentioned earlier that His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And it is He who begins creation and then repeats it, and that is easier for Him﴾ [al-Rum: 27], and here His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Your creation and your resurrection are not but as one soul﴾ [Luqman: 28]. Both indicate the ease of resurrection, and He confirmed that here with His saying, mighty and majestic is He, saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah is Hearing and Seeing﴾. And He, glorified is He, mentioned there His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when harm touches the people, they call upon their Lord, turning back to Him. Then when He lets them taste mercy from Him, at once a party of them associate others with their Lord﴾ [al-Rum: 33]. And here He, mighty and majestic is He, said: ﴿And when a wave covers them like shade, they call upon Allah, sincere to Him in religion. But when He delivers them to the shore, some of them are moderate﴾ [Luqman: 32]. So in each of the two verses He mentioned a category He did not mention in the other, and so on besides that.

How subtle this connection is, in that the first surah mentioned the defeat and victory of the Romans, which were based on fighting between two great kings of the kings of this world who fought over it, and this departed from the requirement of wisdom, for the wise does not fight over a base worldly matter that does not weigh, in the sight of Allah, the wing of a gnat. And this one (Surat Luqman) mentions, according to many opinions, the story of a slave, a wise ascetic in this world, indifferent to it and not turning to it, who counselled his son with what rejects fighting and requires patience and peace. And between the two matters there is an opposition that is not hidden.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. (Alif Lam Mim.) ﴿These are the verses of the wise Book﴾ — that is, the one possessing wisdom. Describing the Book with this, according to some Maghribis, is metaphor, because description with this is for possession, and it (the Book) does not possess wisdom but includes it and contains it. For this reason it was described as wise in the sense of possessing wisdom. Al-Tibi held that it is, on that basis, a metaphor of the implicit kind (istiʿara makniyya). The truth is that it is of the type of ﴿a pleasant life﴾ [al-Haqqah: 21], in the manner of "laban and tamr" (a possessor of milk and dates, i.e., the attribute is understood as possession).

Yes, it is permissible that there be here a metaphor by implication, meaning the one who speaks with wisdom like a living being. It is also permissible that "the Wise" be one of His attributes, and describing the Book with it is of the type of metaphorical attribution (isnad majazi), for it proceeds from Him, glorified is He. Something may be described by the attribute of its origin, as in the words of al-A'sha:

*And a strange thing that comes to kings, wise, which I have composed so that it may be said, "Who is it who said it?"*

And it is permissible that the original be "the wise one who revealed it or who spoke it," so the noun in the genitive pronoun form was omitted and the noun in the attached form was put in its place,

[p. 66]

so it became nominative, then it became a fixed (sukun) in the attributive adjective (al-sifa al-mushabbaha). And it is permissible that "al-Hakim" be an adjective of the pattern fa'il in the sense of maf'il (passive), as they say: "I made the honey thick (ʿaqadtu al-ʿasal), so it is ʿaqid," meaning muʿqad. This is rare. It has also been said that it means ḥakim (one who judges). The full discussion of this verse has been given earlier, in the discussion of its counterpart.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 31, verse 3:

﴿Guidance and mercy﴾ is read in the accusative (naṣb) as a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl) of (āyātu, "the verses"), and the element governing both of them is the sense of indication (ishārah, "pointing to"), as stated by more than one scholar, who also discussed it.

Ḥamzah, al-A'mash, al-Za'faranī, Ṭalḥah, and Qunbul, through the route of Abū al-Faḍl al-Wāsiṭī, and Naẓīf read it in the nominative (rafʿ) as a predicate following a predicate, namely "those are" (li-tilka), according to the view of the majority; or as the predicate of an omitted subject, i.e., "it is," or "he is": guidance and a great mercy ﴿for the doers of good﴾. That is, those who act virtuously (al-ʿāmilīna al-ḥasanāt). The prepositional phrase (al-jārr wa-l-majrūr) is attached to an omitted element that stands as a qualifier (ṣifah) of the two conjoined items.

Al-Alusi on Surah 31, verse 4:

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Those who establish the prayer and give the zakat, and they, in the Hereafter, are certain of it﴾ is either in the genitive (majrur) as a descriptive clause that clarifies (sifah kashifah), or as a substitute (badal) or an explanatory apposition (bayan) for what precedes it. Or it is in the accusative (mansub) or nominative (marfu') by way of a new predication (qat'). In every case, it is an explanation (tafsir) of "the doers of good" (lil-muhsinin), in the manner of the saying of Aws ibn Hajar:

The sharp-witted (al-Al-ma'i) one, who thinks of you such thoughts as if he had seen and heard.

It is related from al-Asma'i that he was asked about al-Al-ma'i, so he recited the verse to him and did not add anything to it. This is clear if what is meant by "the good deeds" (al-hasanat) is their well-known and recognized instances in the religion. As for if what is meant by them is all that is good among actions, then it is not apparent except by considering the things mentioned as standing in the place of the whole, by way of the expression "the whole of the hunt is in the belly of the fox" (kull al-sayd fi jawf al-fira). It has also been said: if the good deeds mentioned are what is intended, then the relative pronoun (al-mawsul) is a descriptive clause that clarifies.

Al-Alusi's commentary (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on Surah 31, verse 5:

Allah the Exalted's saying: ﴿Those are upon guidance from their Lord, and those are the successful﴾ is resumptive (isti'nafan). If by it is meant all the good deeds, and the mention of the things specified was for the sake of their great importance, then the relative pronoun (al-mawsul) is the subject (mubtada'), and the clause "Those are upon guidance" (ulaika 'ala huda) etc. is its predicate (khabar), and the sentence is resumptive, mentioning the attribute that necessitates the beginning of the speech.

It has been said: on both assumptions the relative pronoun is a qualifying attribute (sifah), except that on the first assumption it is explanatory (kashifah), and on the second assumption it is an attribute of praise for the quality, not for the qualified noun. The construction of (yuqinun) upon (hum) is for exclusivity (lil-taqwa), and the pronoun is repeated for emphasis, and to ward off the suspicion that (bil-akhirah) is a predicate and a complement that separates the subject from its predicate. The separating element was not postponed for the sake of the rhyme (al-fasilah).

Some of the eminent exegetes mentioned, regarding Allah the Exalted's saying at the beginning of Surah al-Baqarah: ﴿And in the Hereafter they are certain﴾, that the construction of (yuqinun) upon (hum) indicates that their opponents are not in any shade or shelter of certainty, and that the fronting of "fi al-akhirah" (in the Hereafter) indicates that what their opponents hold is not from the Hereafter at all. This is because fronting the notional agent (al-fa'il al-ma'nawi) and fronting the prepositional phrase before its complement (al-jar 'ala muta'alliqihi) serve to express exclusivity (al-ikhtisas). So consider whether something like this is possible here. What indicates the reason for choosing the demonstrative (ism al-isharah) and the reason for repeating it has already been discussed at the beginning of Surah al-Baqarah. There is further discussion on the verse which will not be hidden from one who reviews what they have said on similar expressions there, reflects, and returns to it, and reflects.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 31, verse 6 (part 1 of 6):**

﴿And among the people﴾, i.e., some of the people, or some people, ﴿are those who buy idle talk﴾, i.e., the one who, or a group who, buys it. This is on the basis that the core of the benefit and the primary intent is that they are characterized by what falls within the scope of the relative clause or the qualifier, not that they are those persons mentioned. The sentence is coordinated with what precedes it in meaning, as if it were said: among the people is one who is guided, and among them is one who is astray and misleads. Or it coordinates one narrative with another. It has also been said that it is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the subject of the indication, meaning: the verses of the Book were indicated while being guidance and mercy.

Page 67

The circumstantial clause is: "among the people is one who buys," etc. ﴿Idle talk﴾, according to what is reported from al-Hasan, is everything that distracts you from the worship and remembrance of Allah, such as idle chatter, jokes, fables, singing and the like. The construction (idafa) is in the sense of "min" (of/from) if by "talk" is meant what is reprehensible, as in the hadith: "Talk in the mosque devours good deeds as an animal devours grass." It is explanatory and partitive if by it is meant what is more general than that, according to the view of some grammarians such as Ibn Kaysan and al-Sirafi. They said: the annexation of something that is a part of the annexed noun is in the sense of partitive "min," as is indicated by the occurrence of the separator (fasl) with it in their speech. What most later scholars hold, and what Ibn al-Sarraj and al-Farisi adopted, and which is the most correct, is that it is in the sense of the lam (of belonging), as Abu Hayyan elaborated in his commentary on al-Tashil, and as the commentator on al-Lumac mentioned.

It is reported from al-Dahhak that ﴿idle talk﴾ is shirk (polytheism). It has also been said that it is magic. Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Abi al-Dunya, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Hakim (who authenticated it), and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman, transmitted from Abu al-Sahba', who said: I asked Abdullah ibn Mas'ud about the words of the Exalted: ﴿And among the people are those who buy idle talk﴾. He said: "By Allah, it is singing." Many have interpreted it this way. The better interpretation is to explain it in a way that encompasses all of these, as we mentioned from al-Hasan, and this is what is required by what al-Bukhari in al-Adab al-Mufrad, Ibn Abi al-Dunya, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan transmitted from Ibn Abbas, that he said: "Idle talk" is singing and the like. In all of these cases, "buying" is a metaphor for preferring it over the Qur'an and substituting it for the Qur'an.

Ibn Asakir transmitted from Makhul concerning the words of the Exalted: ﴿who buys idle talk﴾, that he said: "The striking girls."

Adam, Ibn Jarir, and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan transmitted from Mujahid that he said concerning it: it is his buying a male singer or a female singer and listening to them, and to the like of them from falsehood. In a report mentioned by al-Bayhaqi in the Sunan from Ibn Mas'ud, he said regarding the verse: it is a man who buys a slave-girl to sing to him by night or by day. It is well known that the verse was revealed concerning al-Nadr ibn al-Harith. In the report of Juwaybir from Ibn Abbas: "He bought a singing slave-girl, and he would not hear of anyone who wanted to embrace Islam without taking him to his slave-girl, saying: 'Feed him, give him drink, and sing to him,' and he would say: 'This is better than what Muhammad (ﷺ) calls you to, of prayer and fasting and fighting before him.' So it was revealed."

In Asbab al-Nuzul of al-Wahidi, from al-Kalbi and Muqatil: "He used to travel as a merchant to Persia and buy the news of the non-Arabs, and in some reports, the books of the non-Arabs, and he would narrate them and speak them to the Quraysh, saying to them: 'Muhammad (may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon him) tells you the story of 'Ad and Thamud, and I tell you the story of Rustam and Isfandiyar and the reports of the Kisras.' So they found his talk pleasing and abandoned listening to the Qur'an. Thus it was revealed." It has also been said that it was revealed concerning Ibn Khatal, who bought a slave-girl who sang abuse. The revelation is not precluded from being concerning those who are mentioned in the plural in the words after: ﴿for them are those (who)﴾, as is not hidden from the discerning. Buying, according to most of these reports, is in its literal sense, and in some of them it requires the generalization of metaphor or the combining of literal and metaphorical meanings, as is not hidden from one who examines carefully. Whoever made the female singer and the like the very "idle talk" as an intensification, as the women in the words of the Exalted ﴿The love of desires is made attractive to people, including women﴾ [Al Imran: 14] were made the very adornment, has done so.

In al-Bahr: if by "idle talk" is meant what can be bought, such as singing slave-girls and the books of non-Arabs, then "buying" is literal, and the speech is with an elided modifier, meaning: "who buys the possession of idle talk."

Al-Khafaji said, may Allah have mercy on him: There is no need to posit "possession," because when the singing girl is bought for her singing, the thing bought is in effect the singing itself. Reflect on this. In the verse, according to most scholars, there is a reproach of singing aloud. Many reports and the words of many righteous scholars have been established against it absolutely, not only in some situations and not in others. Ibn Abi al-Dunya and al-Bayhaqi in his Shu'ab transmitted from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "When a man mounts a riding animal without mentioning the name of Allah, a devil rides behind him and says: 'Sing!' If he is not skilled, he says: 'Recite in a sing-song!'" Both of them also transmitted from

Page 68

al-Sha'bi, who said: "From al-Qasim ibn Muhammad, that he was asked about singing, and he said to the questioner: 'I forbid you from it and I dislike it for you.' The questioner said: 'Is it forbidden?' He said: 'Consider, my nephew: when Allah the Exalted distinguishes truth from falsehood, in which of the two does He place singing?'" Both of them also transmitted from him that he said: "Allah the Exalted curses the one who sings and the one for whom it is sung." In the Sunan, from Ibn Mas'ud, he said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Singing causes hypocrisy to grow in the heart as water causes herbs to grow.'" Ibn Abi al-Dunya transmitted something similar from him. It is also narrated from Abu Hurayrah, and al-Daylami transmitted it from him, and from Anas. Ibn al-Qattan weakened it, al-Nawawi said it is not authentic, and al- Iraqi said its attribution to the Prophet is not authentic, because its chain includes one who is unnamed. This indicates that its attribution to Ibn Mas'ud is authentic, and it has the status of a marfu' (attributed to the Prophet), since such a thing is not said on the basis of opinion.

Ibn Abi al-Dunya and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Abu Umamah, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "No one raises his voice with singing except that Allah sends to him two devils who sit on his shoulders, striking his chest with their heels until he stops."

Ibn Abi al-Dunya and al-Bayhaqi transmitted from Abu Uthman al-Laythi, who said: Yazid ibn al-Walid al-Naqis said: "O children of Umayyah, beware of singing, for it diminishes modesty, increases desire, destroys manliness, and it substitutes for wine and does what intoxication does. If you must do it, then keep women away from it, for singing is an invitation to fornication." Al-Dahhak said: "Singing is a waster of wealth, a provoker of the Lord's anger, a corrupter of the heart."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Majah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, and others transmitted from Abu Umamah, from the Messenger of Allah (may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon him), that he said: "Do not sell singing girls, do not buy them, do not teach them, and there is no good in trade in them, and their price is forbidden. Concerning the like of this was revealed the verse: ﴿And among the people are those who buy idle talk﴾ to the end of the verse."

In the report of Ibn Abi al-Dunya and Ibn Mardawayh from Aishah, she said: "The Messenger of Allah (may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon him) said: 'Allah the Exalted has forbidden the singing girl, her sale, her price, her teaching, and listening to her,' then he recited: ﴿And among the people are those who buy idle talk﴾."

This and similar reports return to the reproach of singing.

It has been said: Singing is the spy of the heart and the thief of manliness and intellects. It penetrates into the blackness of hearts and looks into the secrets of hearts, and creeps into the house of imagination, spreading what has been implanted in it of passion, desire, frivolity, and foolishness. So while you see a man with the dignity of gravity, the splendor of intellect, the radiance of faith, and the solemnity of knowledge, whose speech is wisdom and whose silence is a lesson, when he hears singing, his intellect and modesty diminish, and his manliness and splendor depart. He then finds pleasing what he used to find repugnant before listening, reveals what secrets he used to conceal, and moves from the splendor of silence and stillness to much speech, idle talk, and agitation, as if he were a jinn. He may clap his hands and stamp the ground with his feet. Wine does likewise, and more.

The scholars differed about its ruling. Abu al-Tayyib al-Qadi, al-Qurtubi, al-Mawardi, and al-Qadi Iyad related its prohibition from Imam Abu Hanifah, may Allah be pleased with him.

It seems that by "disliking" (karahah) he means prohibition (hurmah). The early scholars often used "disliked" (makruh) to mean "forbidden," as in the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿All of that, its evil is disliked by your Lord﴾ [al-Isra' 17:38]. Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyya mentioned in his book al-Bulghah that most of their companions held the prohibition. In that same work: his companions who were knowledgeable of his school explicitly stated its prohibition and denied the attribution of its permissibility to him, such as al-Qadi Abu al-Tayyib, al-Tabari, and Shaykh Abu Ishaq in al-Tanbih. One of the students of al-Baghawi mentioned in his book named al-Taqrib that singing is forbidden, both its performance and its listening. Ibn al-Salah said in his fatawa, after a lengthy discussion: "Therefore, this listening is forbidden by the consensus (ijma') of the people of binding and loosing (ahl al-hall wa al-'aqd) among the Muslims." End of quote. What I found in the large commentary on al-Jami' al-Saghir by the eminent al-Munawi is that the school of al-Shafi'i holds it to be disliked in the sense of tanzih (non-binding dislike) when there is no fear of temptation (fitnah). In al-Minhaj it is stated: "Singing without instruments is disliked." Al-Allamah Ibn Hajar said: "This is because of what is authentically reported from Ibn Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with him)," and he mentioned the earlier hadith that is attributed to him (mawquf). He also said that it has come as a marfu' report through many chains, which he demonstrated in his book Kaff al-Ri'a' 'an Muharramat al-Lahw wa al-Sama' (Restraining the Rabble from the Forbidden Matters of Amusement and Listening). Then he said: "One claimed that there is no indication in it of its being disliked, because some permissible things, such as wearing beautiful clothes, cause hypocrisy to grow in the heart, yet they are not disliked." This is answered: we do not accept that this causes hypocrisy at all, and even if we accept it, hypocrisy varies. The hypocrisy that singing produces is effeminacy (takhannuth) and what follows from it, which is more ugly and repugnant, as is well known. Then he said: "The two shaykhs, namely al-Nawawi and al-Rafi'i, stated in one place definitively that it is a sin (ma'siyah). Al-Adhra'i said: "As for what is customary when one is attempting a task or lifting a heavy load, such as the hida' (camel-driving chant) of the Bedouins for their camels, and the chanting of women to calm their small children, there is no doubt in its permissibility. Indeed, it may be recommended when it spurs one on in a journey or encourages one toward good, such as hida' on Hajj and in military campaigns. On this basis is understood what has come from some of the Companions." End of quote. The statement of the scholars, "without instruments," implies its prohibition with instruments. Al-Zarkashi said: "However, analogy (qiyas) suggests that only the instrument is forbidden, and singing remains disliked." End of quote.

The disagreement regarding singing is similar to the disagreement regarding listening (al-sama'). Some permitted it, just as they permitted singing, and they used as evidence what al-Bukhari reported from A'ishah, who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) entered upon me while two girls were with me singing the songs of Bu'ath (a battle of the pre-Islamic Arabs). He lay down on the bed and turned his face away." In another narration, in Muslim's collection: "He covered himself with his garment. Abu Bakr entered and rebuked me, saying: 'The flute of Satan in the presence of the Prophet (ﷺ)?' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) turned to him and said: 'Leave them.' When he was unaware, I signaled to the two girls, and they left. It was a day of Eid." End of hadith.

The basis of the argument is that there was singing or listening, and the Prophet (ﷺ) did not rebuke it as Abu Bakr did. Moreover, there is evidence in it for the permissibility of a man listening to the voice of a girl even if she is not a slave-girl (mamlukah), because he (ﷺ) listened and did not rebuke Abu Bakr for listening; rather he rebuked Abu Bakr's rebuke. The two girls continued singing until A'ishah signaled to them to leave. Abu Bakr's rebuke of his daughter, while knowing that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was present, was based on the assumption that this was not with the Prophet's knowledge, since he entered and found him covered with his garment and assumed he was asleep.

In Fath al-Bari, a group of Sufis used this hadith as evidence for the permissibility of singing and listening to it, both with and without instruments. What suffices to refute this is what al-Bukhari also reported shortly after, from A'ishah as well, who said: "Abu Bakr entered upon me while I had two girls from the girls of the Ansar singing what the Ansar had recited on the day of Bu'ath. She said: 'They were not singers.' Abu Bakr said: 'The flutes of Satan in the house of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)?' That was on a day of Eid. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'O Abu Bakr, every people has an Eid, and this is our Eid.'"

So she negated from them, by way of meaning, what she affirmed for them by wording, because singing (al-ghina') is applied to raising the voice, to the melodious chanting that the Arabs call nasb (with an open nun and a silent unmarked letter), and to hida'. The one who does it is not called a singer (mughanni); rather, the name is given to one who recites with drawn-out, broken, stirring, and enticing tones, with what contains allusion to indecencies (fawahish) or explicit reference.

Al-Qurtubi said: Her saying "they were not singers" means they were not among those who know singing as professional singing women known for it. This is her figurative statement about the singing customary among those famous for it, which is that which stirs the dormant and arouses the latent. This type, if it is in poetry that describes the beauty of women, wine, and other forbidden matters, there is no disagreement about its prohibition. As for what the Sufis have innovated in this regard, it is among what is not disputed as forbidden. But carnal souls have overcome many who are associated with goodness, to the extent that acts of madmen and children appeared among many of them, until they danced with synchronized movements and rapid rhythmic steps. Audacity led a group among them to consider these practices to be a means of nearness to Allah and righteous deeds, and to claim that they bring about the fruits of excellent states. This, in truth, is a result of heresy (zandaqah) and the speech of charlatans (ahl al-makhraqah). And Allah is the One sought for help. End of al-Qurtubi's statement. The purpose of the statement of Fath al-Bari is similar, and it is a good statement, except that his saying: "It is only called by that name the one who recites..." etc., is not free from issue, based on the assumption that the general meaning is apparent, both for what in the reciter includes allusion or explicit reference to indecencies, and for what does not include that.

Some eminent scholars said: The report does not indicate absolute permissibility. At most, it indicates its permissibility in a lawful joy, such as at Eids and weddings. So it is evidence for one who permits it at weddings, just as he permitted striking the tambourine (duff) at them. Also, Abu Bakr's rebuke (may Allah be pleased with him) appears to indicate that he had heard from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) a condemnation of singing and a prohibition of it, so he assumed the ruling was general and rebuked. By the Prophet's (ﷺ) rebuke of his rebuke, it became clear to him that the ruling was not general. In the other report there is what indicates that the Prophet (ﷺ) clarified the situation to him together with explaining the wisdom: it is a day of Eid, so such a thing is not rebuked on it, just as it is not rebuked at weddings. Yet despite this, the Prophet (ﷺ) indicated, by wrapping himself in his garment and turning his noble face away, that turning away from this is better. And the listening to the voice of a girl who is not a slave-girl, with this kind of singing, if there is no fear of temptation, is something not objectionable. So let the report be evidence for its permissibility.

Some scholars used as evidence for this what was reported from Anas ibn Malik, that he entered upon his brother al-Bara' ibn Malik, who was one of the shrewd Companions (may Allah be pleased with them all), and he used to sing (yatagharra). There is no concealing what is in this, for this singing (taghanni) is not in the commonly known sense. Similar to it is the taghanni in the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "He is not of us who does not sing (yatagharra) with the Qur'an." Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna and Abu 'Ubayda interpreted taghanni in this hadith as self-sufficiency (istighna'), so it is as if it was said: "He is not of us who does not find sufficiency in the Qur'an over other than it." And this (the singing of al-Bara') is also a form of chanting to relieve loneliness in his own home. Similar to it is what was reported from 'Abd Allah ibn 'Awf, who said: "I came to the door of 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him), and I heard him singing:

"How is my dwelling in Medina, after Jamil ibn Ma'mar has fulfilled his need from it?"

He meant by Jamil the Jumahi, and he was a close companion of his (the poet's). When I asked permission to enter upon him, he said to me: "Did you hear what I said?" I said: "Yes." He said: "Indeed, when we are alone, we say what the people say in their homes."

Al-Izz ibn Abd al-Salam was asked about listening to devotional poetry (inshad) about love, and about dancing. This fear is either fear of punishment, or fear of losing reward, or intimacy and nearness. The last is the most excellent of fears and of listeners, and the influence of the Qur'an upon him is strongest. Whoever is dominated by hope, listening affects him when hope-inspiring and expectation-raising things are mentioned. If his hope is for intimacy and nearness, his listening is the most excellent listening of those who hope. If his hope is for reward, he is in the second rank, and the influence of listening upon the first is stronger than its influence upon the second.

Whoever is dominated by love of God, Exalted is He, for His bounty, listening to the mention of bounty and honor affects him. Or [he is dominated by love] for His absolute beauty, Glory be to Him, and the mention of the nobility of His essence and the perfection of His attributes affects him. This is more excellent than what came before, because the cause of his love is the most excellent of causes. The influence upon him intensifies when distance and remoteness are mentioned.

Whoever is dominated by reverence and veneration, which is the most excellent of all that came before, the states of these people differ in what is heard from its source. Listening from a saint (wali) has a stronger influence than listening from a common person. Listening from a prophet has a stronger influence than from him and from a saint. Listening from the Lord, Mighty and Majestic, has a stronger influence than listening from a prophet, because the speech of one who is awe-inspiring has a stronger effect on the one who stands in awe than the speech of others, just as the speech of the beloved has a stronger effect on the lover than the speech of others.

For this reason, the prophets, the truthful (siddiqun), and their companions did not occupy themselves with listening to frivolous amusements and singing, but were content with the speech of their Lord, Exalted be His majesty.

Whoever is dominated by a forbidden passion, loving a beloved, his longing, fear of separation, and hope of meeting affect him. His listening to these is not harmful. But whoever is dominated by a forbidden passion, such as infatuation with a beardless youth or with a foreign woman, the pursuit of the forbidden affects him, and whatever leads to the forbidden is forbidden.

As for one who finds in himself none of these six categories, his listening is disliked (yukrah), because the common people are mostly dominated by corrupt desires. Some wicked people attend the listening and weep and are moved for corrupt purposes they harbor, and they show off to those present that their listening is to something beloved. These have combined disobedience with giving the impression that they are among the righteous. Whoever mentions the severity of retribution, or is reminded of it, his state becomes the state of those who fear, and his listening becomes their listening. And so on by analogy. They have erred in what they said and lied in what they claimed, because when they hear stirring songs they find two pleasures. It is nothing but one of the purposes of the self, and not a means of drawing near to the Lord, Exalted is He. Whoever does it, if he is one who is followed and is believed to have done it only as a means of drawing near, then he did an evil thing, because it gives the impression that this is one of the acts of obedience, whereas it is one of the most shameful frivolities.

As for shouting, fainting, and the like, they are affectation and showing off. If they are from a state that does not require them, the sin of the doer is twofold: first, that he gives the impression of a stable state requiring them; second, his affectation and showing off.
