According to others, it is disliked. According to this speaker, it is forbidden if it becomes so excessive that it removes manliness (muruwwah, personal dignity and integrity), if it is done by their choice; in that case they are like others. Otherwise, they are not morally accountable. Some eminent scholars asked him to clarify this, and he said: It must be applied consistently to everything reported about the Sufis that contradicts the apparent teachings of the Shari'ah. It should not be used as evidence, because if it proceeds from them while they are accountable, they are like others; and if it proceeds from them while they are absent (from themselves, in ecstasy), they were not accountable for it. What appears to me is that a man's singing with such melodies, if it is to dispel loneliness from himself, is permissible and not disliked, as Shams al-A'immah al-Sarakhsi held. However, on the condition that it is not heard by someone who is feared to be tempted by it, whether a woman or someone else, nor by someone who belittles him and looks down on him; and on the condition that he does not alter a revered name by adding something not originally in it, so that it does not depart from the requirements of the art, such as saying of Allah "Iyyah" and of Muhammad "Muwahhamad". This is in addition to the condition that what is sung is something that can be recited without harm. If it is for people's amusement, on an occasion other than a joyful event, such as a wedding, for a fee or without one, and whether or not he is thereby belittled, then if what is sung is permissible to recite, it is permissible; otherwise it is forbidden, even if temptation is safe. I consider it among the minor sins, as the words of al-Mawardi imply, where he said: "If we hold that songs and entertainments are forbidden, they are among the minor sins and not the major sins. If it is on an occasion of joy, it is permissible, provided temptation is safe, what is sung is permissible to recite, no revered name is altered in it, it is not a cause of belittling a person or violating his manliness, and it does not lead to the unlawful gathering of men and women. If it is a cause of something forbidden, it is forbidden, and the degrees of its prohibition vary according to the degree of prohibition of what it causes." If it is for people, not for amusement, but to energize them to remember Allah Most High, as is done in some circles of tahlil (repeating "there is no god but Allah") in our lands, it is possibly permissible, provided it does not involve corruption. Perhaps it is closer to being disliked. It may be said that in that case it is an act of devotion (qurbah), like the ḥudā, which is what is said behind camels by way of urging them on and the like, when it energizes a journey that is itself an act of devotion, since the means to an act of devotion is agreed to be an act of devotion. It is said: We have not come across any report that circles of dhikr included this on the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), nor in the time of his successors and companions, may Allah be pleased with them, though they were the most eager of people for closeness to Allah through this singing, or through any of its other forms. Hadiths are authentic regarding the ḥudā, and for this reason a group stated without qualification that it is recommended. That they were energetic without it does not prevent that some among them may be made more energetic by it. If it were an act of devotion, they would have done it, at least once, but it is not reported that they did it at all. Furthermore, it is not far-fetched to say that it disturbs those who remember Allah, and the meaning and the contemplation of the dhikr cannot be completed for them with it. Without it, there is no reward for it by consensus. Perhaps what is done on the minarets, which they call tamjid (glorification), is regarded among the ignorant as part of the means of closeness to Allah. Indeed, most of them consider it an act of devotion in its very essence. By my life, to the learned it is far from that. If it is for the need of an illness whose cure is determined by it, there is no doubt about its permissibility. Persistence in the permissible of it harms manliness, just as adopting it as a trade does. As for al-Rafi'i's statement that it does not harm manliness if it suits the person, al-Zarkashi rejected it, saying that al-Shafi'i explicitly stated that the testimony of such a person is rejected, and his companions followed this, because it is a base trade, and its practitioner is regarded by custom as one without shame. It is reported from al-Hasan that a man said to him: "What do you say about singing?" He said: "What an excellent thing singing is. Kinship is maintained through it, distress is relieved through it, and good deeds are done through it." The man said: "I mean the shadd (the ornamented, elaborate style of singing)." He said: "And what is the shadd? Do you know anything of it?" He said: "Yes." He said: "What is it?" The man began to sing, twisting his cheeks and nostrils and narrowing his eyes. Al-Hasan said: "I never thought that a sensible person would drive himself to what I see." Scholars differed on engaging in what harms manliness in several ways. The third is: if testimony is tied to it, it is forbidden; otherwise it is not. Some eminent scholars said: This is the most sound view, because it is forbidden for him to cause the loss of what he has borne and which has become a trust with him for others. It appears to me that if this comes from a scholar who is followed, or if it is a cause of belittling, it is also forbidden. As for listening to it, that is, deliberately listening, not merely hearing it without intent, while temptation is safe, and what is sung is permissible to recite, and it does not cause a person to commit disobedience, then it is permissible. But if a singer continues to sing sinfully, then listening to him is permissible, and persistence in it, as al-Nawawi said, harms manliness, like persistence in permissible singing. The disagreement about engaging in what harms manliness has been mentioned just above. As for listening when temptation is not safe, or when what is sung is not permissible to recite, or when it causes disobedience, that is forbidden, and the degrees of its prohibition vary, and perhaps it reaches the level of a major sin. Among forbidden listening is the listening of the Sufis of our time, even if it is free of dancing, for its corruptions are too many to count, and much of what they listen to of poetry is among the most abominable things recited. Despite this, they consider it an act of devotion, and they claim that those most eager for it are the most fearful or the most hopeful. May Allah Most High fight them; how are they deluded! It is not hidden from one who has thorough knowledge of what has been mentioned from al-Qushayri and others that their listening is blameworthy according to those who believe that he supports them and imagine that they and he belong to one party. Woe to the one whose intercessors are his adversaries, and whose beloved ones are his enemies. As for their dancing to it, they have added a clamor to the lute, and joined to the cracking of the chords of foolishness a madness, may Allah Most High break their power for that. Some eminent scholars stated that the testimony of Sufis who dance to the daf (frame drum), which is said to be permissible, or recommended to be beaten at weddings, circumcisions and other occasions of joy, is not accepted, among them the arrival of a scholar who benefits the Muslims, refuting the one who claimed acceptance. He said: "It is said that according to some, the testimony of Sufis who dance to the daf is accepted, because they believe it is an act of devotion, just as the testimony of a Hanafi who drinks nabidh (a fermented drink) is accepted because he believes it is permissible. Likewise, everyone who does what he believes to be permissible." (end of quote). It was refuted: this is a foul error, because the belief of the Hanafi arises from valid taqlid (following a school of law), whereas this is not the case for others. Their belief stems only from ignorance and negligence, so it is a false imagination, to which no attention should be paid. (end of quote). Then I say: It is not far-fetched that a person in a state may be stirred by listening, and that it moves him to dance, clap, faint and shout, tear his clothes, or do something similar that is disliked or forbidden. What appears to me in this matter is that if he knows of himself that such things proceed from him, then the ruling on his listening is the ruling on what follows from it. If he is in doubt about it, then the safer course for him, if we do not say it is disliked, is not to listen. Thus, in the hadith: "Leave what makes you doubt for what does not make you doubt." Then, if something of that happens to him merely by hearing without intent, and he cannot prevent it at all, there is no blame or reproach for him, and his ruling in this is the ruling for one who is overtaken by an involuntary sneeze or cough. Blame and reproach are not removed from him only if this happens while he is absent; so a person in whom it occurs while he is not absent does not have to renew his wudu' (ablution) for prayer, for example. Consider the case where it overtakes him during prayer without absence: is its ruling the ruling of sneezing or coughing when it overtakes him during prayer or not? What I have heard from some elders is the second, so reflect. Some people are overtaken by something of what has been mentioned when they hear the Qur'an, either in general, or when it is recited with a beautiful voice. Yet this rarely happens from hearing the Qur'an or anything else for a perfect person. It is reported from A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, that it was said to her: "Some people, when they hear the Qur'an, fall unconscious." She said: "The Qur'an is too noble for men's minds to be stolen by it. Rather, as Allah Most High said: ﴿The skins of those who fear their Lord shudder from it; then their skins and their hearts soften to the remembrance of Allah﴾ [az-Zumar: 23]." It is often due to the weakness of a person's capacity to bear what comes upon him. Some pretenders do it for show. It is reported from Ibn Sirin that he was asked about someone who hears the Qur'an and faints. He said: "Our agreement with them is that they sit on a wall and the Qur'an is recited to them from beginning to end. If they faint, then it is as they claim." The hadith of Ibn Mas'ud does not contradict the permissibility of singing and listening to it in some cases: "Singing produces hypocrisy in the heart just as water produces herbage." No, because the word "singing" in it is restricted, and what is meant by it is wealth, the opposite of poverty. This is refuted by the fact that the hadith was reported in another version with the addition: "(And remembrance produces faith in the heart just as water produces crops)." The contrast of singing with remembrance clearly indicates that what is meant is melodious chanting. Moreover, as some memorizers of hadith said, the narration is with a long vowel. Rather, what is meant is that singing by its nature leads to hypocrisy, that is, practical hypocrisy, in that it moves a person to treachery, breaking promises, lying and the like. It does not necessarily follow that this always results. Perhaps the comparison in his words "just as water produces herbage" points to this, for water does not always produce herbage, and there are many similar examples in speech. The one who permits it in some cases permits it only where this does not result. Yes, there is no doubt that the safest course for something of this nature, after all that has been said, is to have no desire for it. So it has been said. It has also been said: It is possible that by hypocrisy is meant faithful hypocrisy (i.e., a kind of hypocrisy among those who have believed), and this is supported by its being contrasted with faith in some versions. The purpose of the hadith would then be to discourage singing, since people were recently converted from the Jahiliyyah, when singing was used for amusement and gathered around at drinking gatherings. The way it produced hypocrisy at that time is that many of them, because of their recent experience of the pleasure of singing and the amusement, drinking and other kinds of sin that accompanied it, had their hearts moved toward what they had been in, and yearned for it like the she-camels in their longing, and they disliked faith because it barred them from that. Because of the strength of Islam's power, they could not openly show what they concealed, nor cast faith behind their backs and move toward what they had turned away from. So they had no choice but hypocrisy, for what they had gathered upon, out of fear of apostasy and longing. Reflect on this, and may Allah Most High guide you. As for the verse, if the basis of the argument from it is calling singing "lahw" (idle talk, amusement), then how many forms of amusement are lawful! If the threat is over buying it and choosing it, we do not concede that this applies to merely buying it, since it may be about buying it in order to lead astray from the path of Allah Most High. There is no doubt that this is among the major sins, and we have no dispute about it. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "What is most likely is that the verse was revealed about idle talk combined with disbelief, and this is why the words of the verse became so severe with His saying: (in order to mislead) and so on." (end of quote).

Among the things we have mentioned, it becomes known what the argument is worth for prohibiting musical instruments such as the rabab, the jank (harp), the sintir, the kamanja (viol), the mizmar (reed pipe), and other instruments that stir emotion, on the basis of what is reported from Ibn Abbas and al-Hasan that they interpreted (lahw al-hadith) ("idle talk") as referring to them. Yes, the use and listening to them for purposes other than those mentioned is forbidden, for it is authentically transmitted through several chains, contrary to what the misguided, misleading Ibn Hazm erred in. Al-Bukhari reported it in suspended form (mu'allaq), while al-Isma'ili, Ahmad, Ibn Majah, Abu Nu'aym, and Abu Dawud transmitted it with sound chains of narration, with no flaw in them. A group of other imams also authenticated it, as some of the memorizers of hadith said, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "There will certainly be among my community people who will deem lawful silk (al-khazz), wine, and musical instruments (al-ma'azif)."

This is explicit in forbidding all instruments of idle entertainment that stir emotion. Among what closely resembles an explicit statement in this regard is what Ibn Abi al-Dunya narrated in his book (Dhamm al-Malahi) from Anas, and what Ahmad and al-Tabarani narrated from Ibn Abbas and Abu Umamah, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ): "There will certainly be in this community sinking of the earth, hurling of stones, and transformation (into animals), and that will be when they drink intoxicants, take female singers, and play musical instruments."

These are the instruments of entertainment you have heard of, and among them is the Persian cymbal (al-sanj al-ajami), which is of brass with strings placed on it and struck with, according to what many have held, in contrast to al-Mawardi, who said: the sanj is disliked when accompanied by singing, but is not disliked when alone, because on its own it is not stirring. Perhaps he meant by it the Arab type, which consists of two pieces of brass struck against each other; for apparently it is that which is not stirring when alone, but it increases the stirring of singing. It is mentioned that the effeminate men (al-mukhannathun) use it in some lands, and it is not far-fetched to say it is forbidden. Among them is the yara' (reed flute), which is the shabbaba (fife), for it is stirring on its own. Indeed, some people of music theory said: it is a complete instrument comprising all tones except a few. The Imam al-Dawlaqi, who is among the great scholars, has elaborately set out the evidences for its prohibition. Among them is analogy (qiyas), which is either stronger or equal. He said: "How astonishing it is that someone among the people of knowledge claims that the shabbaba is lawful!" End of quote.

From this it becomes known what is wrong in the statement of Taj al-Subki in his (Tawshih): "No evidence for the prohibition of the yara' has been established before me despite extensive searching, and what I consider is that it is lawful. If a forbidden element is combined with it, then each of them has its own ruling." Then, in my view, the better course for one who is not among the people of spiritual taste (dhawq) is to abstain from it entirely, because the most it produces is a sensual pleasure, and that is not among the legally sought objectives. As for the people of spiritual taste, their state is to be accepted, and they act according to what they find within themselves. End of quote.

It is related from al-Izz ibn Abd al-Salam and Ibn Daqiq al-Id that they used to listen to it, but the apparent reading is that this is a lie without basis, and some eminent scholars decided on this. It is not far-fetched that it is permissible when played in a manner that is not the recognized method of stirring, as with children and shepherds.

Among them is the 'ud (lute), which is an instrument of entertainment other than the tunbur, though some have applied the term to it. As for the report of the impure Ibn Tahir from Shaykh Abu Ishaq al-Shirazi that he used to listen to the 'ud, it is among his lies and recklessness, like his claim of consensus of the Companions and the Successors on the permissibility of singing and entertainment. Similar in recklessness and fabrication, and in asserting falsehoods with certainty, is Ibn Hazm. As for the daff (frame drum), it is permissible to strike it by a man and a woman, not by a woman alone, in contrast to al-Halimi; and listening to it at a wedding and marriage, and likewise for other occasions of joy, is permissible according to the more correct view. It is also permitted with the zu al-jalajil (tambourine with jingles), which is either something like rings placed inside it, like the Arab daff, or wide brass cymbals placed in the grooves of its circle, like the Persian daff. A group has decided it is permissible, while others have decided it is forbidden, and I hold this view, for as al-Adhra'i said, it is more stirring than most of the instruments on which agreement has been reached about their prohibition.

Some Sufis wrote treatises on the permissibility of lutes, flutes, and other instruments of entertainment, and in them they brought astonishing falsehoods against Allah the Exalted, against the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), against his Companions (may Allah be pleased with them), the Successors, and the practicing scholars. Those who imitated them in this were people whom Satan has played with and whom desire has cast into the pit of deprivation; he is far removed from the truth, and between him and the reality of Sufism there is a thousand thousand stations. When the statement of some great figure permitting something of this has been verified for you, do not be deceived by it, for it contradicts what the Imams of the four schools of law and others among the eminent scholars hold, supported by strong evidences "falsehood cannot come at it from before it or from behind it." Everyone's word is taken or left except that of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Whoever has been given sound reason and a heart free from corrupt desires does not doubt that this is not part of the religion, and that it is far removed by many stages from the aims of the Sharia of the master of the messengers (ﷺ), upon him, his family, and all his companions.

Some of those who permit the shabbaba have relied on what Ibn Hibban included in his Sahih, from Nafi', from Ibn Umar (may Allah be pleased with them both): that he heard the sound of a shepherd's pipe, so he put his two fingers in his ears, turned away from the road, and kept saying, "O Nafi', do you hear?" I said, "Yes." When I said, "No," he returned to the road and said, "Thus I saw the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) do." Ibn Abi al-Dunya and al-Bayhaqi also transmitted it from Nafi'. Al-Hafiz Muhammad ibn Nasr al-Salami was asked about it and said: "It is a sound hadith." The argument from it is that the Prophet (ﷺ) did not order Ibn Umar, who at that time, as the aforementioned hafiz said, was seventeen years old, to block his ears, nor did he forbid the one who was playing. If that were forbidden, he would have commanded and forbidden, upon him be prayers and peace. As for his (ﷺ) blocking his ears, it may be that he was in a state of remembrance or contemplation, and the hearing would have distracted him, upon him be prayer and greetings. It may also be that he did it (ﷺ) as a form of purification.

Al-Adhra'i said: "By this hadith our companions (the Shafi'is) have argued for the prohibition of the mazamir, and upon it they built the prohibition of the shabbaba." End of quote.

My own view is that it is not an explicit text on its prohibition, because blocking the ears at the time of hearing is a matter of his action (ﷺ); it is not something in which the nature of the matter was made clear, nor has it been established that it was specific to him, upon him be prayer and peace, nor is it something made clear as an explanation of a text in regard to which of the categories it belongs to: obligation, recommendation, or permissibility. If its nature is known, then it must be either obligation, recommendation, or permissibility. It cannot be obligation, which would entail the prohibition of hearing the yara', since no one holds that it is obligatory upon anyone to block his ears on hearing something forbidden, for he is safe from sin by not intending it. They have said: "What is forbidden is listening (istima'), not mere hearing without intention." In al-Zawajir: "What is prohibited is listening (al-istima'), not hearing (al-sama') without intention, by consensus." Hence our companions, meaning the Shafi'is, have explicitly stated that whoever has forbidden instruments near him and cannot remove them is not obliged to move away, and does not sin by hearing them without intention and attentive listening. The apparent reading is that the matter is the same according to all the Imams. Yes, they have a distinction regarding sitting in a place where such things are present. In Tanwir al-Absar and its commentary al-Durr al-Mukhtar: "If he is invited to a banquet where there is play and singing, he should sit and eat, even at the table, but it is not appropriate for him to sit; rather he should leave, turning away, in accordance with His words: ﴿So do not sit after the reminder with the wrongdoing people﴾ [al-An'am 6:68]. If he is able to prevent it, he should do so; if he cannot, he should endure, if he is not one who is followed as an example. If he is one who is followed, and cannot prevent it, he should leave and not sit, because it causes disgrace to the religion. What is related from Imam Abu Hanifa (may Allah be pleased with him) was before he became someone followed as an example. If he knows in advance, he should not attend at all, whether or not he is one who is followed." End of quote. Thus it is determined that it is either recommended or permissible, and both of these do not entail prohibition. It may be that it is forbidden or disliked, and blocking the ears upon hearing it is recommended as a precaution against being drawn into forbidden or disliked listening. If its nature is not known, then concerning what is like this, the schools of thought with respect to the community are five: obligation, recommendation, permissibility, suspension, and a distinction, which is that if the intention of seeking nearness to Allah appears, it is recommended, and otherwise it is permissible. What we have mentioned makes clear the position on every school.

What is most likely in opinion is that if what the report refers to is the piping of the shepherd's pipe with refinement and the production of tones that stir desires, as is done today by those who make it their profession, then listening to it is forbidden, and the blocking of the ears mentioned in it may have been from him (ﷺ) as teaching the community one of the known methods of precaution, lest it lead them to listen. Otherwise, listening is by way of the Prophet's infallibility something that cannot be conceived in regard to him (ﷺ). Whoever knows the rank of the Companions, and is acquainted with their path and their eagerness to follow him (ﷺ), does not doubt that Ibn Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) also blocked his ears in imitation. In that case, the Prophet's (ﷺ) words to him, which the report indicates, "Do you hear?", would mean "Listen, do you hear?" The words "Listen" were omitted because the situation indicates it, since one who blocks his ears does not hear. He (ﷺ) only permitted him to do this because of the need. This is nearer than the possibility that the blocking of the ears was from the Prophet (ﷺ) because he was in a state of remembrance or contemplation, and the hearing would distract him (ﷺ).

As for his (ﷺ) not forbidding the one who was piping, nor denouncing him, its indication of permissibility is not accepted, for it is possible that the sound came from afar, and between the piper and him (ﷺ) there was something preventing reaching him, or he did not recognize him (ﷺ), since the sound came from behind a screen, and ability to denounce is not established in that case. It is also possible that the prohibition was already known, and the Prophet (ﷺ) was known to persist against it, or that the persistence of that person in his act was known, and this would be like the people of the dhimma going to their churches; in such a case, silence and non-denunciation do not indicate permissibility by consensus. Whoever holds that the disbeliever is not accountable for the branches of the law says: it is possible that that piper was a disbeliever, and that silence regarding him is not evidence of permissibility. If the piping of it is not with refinement and the production of tones that stir desires, then there is no difficulty in saying that it is permissible in both performance and listening, and blocking the ears in regard to it is for the utmost purity fitting to him (ﷺ). As for al-Adhra'i's answer that his words in the report, "a shepherd's pipe," do not specify that it is the shabbaba, since shepherds play with the shu'aybiyya and others, which implies that what is called shu'aybiyya is permissible and settled, there is room for consideration, for it is a term for several small reeds, and it has a stirring effect according to the skill of the one who plays it. It is therefore either a shabbaba or a mizmar without doubt, and the permissibility of this is a matter of dispute.

After all this, we say:

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 31, verse 6 (part 6 of 6):

The report mentioned was narrated by Abu Dawud, who said that it is *munkar* (a report whose narration is rejected, the term meaning a weak report that contradicts a more reliable one). In any case, there is no proof in it for either side. God Almighty has spared the believers from fighting. Furthermore, if you are afflicted with any of this, then beware, and again beware, of believing that doing it or listening to it is an act of devotion (*qurba*), as those believe who have no share (of religion) among the Sufis. Had the matter been as they claim, the Prophets would not have neglected to do it and to command their followers to do it. Nothing of this has been transmitted from any of the Prophets, peace be upon them, nor has any of the revealed Books sent down from heaven alluded to it. God Almighty has said: ﴿Today I have perfected your religion for you﴾ (5:3). Had the use of musical instruments that cause ecstasy, or listening to them, been part of the religion and of what brings one closer to the presence of the Lord of the worlds, he (ﷺ) would have explained it and made it fully clear to his community. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "By Him in whose hand is my soul, I have not left anything that brings you closer to Paradise and distances you from the Fire except that I have commanded you to do it, and I have not left anything that brings you closer to the Fire and distances you from Paradise except that I have forbidden you from it."

What has been mentioned falls under the second category, as will not be hidden from one who has a sound heart and an upright mind. So reflect, be fair, and beware of objecting before you have inquired and understood. We will return, God willing, to discussing this matter. May God Almighty facilitate that for us by the sanctity of His beloved, the greatest one (ﷺ).

Some have used the verse as evidence for the view that *lahw al-hadith* (idle talk) refers to the books that an-Nadr ibn al-Harith bought, to argue for the prohibition of reading the histories of the ancient Persians, and of hearing and reciting what is in them. There is discussion on this point. It should not be hidden that these books contain much falsehood, so occupying oneself with them for no religious purpose is engaging in vanity. Ibn Nujaym counted this, in his treatise on the sins, among the minor sins, and illustrated it by mentioning the luxury of kings and the wealthy. Understand this.

Among the strange and remote views is that of the author of *al-Tahrir*, who took *ishtira* (buying) to mean *bay'* (selling). He said:

"It appears to me that by *lahw al-hadith* He (Glorified be He) meant the narratives that they displayed in strengthening their religion, in commanding its perpetuation, and in altering the description of the Messenger (peace be upon him), and in claiming that the Torah indicates that he is from the descendants of Isaac (peace be upon him). They intended by these to turn their followers away from faith. The term *ishtira* was used because they would take bribes and rewards for this from their kings." He said: "This is supported by the words of God Almighty: ﴿to mislead from the way of God﴾." But it is, as you see, as it is.

By "His way" (God's way) is meant His religion, Mighty and Majestic, or the recitation of His Book, Glorified be He, or what encompasses both. The *lam* in (*liyudilla*) is for causation (*lam al-ta'lil*). Ibn Kathir and Abu Amr read *liyaḍilla* with a *fatha* on the *ya'*. The meaning is that he remains in his error and increases in it, for the one spoken of was already astray before. Here the *lam* is for consequence (*lam al-'aqiba*). That it is in its original sense, as has been said, is remote. Al-Zamakhshari allowed that, in this reading, *liyaḍilla* was put in the place of *liyudilla* because whoever misleads is necessarily astray. Thus he indicated the consequence (*radif*, the implied concomitant) by the concomitant, namely the error, and by the implied meaning, namely the misleading. The basis of this indication is that by error is meant the doubled error concerning one who turns entirely away from the way of God Almighty and abandons it altogether. This error is never separate from misleading, and vice versa. By this the objection of the author of *al-Fara'id* is dispelled, who said that error entails only error. In this reading the two readings agree, and the *lam* remains in its literal sense. In both cases it is connected to His words, Glorified be He: ﴿he buys﴾.

His words, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿without knowledge﴾ may be connected to this as well, meaning he buys that without knowledge of the state of what he buys. Or it may be connected to trade, since he exchanged error for guidance and falsehood for truth. It may also be connected to (*liyudilla*), meaning to mislead from His way, Glorified be He, while ignorant that it is His way, Mighty and Majestic, or ignorant that he is misleading, or ignorant of the truth.

﴿and take it﴾ (*wa yattakhidha-ha*)
Page 80

is in the accusative, coordinated with *yudilla*, and the pronoun refers to "the way," since it may be masculine or feminine. It was also permitted that it refers to "the verses." It has been said that it may refer to "the narratives," since *hadith* is a collective noun meaning narratives. But this is, as you see, as it is.

﴿in mockery﴾ means: as something mocked. Some of the Seven Readers read (*yattakhidha-ha*) in the nominative, coordinated with *yashtari*. It was also permitted that it is in the nominative by an implied pronoun (*huwa*).

﴿For them there is a humiliating punishment﴾ because of what they characterized themselves by: their contempt for the truth by preferring falsehood over it, and their enticing of people toward it. The recompense is of the same kind as the deed. ﴿Those﴾ (*ulaʾika*) refers to "whoever" (*man*). The sense of distance in the demonstrative is for indicating the remoteness of their rank in wickedness. The plural in the demonstrative and the pronoun is in accordance with its meaning, just as the singular in the two verbs is in accordance with its wording. The same applies to His words, Exalted be He:

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 31, verse 7:

﴿And when Our verses are recited to him﴾: In this verse there is observance of the wording (mura'at al-lafz), then observance of the meaning (mura'at al-ma'na), then observance of the wording again. A parallel to this in that respect is His saying, Exalted is He, in surah [al-Talaq: 2] (wa-man yu'min billahi) "and whoever believes in Allah," and the rest of the verse. Abu Hayyan said:

"We do not know of anything in the Qur'an that is treated first according to the wording, then according to the meaning, then according to the wording again, other than these two verses."

Al-Khafaji said: "That is not so, for it has parallels." That is, "and when Our verses, which are of great significance, are recited to the aforementioned purchaser of idle tales" ﴿wa-lla﴾ he turned away from them, not regarding them as important, ﴿mustakbiran﴾ being arrogant to an excessive degree. Here the form istaf'ala is used in the sense of tafa''ala. ﴿ka-an lam yasma'hā﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in (wa-lla), or from the pronoun in (mustakbiran), meaning: his state in turning away, or in his arrogance, resembles that of one who did not hear them, while in fact he did hear. In this there is an allusion to the fact that one who hears them cannot be imagined to turn away or be arrogant, because they contain matters that necessitate turning toward them and submitting to them, following the manner of al-Khansa's saying:

"O tree of al-Khabur, why are you in leaf, as if you had not grieved over the son of Tarif?"

(Ka-an) in its light form (al-mukhaffafa) is inoperative, and there is no need to posit a pronoun of the matter (damir sha'n) in it, though some do posit it. ﴿ka-anna fi udhunayhi waqran﴾ meaning: deafness preventing hearing. The original meaning of waqr is a heavy load; it was borrowed for deafness, and then it became dominant until it became literally applied to it. This clause is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in (lam yasma'hā), or it is a substitute for it, a substitution of the whole for the whole, or an explanation of it. It may also be a circumstantial clause from one of the two preceding, and it may be that both clauses are independent (mustan'afatan). The purpose of the second clause is escalation in censure. The heavy form (ka-anna) in the second clause is used because of its suitability to heaviness in its meaning. Nafi' read «fi udhnayhi» with the dhal unvowelled (sukun) as a lightening.

﴿So give him tidings of a painful punishment﴾: that is, inform him that a punishment extremely painful in its affliction will surely befall him. The mention of "tidings" is sarcastic (li-l-tahakkum).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 31, verse 8:

﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾ is an exposition of the state of the believers in His signs, following the exposition of the state of the disbelievers in them. That is: those who believed in His signs and acted in accordance with their requirements, ﴿for them﴾ in return for their faith and their deeds mentioned, ﴿are gardens of bliss﴾, i.e. abundant bliss. The annexation of the gardens to it is on account of their containing it, like your saying: "books of jurisprudence" (kutub al-fiqh).

In this there is an indication that they possess its bliss by way of demonstration (burhani), which is more eloquent than: "for them is the bliss of the gardens," since that does not require that the gardens themselves be their property, for one may enjoy a thing without owning it. It has also been said, regarding the aspect of greater eloquence, that it is because bliss has been made the source in it, by which the gardens are distinguished, so this conveys the abundance of bliss and its fame. Whatever the case, "gardens of bliss" are the well-known Gardens.

Ibn Abi Hatim related, from Malik ibn Dinar, who said: "The Gardens of Bliss lie between the Gardens of Firdaws and the Gardens of 'Adn, and in them are maidens created from the rose of Paradise. It was said: 'And who will dwell in them?' He said: 'Those who were minded toward sins, but when they remembered My greatness, they watched over Me; and those whose loins were bent in My fear.'" And Allah the Exalted knows best the soundness of the report. The clause is the predicate of "inna" (indeed). It has been said that the better view is to make "for them" the predicate, because "gardens of bliss" is raised by it as its agent (fa'il).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 31, verse 9:

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿abiding therein﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) referring either to the pronoun in the genitive (ضمير مجرور) or the concealed pronoun in (lahum, "for them"), on the basis that it is a fronted predicate (khabar muqaddam); or it refers to (jannatu, "gardens"), on the basis that it is the agent (fa'il) of the adverbial phrase, since it relies on being in the predicate position, and the governing element is what the preposition (lam) is attached to.

Zayd ibn 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with both of them, read ﴿khalidun﴾ with a waw, and it is by the estimate of (huwa, "He"). ﴿Promise of Allah﴾ is an emphatic infinitive (masdar mu'akkid) emphasizing itself, i.e., emphasizing what is like its own self, and this is the explicit sentence in its meaning, namely His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿for them are gardens of bliss﴾, for it is explicit in the promise.

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿truly﴾ is also an emphatic infinitive emphasizing that sentence, except that it is counted as emphasizing something other than itself, since not every promise is true in itself.

It has been permitted that it emphasizes the emphasized promise of Allah, and that it emphasizes that sentence, being counted among what emphasizes itself on the basis of its indication of certainty and firmness in several respects; but this is remote. In al-Kashshaf: this is not sound, because emphatic reports do not escape the possibility of being false, so reflect. ﴿And He is the Mighty﴾, whom nothing overcomes so as to prevent Him from fulfilling His promise and making true His threat, ﴿the Wise﴾, who does only what wisdom and benefit require. This restriction is understood from the implication (fahwa), and the sentence is a concluding phrase (tadhyil) affirming the truth of His promise, which is specific to those mentioned, indicating the threat against their opposites.

﴿He created the heavens without pillars [that you can see]﴾, etc. This is a resumptive clause (istinaf), brought in to serve as evidence for what has been mentioned about His might, which is the perfection of power, and His wisdom, which is the perfection of knowledge and the perfect execution of work. It also paves the way for and establishes the principle of monotheism (tawhid), refutes the matter of associating partners with God (shirk), and rebukes its adherents. The word ʿamad (pillars) is the plural of ʿimad, like ahab is the plural of ihab. It is that by which something is supported, i.e., propped up. One says "I propped up (ʿammadtu) the wall" when you buttress it. The meaning is that He created them without supports. The plural form is due to the multiplicity of the heavens.

The Exalted's statement ﴿you see them﴾ is a resumptive clause answering an implied question: "What is the proof of that?" It is therefore driven toward establishing that they are without pillars, because if they had pillars, they would be seen. The clause has no place in terms of i'rab (grammatical analysis). The pronoun in the accusative refers to the heavens, and the seeing is visual (basariyya), not cognitive (ʿilmiyya), so that there is no need to omit one of its two objects. It is also permissible for the phrase to be an adjective of ʿamad, with the pronoun referring to them, meaning: He created them without visible pillars. This restriction hints that He supported them with a pillar that is not seen, namely the pillar of power (ʿamad al-qudra). This is narrated from Mujahid. Another view is that the pillar of the heavens in every age is the perfect human of that age. Hence, when the perfect human ceases to exist, which is at the cessation of the human species, the heavens will be folded like the folding of a scroll for books. This is a statement that has no support from the Book or the Sunnah, as far as we know, and "above every possessor of knowledge is One who knows" (Qur'an 12:76).

﴿And He cast into the earth firm mountains﴾: this is an explanation of His wonderful creative act in the stability of the earth, following the explanation of His wise creative act in the stability of the heavens. That is, He cast into it lofty mountains, or firm (thawabit) ones, lest ﴿it should shake with you﴾, or so that it would not shake, i.e., be agitated. ﴿With you﴾: were He, glory be to Him and exalted, not to cast mountains into it, [the earth would shake], because wisdom required that it be created in a state such that, if it were empty of mountains, it would sway due to the surrounding waters that cover most of it, and the violent winds whose blowing wisdom requires, or something similar. Among this may be counted the movement of a heavy weight upon it. Some philosophers have mentioned that, based on the sphericity of the earth and the necessity that its center of gravity coincide with the center of the world, its movement along with the mountains upon it would result from a heavy movement from one side of it to another, because the center of gravity would then change. However, this has not appeared, because the moving weights upon it are as nothing in relation to it along with what is in it. Perhaps whoever counts the movement of a heavy weight upon it among the causes of swaying would, were it empty of mountains, say: it is not far-fetched that a heavy weight moves upon it, like water that flows from one place to another and gathers until it becomes a great sea, together with what is added to that from the great quantities of sand and dust carried by the winds, which would have a measure worth considering in relation to the earth empty of mountains, so it would move with its movement in the opposite direction. Furthermore, swaying without the firm mountains, through such things as water and winds, is conceivable on the assumption that the earth is spherical, as Ghazali held. Likewise he held that the heaven is spherical. A narration from Ibn ʿAbbas indicates this, and most philosophers adopted it, citing what is in al-Tadhkira and its commentaries and elsewhere. It is what sense perception and intuition support. And on the assumption that it is not spherical, as others held, they differed about its shape. The details of this are to be sought in their proper places.

There is no indication in the verse that the wisdom of casting the firm mountains into it is limited to its safety from swaying, for there are countless wisdoms for that.

Likewise there is no indication in it that it does not move in a circular motion permanently, as the followers of Pythagoras held, and behind that are doctrines far more evidently false. Yes, the textual and rational proofs for that are numerous.

﴿And He spread throughout it﴾, i.e., He brought into existence and manifested. The root of baththa is to stir up and to scatter, and from it comes ﴿then they became scattered dust﴾ (Qur'an 56:6) and ﴿like scattered moths﴾ (Qur'an 101:4). In placing it later [in the verse] there is a hint that it depends on the removal of swaying.

﴿Of every creature﴾: of every kind among its kinds.

﴿And We sent down from the sky﴾: water, which is rain. By "sky" is meant the direction of height. It is permissible to interpret it as a canopy. That the sending down is from it is by way of some interpretation, and abandoning interpretation should not be relied upon unless there is evidence that compels us to it, because that contradicts observation.

﴿Then We made to grow therein﴾, i.e., by means of that water, ﴿of every noble pair﴾, i.e., every noble kind, ﴿noble﴾, i.e., honorable, of abundant benefit. The shift to the pronoun of majesty in the two verbs serves to highlight greater care for both, given their repetition, along with what they contain of the soundness of the state of animals and the cultivation of the earth, which is not hidden.

This refers to what has been mentioned of the heavens, the earth, and the other enumerated matters, "is the creation of Allah," meaning His creature. "Then show me" means inform me and tell me. The *fa* (then) responds to an implied condition, meaning: if you know this, then show me what "those you took besides Him" have created. You have taken them as partners to Him, glorified is He, in worship, to the point that they have come to deserve worship through it.

Regarding *mādhā* (ماذا), it may be a single interrogative noun, functioning as the object of *khalaqa* (created) and placed at the front of the sentence because it is an interrogative. Alternatively, (ما) alone may be an interrogative noun serving as the *mubtada'* (subject of a nominal sentence), with (ذا) as a relative noun serving as its *khabar* (predicate), and the clause is then *mu'allaq* (suspended from the verb's action) and serves as the second object of *arūnī* (show me). Or the whole (ماذا) may be a relative noun, which Abu Hayyan says is used this way only rarely, functioning as the second object of *arūnī*. In both of the latter cases the returning pronoun is omitted.

As for His words, ﴿Nay, the wrongdoers are in manifest error﴾, this is a turning away from rebuking them with what has been mentioned, to recording against them a clear error. This calls for turning away from addressing them with the reasonable and true premises, because it is impossible that they would understand anything from them, so that they might be guided by them to knowledge of the falsehood of what they hold, or be affected by the censure and rebuke so that they desist from it. The apparent noun was placed in the position of their pronoun to indicate that, by their associating partners with Allah, they are placing things in other than their proper place, exceeding the limits, and wronging themselves by exposing themselves to the everlasting punishment.

**Verse 12: "And We had certainly given Luqman wisdom."**

This is a new sentence, brought in to show that polytheism is false by transmitted evidence, following the earlier indication of its falsehood by reason.

Luqman is a non-Arabic name, not an Arabic one, and is said to be derived from *luqam* (a type of morsel). He is, it is said, the son of Ba'ura'. Wahb said: he was the son of the sister of Ayyub, upon him be peace. Muqatil said: he was the son of Ayyub's maternal aunt. Abd al-Rahman al-Suhayli said: he is the son of Anqa ibn Sarun. It is also said that he was among the descendants of Azar. He lived a thousand years and encountered Dawud, upon him be peace, and took knowledge from him. He used to give legal rulings (*fatwa*) before his mission (*mab'ath*), but when he was sent as a prophet he stopped giving rulings. It was said to him, "Why?" He replied, "Shall I not be content when I am spared?" It is also said that he was a judge among the Children of Israel, and this is related from al-Waqidi, except that he said: his time was between Muhammad and Isa, upon them both be peace. Ikrima and al-Sha'bi said that he was a prophet. Most scholars hold that he lived in the time of Dawud, upon him be peace, and that he was not a prophet.

It has been disputed whether he was free or a slave. Most hold that he was a slave. They also differed about his appearance. It was said that he was Ethiopian, and this is related from Ibn Abbas and Mujahid.

Ibn Mardawayh transmitted this, from Abu Hurayra, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ). Mujahid mentioned in describing him that he had thick lips and flat feet. It was also said that he was Nubian, with cracked feet and thick lips, and this came in a report from Ibn Abbas, Ibn al-Musayyib and Mujahid.

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr, who said: I asked Jabir ibn Abdullah, "What has reached you about the affair of Luqman?" He said: he was short, flat-nosed, from the Nubians. He (Ibn Abi Hatim) and Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Ibn al-Musayyib that he said: Luqman was black, one of the blacks of Egypt, with thick lips. Allah the Exalted gave him wisdom and withheld prophethood from him.

They differed about what work he used to do. Khalid ibn al-Rabi' said he was a carpenter (*najjar*), with a *ra*. In the *Ma'ani* of al-Zajjaj, it is said he was a *najjad* with a *dal*, which is on the pattern of *kattan*, meaning one who works on carpets and cushions and sews them.

Ibn Abi Shayba, Ahmad in *al-Zuhd*, and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Ibn al-Musayyib that he was a tailor, which is more general than *najjad*. From Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, it is related that he was a shepherd. It is also said that he used to gather firewood for his master every day, one bundle. I have no confidence in any of these reports, and I have only related them following those commentators, the good ones, who transmitted them. However, I prefer that he was a righteous man, wise, and not a prophet.

*(Al-Hikma)* (wisdom): according to what Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Ibn Abbas, it is intellect, understanding and shrewdness. Al-Firyabi, Ahmad in *al-Zuhd*, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Mujahid that it is intellect, jurisprudence (*fiqh*) and correctness in speech. Al-Raghib said: it is knowledge of existing things and the performance of good deeds. The Imam said: it is an expression for the harmonizing of action with knowledge. Then he said: if we wish to define it by what includes the wisdom of Allah the Exalted, we say: the attainment of action in accordance with what is known. Abu Hayyan said: it is the speech by which one is admonished and becomes alert, and which people pass on to one another for that purpose. It is said: it is the perfecting of a thing in knowledge and action. It is said: it is a perfection attained by the completion of the human soul through acquiring theoretical sciences and gaining complete disposition toward virtuous acts according to its capacity. Many of the sages defined it as knowing the realities of things as they are, to the extent of human capacity. They have other definitions, and what is for and against them, in terms of criticism and endorsement, is mentioned in their books.

From his wisdom is his saying to his son: "O my son, the world is a deep sea, and many people have drowned in it. So make your ship in it the fear of Allah the Exalted, let its hull be faith, its sail reliance upon Allah the Exalted, perhaps you will be saved, though I do not think you will be saved." And his saying: "Whoever has an admonisher within himself will have a guardian from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. Whoever gives people their due from himself, Allah the Exalted will increase him in honour by that. Humility in obedience to Allah the Exalted is closer than seeking honour through disobedience." And his saying: "A father's beating of his child is like manure for the crop." And his saying: "O my son, beware of debt, for it is humiliation by day and worry by night." And his saying: "O my son, hope in Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, with a hope that does not lead you into His disobedience, and fear Allah, glorified be He, with a fear that does not make you despair of His mercy, exalted be His station." And his saying: "Whoever lies loses the water of his face, and whoever is bad-tempered, his grief multiplies. Moving rocks from their places is easier than making understand one who does not understand." And his saying: "O my son, I have carried gravel, iron and everything heavy, but I have carried nothing heavier than a bad neighbour, and I have tasted bitterness, but I have tasted nothing more bitter than poverty. O my son, do not send an ignorant messenger; if you do not find a wise man, be the messenger of yourself. O my son, beware of lying, for it is as delicious as the meat of a sparrow, but its eater will soon be burned by it. O my son, attend funerals and do not attend weddings, for funerals remind you of the Hereafter and weddings make you covet this world. O my son, do not eat to satiety upon satiety, for throwing it to the dog is better than your eating it. O my son, do not be sweet lest you be swallowed, nor bitter lest you be spat out." And his saying to his son: "Let no one eat your food but the pious, and consult the scholars about your affair." And his saying: "There is no good in learning what you do not know, while not acting on what you already know; the likeness of that is a man who gathered firewood, took a bundle and went to carry it, but was unable to, so he added another to it." And his saying: "O my son, if you want to befriend a man, first anger him. If he treats you fairly in his anger, then befriend him, otherwise beware of him." And his saying: "Let your word be good, and let your face be open, and you will be more beloved to people than one who gives them gifts." And his saying: "O my son, place yourself in relation to your companion as one who has no need of you, yet whom you cannot do without. O my son, be like one who does not seek people's praise nor earn their blame; his soul is in hardship because of him, and people are at ease from him." And his saying: "O my son, restrain what comes out of your mouth, for if you keep silent you are safe, and you should only say what benefits you."

And other sayings beyond number.

**"That give thanks to Allah."** That is, "Give thanks," with *an* being explanatory (*tafsiriyya*), and what follows it explains the giving of wisdom. It contains the sense of saying without its letters, whether it was by inspiration, revelation, or teaching.

It is permitted that it be an explanation of wisdom in terms of what the command contains. Al-Zajjaj made *an* verbal (*masdariyya*), with an implied causal *li* (for), and the meaning of command is not lost, as has been verified previously. Sibawayh related: "I wrote to him with *an qum* (that stand up)." The preposition phrase is attached to "Our signs." It is also permitted that it be verbal without any implied particle, the verbal noun being an inclusive apposition (*badal ishtimal*) of "wisdom," but this is far-fetched.

**"And whoever gives thanks..."** etc.: a resumptive clause (*isti'naf*) confirming the content of what came before, requiring compliance with the command. That is, whoever gives thanks to Him, the Exalted, **"then he gives thanks only for his own self"**, because its benefit lies in the binding of the blessing, the drawing of increase, and success in the Garden of eternity, which are confined to it. **"And whoever disbelieves, then indeed Allah is Rich"** beyond every thing, so He has no need of thanks to be harmed by the disbelief of the disbeliever, **"Praiseworthy"**, deserving of praise even if no one praises Him, or praised in act, all created beings declaring His praise in the tongue of their state; so *hamid* is a form meaning *mahmud* (praised) in both respects. The lack of mention of His being thanked, exalted and glorified, is because praise includes thanks; rather, it is its head, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Praise is the head of gratitude; a servant does not give thanks to Allah if he does not praise Him."

Affirming praise for Him is thus definitively affirming thanks for Him. In choosing the past tense in this second part, it has been said that it indicates the ugliness of ingratitude, and that it should not be found except as a predicate of *kana* (was). It has also been said that it indicates that disbelief is abundant and established, unlike gratitude: **"And few of My servants are grateful"** (Saba' 13).

The response of the conditional is omitted, and what stands in its place is His saying, exalted be He, "then indeed Allah..." The original would be: "And whoever disbelieves, then his disbelief is only against himself, because Allah is Rich, Praiseworthy." The sum of it: whoever disbelieves, the harm of his disbelief returns upon him, because He, the Exalted, is Rich, who has no need of thanks so that He could be harmed by disbelief, and Praiseworthy by the measure of entitlement or by the speech of the tongues of states. So both attributes relate to the second part.

It is permitted that "Rich" be a causal explanation of His saying, glorified be He, "then he gives thanks only for his own self," and that His saying, exalted and glorified be He, "Praiseworthy," be an explanation of the implied response of the conditional, by the indication of its counterpart, which is: "then he disbelieves only against his own self." And it is permitted that each of them be attached to each of them. There is no hidden what is in that of artificiality, to which there is no call, and for which no indication stands. So reflect.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 31, verse 13:

﴿And when Luqman said to his son﴾: his name was Taran, according to al-Tabari and al-Qutaybi. It is also said to be Mathan with a *tha'* (ث), and it is said to be An'um, and it is said to be Ashkum. These two are of the form *af'al*. It is also said to be Mashkam, with a *mim* instead of the *hamzah*. "*Idh*" (إذ, "when") is an object (*ma'mul*) of a verb "*udhkur*" (اذكر, "remember") which is omitted. It is also said that it may be an adverbial complement (*zarf*) of "*atayna*" (آتينا, "We gave"), and the sense is: "We gave him wisdom when he said," and this was abbreviated because the preceding clause indicates it. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿while he was admonishing him﴾ is a circumstantial clause (*jumlah haliyyah*). *Al-wa'z* (الوعظ, admonition), as al-Raghib said, is a rebuke combined with frightening. Al-Khalil said: it is reminding of good in what softens the heart. ﴿O my son﴾: the diminutive here is a diminutive of tenderness and affection, not a diminutive of belittling:

"But when the love of a thing overwhelms you,
the letters of diminution take hold of it out of the intensity of longing."

And another said:

"I did not say 'my beloved' (*Hubayybi*) as a diminishing;
rather, the name of a thing becomes sweeter by diminution."

Al-Bazzi recited here "*Ya bunayy*" (يا بُنَيْ) with a sukun (silent ending), and in what follows, "*Ya bunayyi innaha*" (يا بُنَيِّ إنها) with a kasrah on the *ya'*. And "﴿O my son, establish prayer﴾" (Luqman 17) with a fathah on it. Qunbul read with a sukun in the first and third, and with a kasrah in the middle. Hafs, and al-Mufaddal from Asim, read with a fathah in all three, on the reckoning of "*ya bunayyan*" (يا بنيًّا), with the fathah standing in place of the alif. The rest of the seven readers read with a kasrah in them. ﴿Do not associate anything with Allah﴾: it was said that his son was a disbeliever, and therefore he forbade him from association, and he continued to admonish him until he became a Muslim. The same was said of his wife.

Ibn Abi al-Dunya narrated in *Na't al-Khaifin* from al-Fadl al-Raqqashi, who said: Luqman continued to admonish his son until he died.

He also narrated from Hafs ibn Umar al-Kindi, who said: Luqman placed a bag of mustard seeds, and he began to admonish his son with an admonition, and he would take out one mustard seed. The mustard seeds ran out, and he said: "O my son, I have admonished you with an admonition which, if I had admonished it to a mountain, it would have split apart." So his son split apart. It was said that he was a Muslim.

The prohibition of association is a warning to him against its occurrence from him in the future. The apparent reading is that the *ba'* (ب) in "*bi-Allah*" is attached to what precedes it. Whoever pauses at "﴿do not associate﴾" makes the *ba'* an oath particle, meaning: "I swear by Allah, exalted is He," ﴿indeed association is a great injustice﴾. The apparent reading is that this is from the speech of Luqman, and the speech of Muslim in his *Sahih* implies it. The statement is a justification for the prohibition, or for abstaining from association. It was also said that it is a statement from Allah, exalted is His glory, disconnected from the speech of Luqman but connected to it in emphasizing the meaning. Association is an injustice because it involves placing a thing in other than its proper place, and it is great because it involves equating between the One from whom is every blessing, glorified is He, and one who has no blessing at all.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 31, verse 14:

﴿And We enjoined upon man concerning his parents﴾ etc. is a resumed statement, introduced as a digression (istitrad) in the midst of Luqman's admonition, to emphasise what it contains of the prohibition of association (shirk). It is therefore part of the speech of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, which He did not say to Luqman. It has also been said that it is part of His speech, exalted be He, addressed to him, and it is as if it were said: "We said to him: Be grateful," and "We said to him: We enjoined upon man," etc. In al-Bahr (of Abu Hayyan): When Luqman explained to his son that shirk is wrongdoing and forbade him from it, that was an exhortation to obey Allah, the Exalted. Then he explained that obedience is also owed to the two parents, and explained the reason for that. Thus it is part of Luqman's speech, which he enjoined upon his son, and Allah, the Exalted, reported it. Both opinions, as you see, are [weak]. The meaning: We commanded man to care for his parents. ﴿His mother bore him in weakness﴾, i.e., in frailty, ﴿upon weakness﴾, i.e., upon frailty. The verbal noun (masdar) is a circumstantial clause (hal) referring to "his mother," with an implied genitive, i.e., "in a state of weakness." It has been permitted to make the noun itself a circumstantial qualifier for emphasis, but this is contrary to analogy, since the norm for a circumstantial qualifier is that it be a derived noun (mushtaq). It may also be an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq) of an implied verb, i.e., "she grows weak in weakness," and the clause is also a circumstantial qualifier of "his mother." In any case, what is meant is that she grows weaker and weaker as the weight of the burden increases until the time of labour. It has been said: a continuous weakness, which is the weakness of pregnancy, the weakness of labour, and the weakness of postpartum bleeding. It has also been permitted that it be a circumstantial qualifier of the pronoun in "bore him" (hamalathu), referring to "man," and this is what is required by what Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Mujahid, that he said: "Weakness" is the child, "upon weakness" is the mother and her frailty. The meaning is that she bore him while he was weak, upon another weak one like him. The intention is not that she bore him while his weakness was increasing, so as to be objected that his weakness does not increase but decreases. ʿIsa al-Thaqafi and Abu ʿAmr, in one narration, read: "wahnan ʿala wahnin" with a fatha on the ha' in both, so it may be from the pattern of vowelling the middle radical when it is a guttural letter, as in "al-shaʿr" and "al-shaʿar," according to the regular rule of the Kufans, as Ibn Jinni held; and it may be the verbal noun of "wahina" (with kasra on the ha') in the present "yawhanu" (with fatha), since its verbal noun came in that form. This is like saying "taʿiba yataʿabu taʿaban," as it has been said. The words of the author of al-Qamus appear to indicate that neither verbal noun is specific to one of the two verbs. He said: "al-wahn" is weakness in work, and it may be vowelled, and the verb is like "waʿada," "waritha," and "karuma."

﴿And his weaning﴾, i.e., his weaning and the cessation of his suckling. Al-Hasan, Abu Raja', Qatada, al-Jahdari and Yaʿqub read "wa-fasluhu," which is more general than "fisal," while "fisal" is more appropriate here, because it is a term specific to breastfeeding, even though both go back to one root, as Al-Tibi said. ﴿In two years﴾, i.e., at the completion of two years, that is, at the beginning of the time of their completion. The apparent meaning of the verse is that the period of breastfeeding is two years. This is the view of al-Shafi'i, Ahmad, Abu Yusuf and Muhammad, and it is the preference of al-Tahawi. It is narrated from Malik. Abu Hanifa held that the period of breastfeeding by which marriage prohibitions are established is thirty months, based on His saying: ﴿And his carrying and weaning is thirty months﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 15]. The basis of the argument from it is that He, glorified and exalted, mentioned two things and assigned a period for them both, so each of them has its full period, like a term set for two debts owed by two persons: if one says "I have deferred the debt owed to me by so-and-so, and the debt owed to me by so-and-so, for a year," it is understood that the year is complete for each. Or as when one says to a man: "I owe you a thousand dirhams and ten qafiz (of wheat) until a year," and the debtor acknowledges it for the term; when the year passes the term of both is complete. However, a deficiency occurred in one of them, namely the period of pregnancy, based on the saying of ʿAʾisha, which is not said except on the basis of transmission: "A child does not remain in its mother's womb for more than two years, even by the measure of a spindle whorl." So the period of weaning remains on its apparent basis. What is mentioned here is the minimum of its period, and there is a discussion about this.

﴿Give thanks to Me and to your parents﴾ is an explanation (tafsir) of "We enjoined," as al-Nahhas preferred, so "an" is explanatory. It has been permitted that it be verbal (masdariyya) with an implied lam of causation before it, and it is connected to "We enjoined." It has also been permitted without an implied particle, with the verbal noun as a substitute for "your parents," a substitution of inclusion (badal al-ishtimal). In this case it is as if it were said: "We enjoined man concerning his parents by thanking them." The thanks owed to Allah, the Exalted, is mentioned because the validity of thanking them depends on thanking Him, the Mighty and Majestic, just as it has been said in the reverse: "He who does not thank people does not thank Allah, the Exalted." For this reason He joined them in the injunction. There is much remoteness in this, but as for the claim that the command rules out explanation, causation, and substitution, this is nothing, as we pointed out shortly before. On all three possibilities, His saying ﴿His mother bore him﴾ up to ﴿two years﴾ is a parenthetical clause emphasising the injunction concerning the mother in particular, because it mentions what she endured in his upbringing and his carrying. For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) said, as in an authentic hadith narrated by al-Tirmidhi and Abu Dawud, from Bahz ibn Hakim, from his father, from his grandfather, to one who asked him whom he should treat with kindness: "Your mother," and he answered his question with it three times.

It is narrated from some of the Arabs that he carried his mother on his back to the Hajj, while chanting in his camel-driving song:

I carry my mother, and she is the one who bears (the burden),
She feeds me the milk and the (other) nourishment,
And a parent is not repaid for his favour.

And may Allah, the Exalted, bestow His blessing upon the one who said:

Your mother has a right, if you knew it, great indeed,
Your much (of kindness) to her is, O man, little.
How many a night she spent, troubled by your weight, complaining,
For her, from its pains, there is a groan and a sigh.
If you knew the hardship upon her in the birth,
From its agonies the heart flies away.
How often she washed the filth from you with her right hand,
And her lap was for you a bed.
She ransoms you from what she suffers, with her own self,
And from her breast there is a drink for you, a flowing spring.
How many a time she went hungry and gave you her food,
Out of tenderness and compassion, while you were small.
Woe then to one who has sense yet follows his desire,
And woe to one blind of heart while he sees.
So hold fast to her, desire abundantly her supplication,
For you, in what you ask through it, are indeed in need.

Scholars differed about the meaning of the gratitude commanded. It was said that it is obedience, and doing what pleases: prayer and fasting with respect to Allah, and kinship and kindness with respect to the parents. It is narrated from Sufyan ibn ʿUyayna: "Whoever prays the five prayers has given thanks to Allah, the Exalted, and whoever supplicates for his parents after them has given thanks to them." Perhaps this is an explanation of some instances of gratitude. ﴿To Me is the final return﴾ is a justification (taʿlil) for the obligation of compliance with the command, i.e., the return is to Me and not to another; so I shall recompense you for what proceeds from you that contradicts My command.

﴿And if they strive with you to make you associate with Me that of which you have no knowledge﴾, i.e., with its being deserved as a partner, or with His partnership with Him, may He be exalted, in the entitlement to worship. The prepositional phrase "with it" (bihi) is connected to His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿knowledge﴾ (ʿilm). "What" (mā) is the object of "you associate" (tushrika), as Ibn al-Hajib (Ibn al-Ḥājib) preferred. Then he said: "If 'you associate' were taken to mean 'you disbelieve,' and 'what' were taken as indefinite, or as the relative pronoun in the sense of 'that which,' meaning disbelief, or the disbelief, and it were in the accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar), it would be a good reading. The sentence, in that case too, would involve an elided noun (muḍāf), meaning: 'And if your parents strive with you to make you disbelieve in Me with a disbelief for which you have no [warrant], or the disbelief of which you have no knowledge of its validity or its truth.' ﴿Do not obey them in that﴾. The intended meaning is the continuance of the negation of knowledge, not the negation of its continuance, so that association is only by imitation (taqlīd)."

In al-Kashshaf (al-Kashshāf): "God, glorified is He, intended by the negation of knowledge the negation of that which is associated, i.e., 'do not associate with Me that which is not anything,' meaning the idols, as in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿what they call upon besides Him is nothing﴾ [al-ʿAnkabūt: 42]." Al-Ṭībī (al-Ṭībī) made it, on this reading, a case of negating a thing by negating its necessary consequence, because knowledge follows the known: when a thing is nonexistent, it cannot be the object of knowledge while it exists. It is reported from Ibn al-Munir (Ibn al-Munīr) that it belongs to the type of the saying:

*ʿAlayya lāḥibun lā yuhtadā bi-manārihi*
("Upon me is a faint trail, whose landmarks cannot be followed.")

That is, "that which is not a god," so that you would have knowledge of its divinity. In al-Kashf: al-Zamakhsharī (al-Zamakhsharī) intended that the negation of a partner was exaggerated to the point that it was made like nothing, then exaggerated further to the point of that about which knowledge cannot be related at all. The nonexistent can be known, and it can be said that it is a thing, so it is placed in the category of the unknown absolutely, and this is not of the kind of negating knowledge in order to negate existence. This is a good formulation, and in it there is a great exaggeration from him, which shows the preference of this course in this context over the style of:

*Wa-lā tarā al-ḍabba bihā yanjaḥiru*
("And you do not see the lizard burrowing into it.")

End of quotation. Understand this, and do not be heedless. ﴿And keep company with them in this world in a kindly manner﴾, i.e., companionship that is approved by the Sharia and required by generosity and manliness, such as feeding them, clothing them, not being harsh with them, not scolding them, visiting them when they are ill, and burying them when they die. The mention of "in this world" serves to make the matter of companionship seem light, and to indicate that it is for a few days, soon to end, so that bearing its hardship does no harm, because its days are few and quickly pass. It was also said: it indicates that kindness to them is in worldly affairs, not in religious ones.

It was also said: it was mentioned in contrast with His saying, may He be exalted: "Then to Me is your return." ﴿And follow the way of him who turns back to Me﴾, i.e., who returned to Me in monotheism and sincerity, in obedience. Its sum is: follow the way of the sincere, not their way. ﴿Then to Me is your return﴾, i.e., your return and their return. Some added "who turns back" (man anāba), which is contrary to the apparent meaning. In any case, in it the address to the second person prevails over the third person. ﴿So I will inform you﴾ at your return ﴿of what you used to do﴾, by recompensing each of you for what proceeded from him of good and evil.

The verse was revealed concerning Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ. Abū Yaʿlā, al-Ṭabarānī, Ibn Mardawayh and Ibn ʿAsākir reported from Abū ʿUthmān al-Nahdī that Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ said: "This verse was revealed about me: ﴿And if they strive with you﴾ to the end of the verse. I was a man dutiful to my mother. When I embraced Islam, she said: 'O Saʿd, what is this religion you have invented? You will either abandon this religion of yours, or I will not eat or drink until I die, and you will be reproached for me, and it will be said: O slayer of his mother!' I said: 'Do not do that, O mother, for I will not abandon this religion of mine for anything.' She remained for a day and a night without eating, and in the morning she had become exhausted. She remained another day and night without eating, and in the morning her exhaustion had grown severe. When I saw that, I said: 'O mother, you know by God that if you had a hundred souls, and they departed one soul after another, I would not abandon this religion of mine for anything. So if you wish, eat, and if you wish, do not eat.' When she saw that, she ate, and this verse was revealed."

Some have mentioned that this verse and what precedes it, namely His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We have enjoined upon man﴾ to the end of the verse, were revealed concerning him. It was said: because the revelation concerned him, the phrase ﴿who turns back﴾ (man anāba) was said with the singular pronoun, since by it Abū Bakr, may God be pleased with him, is intended, for Saʿd's embracing Islam was through his [Abū Bakr's] embracing Islam.

Al-Wāḥidī reported from ʿAṭāʾ, from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: "He intends by ﴿who turns back﴾ Abū Bakr. That is because when he embraced Islam, ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAwf, Saʿīd ibn Zayd, ʿUthmān, Ṭalḥa and al-Zubayr saw him, and they said to Abū Bakr: 'Have you believed and affirmed Muḥammad (ﷺ)?' Abū Bakr said: 'Yes.' So they came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and they believed and affirmed. Then God, may He be exalted, revealed, saying to Saʿd: ﴿And follow the way of him who turns back to Me﴾, meaning Abū Bakr, may God be pleased with him."

Ibn Jurayj said, as reported from him by Ibn al-Mundhir: ﴿who turns back﴾ is Muḥammad, peace and blessings be upon him. Others, and not one alone, said: it is he (ﷺ) and the believers. The apparent meaning is generality.

[Page 88]

"O my son" etc. — this is a reference back to the story, mentioning the rest of what is meant to be related of Luqman's counsels, following the establishment, at its opening, of the prohibition of association (shirk) and its emphasis through the parenthetical clause. ﴿Indeed it﴾, i.e., the quality of wrongdoing and of goodness, is understood from the context. It was also said — and it is as you see — that "it" refers to what you asked about: it has been related that Luqman's son asked him: "Do you see that a grain falls into the depths of the sea; will Allah the Exalted know of it?" So he said: "O my son, indeed it" — i.e., what you asked about — ﴿if it be the weight of a grain of mustard seed﴾, i.e., if it be in smallness like a mustard seed. The mithqal (mithqal, the weight by which other things are measured, because their weights are equal) is known in common usage.

Naafi', al-A'raj and Abu Ja'far read "mithqalu" with the nominative, on the basis that the pronoun refers to the matter (al-qissah), and "taku" (تَكُ) is the imperfect of kana in its complete (intransitive) usage; the feminine marking is due to the feminine gender of the noun added as subject, as in the verse of al-A'sha:

"And it chokes with the word you have spread, just as the spear's blade chokes with blood."

Or the feminization is due to interpreting it as "weight" (zinah), or as "the good deed and the bad deed." ﴿Then it will be in a rock, or in the heavens, or in the earth﴾, i.e., then it will be, together with being in the utmost degree of smallness and insignificance, in the most hidden and most secure place, such as the hollow of a rock, or wherever it may be in the upper world or the lower world. It was also said: in the most hidden and most secure place, such as the hollow of a rock, or its highest part, like the convex surface of the heavens, or its lowest part, like the concave surface of the earth. It is not hidden that the wording gives no indication of specifying the convex or the concave; perhaps the context requires it, since the purpose is hyperbole.

The saying of the Exalted, "in the heavens," does not contradict this, because they are mentioned according to locality, or for the sake of correspondence (mushakalah), or "in" here means "upon," and it is expressed with it to indicate firm establishment. Along with this apparent meaning, there is what has preceded. In al-Bahr (al-Bahr al-Muhit): he begins with what the listener first conceives, which is the being of a thing in a rock, namely what is hard of stone and difficult to extract from; then he follows it with the upper world, which is stranger to the listener; then he follows it with what is the place of things for the witness, namely the earth. It was also said: the hiddenness of a thing and the difficulty of reaching it come by way of its extreme smallness, its remoteness from the seer, and its being in darkness, and its being shielded.
