So "the weight of a grain of mustard seed" is an indication of extreme smallness; "in a rock" is an indication of the screen; "in the heavens" is an indication of distance; "in the earth" is an indication of darkness, for the interior of the earth is the most darkened of places. Or it may be said: the rock here is not a specific rock. From Ibn Abbas and al-Suddi it is reported that this rock is the one upon which the earth rests. Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn Abbas that the earth is upon a fish (nun), the fish is upon a sea, the sea is upon a green rock, from whose greenness the water's greenness comes, the rock is upon the horn of a bull, and that bull is upon the dry earth (al-thara), and none knows what is beneath the dry earth except Allah the Exalted.

Some interpreters explained the rock as this very rock. It was also said: it is a rock in the wind. Ibn Atiyyah said: all of these are weak, their chains not being established; the meaning of the speech is only hyperbole and thoroughness in making it understood, i.e., His power, Mighty and Majestic, reaches whatever is within the folds of a rock, and whatever is in the heaven, and whatever is in the earth. End of quote. My own view, however, is that these reports and their like are fabricated; the earth is only within the embrace of water, the water is only within the hollow of air, and the matter ends at the Throne of the Merciful, Majestic and Exalted, and all of it is in the grasp of the power of Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

Abd al-Rahim al-Jazari read "fatakinn" (فَتَكِنَّ) with a kasrah on the kaf and a shaddah with fatha on the nun; Muhammad ibn Abi Fajjah al-Ba'labakki read "fatukan" (فَتُكَنَّ) with a dammah on the ta and fatha on the kaf, the nun shaddah; Qatadah read "fatakin" (فَتَكِنْ) with fatha on the ta, kasrah on the kaf, and sukun on the nun, and this reading is also related from al-Jazari. The verb in all of these is from wakana, when the bird settles in its nest (wakrah), i.e., its nest. So there is metaphor or a sent (majazi mursal) in the speech, as in "mishfar" (lip). The pronoun refers to the one spoken of earlier. It is also permitted that it refers to the son, and the meaning is: if you hide, or conceal, at the time of reckoning, Allah the Exalted will bring you forth. It is not hidden that this does not suit the answer, namely the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Allah will bring it﴾, i.e., will produce it, and will call it to account for it. This is either on its literal sense, or the meaning is that He makes it like something present and witnessed, by its mention and acknowledgment. ﴿Indeed Allah is Subtle﴾, whose knowledge reaches every hidden thing, ﴿Aware﴾, knowing its true nature.

From Qatadah: Subtle in extracting it, Aware of its place of rest. It was also said: Gracious to His servants, so He is gracious in bringing it forth by one of the two disputants; Aware, knowing the hidden things; and that is as you see. The sentence is an explanatory cause justifying the bringing of it. Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ali ibn Rabah al-Lakhmi: when Luqman admonished his son and said, "Indeed it, if it be..." (the verse), he took a grain of mustard seed and brought it to al-Yarmuk, a valley in Syria, and placed it in its side; then he remained as long as Allah willed, then he mentioned it, and extended his hand, and a fly came and placed it in his palm. And Allah knows best.

After He commanded him with tawhid, which is the first thing obligatory upon the responsible person, within the prohibition of shirk, and alerted him to the perfection of Allah's knowledge and power, Mighty and Majestic, He commanded him with prayer, which is the most perfect of acts of worship, being a completion from the aspect of action after its completion from the aspect of belief; so He said, winning him over:

O my son, establish the prayer (﴿يا بُنَيَّ أقِمِ الصَّلاةَ﴾), for the perfecting of yourself. It is related that he said to him: "O my son, when the time of prayer comes, do not delay it for anything; pray it and be relieved of it, for it is a debt. Pray in congregation, even if it is at the tip of a spear-butt (zujj)." ﴿And enjoin what is good and forbid what is evil﴾, for the perfecting of others. The apparent meaning is that the good and the evil are not specific ones.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Jubayr that he said: "﴿Enjoin what is good﴾ means monotheism (tawhid), and ﴿forbid what is evil﴾ means polytheism (shirk)." ﴿And be patient over what befalls you﴾ of hardships and trials, especially in what you have been commanded: establishing the prayer, enjoining what is good, and forbidding what is evil. That the last two require patience over what has been mentioned is evident. As for the first, it is because completing the prayer and guarding it may be difficult, and for this reason God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And indeed it is burdensome except for the humble (khashi'un)﴾ [al-Baqarah: 45]. Ibn Jubayr also said: "Be patient over what befalls you in the matter of enjoining what is good and forbidding what is evil. He means: when you enjoin a good or forbid an evil, and harm and hardship befall you because of that, then be patient over it." ﴿Indeed that﴾, i.e., the patience over what befalls you according to Ibn Jubayr, and this suits the singular form of the demonstrative. The remoteness implied in it indicates the remoteness of its rank in excellence. Or the demonstrative refers to patience and to all that he was commanded to do; the singular is for the interpretation with what has been mentioned, and the remoteness is as you have understood. ﴿Is of the resolute matters (min 'azm al-umur)﴾, i.e., of what God, exalted is He, has resolved and decided as a binding decree. This meaning of resolve ('azm) is among what is attributed to God, exalted is He, and among it is what has come in the "resolutions of God" ('azamat Allah), mighty and majestic is He.

Here the intended sense is the resolved things (al-ma'zum), using the verbal noun in the sense of the passive participle, and the idafah is from the idafat al-sifah ila al-mawsuf (attribution of a qualifier to the thing qualified), i.e., the resolved matters.

It is also permitted that 'azm carries the sense of the active participle, i.e., "one who resolves matters" ('azim al-umur), from 'azama al-amr, meaning he exerted himself and resolved the matters. This is an isnad majazi (metaphorical attribution), like makr al-layl (the night's scheming), not an idafah in the sense of "in." Though it is valid, it has been said: he means of the noble characteristics and the resolutions of the people of prudence who travel the path of salvation. Abu Hayyan preferred that he meant the necessary implications of the obligatory matters. He transmitted from some of them that 'azm is ḥazm in the dialect of Hudhayl, and that ḥazm and 'azm are two roots. What al-Mubarrad said, that the ʿayn was changed into a ḥā', is not valid, since the derivations of each of the two words are regular, so neither is the root of the other. The sentence is a justification for the obligation of compliance with what preceded, and in it there is an emphasis on its importance.

Al-Alusi, *Ruh al-Ma'ani*, on Surah 31, verse 18:

﴿And do not turn your cheek away from people﴾: that is, do not incline it away from them, and do not turn the side of your face toward them as the arrogant do. This is what Ibn 'Abbas said, along with a group of others, and they recited:

"And when the tyrant turned his cheek aside, we straightened him from his inclination, and he became straight."

Here it is from *al-ṣaʿar* (a disease, "ṣaʿar," that afflicts the camel, causing it to twist its neck to one side), meaning *al-ṣayd*. It is used metaphorically for arrogance, as *al-ṣaʿar* is. Ibn Khuwayzimandad said: he was forbidden to humble himself without need, so that he twists his neck. The first explanation is preferred because it fits better with what follows. The *lam* in *lil-nas* ("for people") is causal (*taʿlīliyya*), and the meaning is: do not turn your cheek away out of aversion to people or as a way of cutting them off.

Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read *tuṣāʿir* with an *alif* after the *ṣād*. Al-Jahdari read *tuṣʿir*, the present tense of *aṣʿara*. All of these are one in meaning, like *ʿalāhu*, *ʿālāhu* and *aʿlāhu*.

﴿And do not walk upon the earth﴾, which is the lowest of places in rank, ﴿exultantly﴾: that is, with joy and insolence. *Maraḥan* is a verbal noun (*maṣdar*) standing in the position of a circumstantial qualifier (*ḥāl*) for emphasis, or because it is interpreted as a descriptive word. Alternatively, it is an absolute object (*mafʿūl muṭlaq*) of a deleted verb, "you exult exultantly," and the clause is then in the position of a circumstantial qualifier. Or it is a causative object (*mafʿūl lahu*): "for the sake of exultation." It has also been read as *marihan* with a kasra on the *rāʾ*, as a descriptive word in the position of a circumstantial qualifier. ﴿Indeed, Allah does not love every arrogant boaster﴾: this is a reason for the prohibition or what necessitates it. *Mukhtāl* is from *khuyalāʾ*, which is strutting in walking out of pride. Al-Raghib said: arrogance is the imagining of a virtue that appears to a person in himself. From this the word *khayl* (horses) is derived, because it is said that no one rides a horse without finding in himself a sense of pride. *Fakhūr* is from *fakhr*, which is boasting about things external to a person, such as wealth and status. This includes a person enumerating what he has been given, since it is evident that this is boasting about wealth. From Mujahid: the *fakhūr* is interpreted as the one who enumerates what he has been given and does not thank Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

In the verse, according to al-Zamakhshari, there is *lafʿ wa-nashr* (a rhetorical device of folding and unfolding, in which two items are mentioned and then each is matched to its counterpart) in reverse order, since he said: *mukhtāl* corresponds to the one who walks exultantly, and likewise *fakhūr* corresponds to the one who turns his cheek away in arrogance. This is said to be for the sake of the verse-endings (*fawāṣil*, the rhyming ends of verses). That the counsel was not in the Arabic tongue does not preclude this, as is not hidden.

It is also permitted that there is an ordered *lafʿ wa-nashr*, since *ikhtiyāl* (strutting) suits arrogance and self-admiration, and likewise *fakhr* (boasting) suits walking exultantly.

The statement is on the negation of a universal affirmation, and the meaning is a universal negation. It is also permitted that it remains on its apparent meaning. The form *fakhūr* is for the sake of the verse-ending, and because what is disliked of boasting is its abundance, since a little of it is frequently occurring. So Allah, exalted is He, showed kindness by pardoning it, as He showed kindness by permitting the strutting of the warrior between the two lines, and by permitting boasting about things such as wealth for a good purpose.

[Page 91]

﴿Walk with moderation in your gait﴾, after refraining from exultant strutting (*maraḥ*) in it. That is, moderate it between the creeping (*dabīb*, a slow, dragging step) and hurrying, from *al-qaṣd*, which means moderation. Several narrations have come down on this, but most of them have weaknesses that remove them from being valid as evidence, as will not be hidden from anyone who consults *Sharḥ al-Jāmiʿ al-Ṣaghīr* by al-Munawi.

From the Prophet ﷺ: "Hastening in walking removes the radiance (*bahāʾ*) of the believer."

That is, his dignity and his beauty. It produces contempt in the eyes of people, and this seems to be because it indicates lightness. This is closer to the view of al-Munawi, who said that it causes fatigue, which alters the body and bearing.

Ibn Masʿud said: "They used to forbid the *khabab* (a fast, bounding gait) of the Jews and the *dabīb* of the Christians, but [they walked] in a manner between these."

As for what is in *al-Nihayah* that ʿAisha looked at a man who was nearly dying from feigned weakness, and she said, "What is wrong with this one?" It was said, "He is one of the reciters (*qurrāʾ*)." She said, "ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, was the chief of the reciters. When he walked, he walked briskly; when he spoke, he made himself heard; and when he struck, he hurt." So the hurrying intended here is what is above the creeping of one who pretends to be dead, who lowers his voice and minimises his movements, imitating the appearance of the devout, as if he strains to attain the qualities that bring him close to the attributes of the dead, in order to give the impression that he has grown weak from excessive worship. This does not contradict the verse. Likewise, what has been reported describing the Prophet ﷺ, that when he walked he seemed to be descending from a slope, does not contradict it. Nor does the saying of Allah, Exalted is He: ﴿And the servants of the Most Merciful are those who walk upon the earth in humility﴾ [al-Furqan: 63] contradict it, since humility in it does not mean walking like the creeping of an ant.

Some of the distinguished scholars mentioned that what is blameworthy is the habit of hurrying to excess. Al-Sakhawi said: "The place of censure of hurrying is when slowness of pace does not threaten missing a religious matter." But you know that hurrying which removes khushuʿ (humble attentiveness) in order to catch a rak'ah with the imam, for example, is among what they said is not to be done, so do not be heedless.

From Mujahid: moderation in walking is humility in it. It was also said: the gaze is placed at the place of the foot. What is relied upon is what has preceded.

It has been read as **"wa-aqṣid"** with a hamza (*qaṭʿ al-hamzah*), and Ibn Khalawayh attributed this reading to the Hijazi reciters. It comes from *aqṣada al-rāmī*, when the archer aims his arrow toward the target and directs it at it in order to hit it. That is: aim (*sadded*) in your walk. The meaning is: walk a good walk. It seems that the intention is moderation between the quick walk and the slow walk, so that the two readings agree.

﴿And lower your voice﴾, that is, reduce it and diminish it. It is said: "So-and-so *yaghuḍḍu* (lowers) so-and-so," when he belittles him, diminishes him, and lowers his rank.

In *al-Bahr* it is said: *al-ghaḍḍ* is the restraining of the sharpness of a thing, such as the voice or the gaze. It is used transitively by itself, as in the line:

*So lower the glance, for you are of Numayr.*

And transitively with *min*, as is clearly the statement of al-Jawhari: "He lowered (*ghadda*) from his voice." The apparent view is that what is in the verse is of the second type. Some have strained to make *min* here partitive, and another claimed that it is redundant in an affirmative sentence.

The Arabs used to take pride in loudness of voice and praise it in the pre-Islamic period. From this is the saying of the poet:

*Loud of speech, loud of sneezing,*
*loud of bearing, loud of gifts.*

*And he steps over the ʿamm (his people) with the stride of the ostrich,*
*and he rises above men with a general form.*

The wisdom in lowering the voice, as commanded, is that it is more beneficial to the speaker and more agreeable to the listener's soul and understanding.

﴿Indeed, the most hateful of voices﴾, that is, the most ugly of them. It is said: "a hateful face" (*wajhun munkar*), that is, an ugly one. In *al-Bahr* it is said: it is an *afʿal* formed from the passive form of the verb, like their saying *ashghal min dhāt al-niḥyayn* (busier than the owner of the two jars). Its formation from this is irregular. Some said: that is, the hardest of them on the hearing and the most repellent, from *nakura* with a *ḍamma* (*nakārah*). From this is the verse ﴿On the day when the caller calls to a thing unfamiliar﴾ [al-Qamar: 6], that is, a hard matter that is not known.

By "voices" is meant the voices of animals, that is, the most hateful of the voices of animals ﴿is the braying of donkeys﴾. *Ḥamīr* is a plural of *ḥimār*, as the lexicographers stated explicitly, and no one disagreed about this except al-Suhayli, who said that it is *faʿīl* as a collective noun (*ism jamʿ*), like *ʿabīd* (servants). The lexicographers may also apply the term "plural" to a collective noun.

The sentence is a justification for the command to lower the voice, in the most eloquent and emphatic manner, since those who raise their voices are compared to donkeys, which are a proverbial example of severe blame and abuse. Their voices are likened to braying, which begins with an exhalation and ends with an inhalation. Then the statement is stripped of the word of comparison and presented in the form of a metaphor. In this there is the exaggeration in blame and disparagement, the excess in discouraging raising the voice, and the encouragement against it.

The singular "voice" together with the plural of what it is attributed to indicates the strength of the resemblance among the braying of donkeys, so that they seem to be one single voice, which is the most hateful of voices.

Al-Zamakhshari said: this is because the intention is not to describe the state of the voice of each individual member of this species, so that it would be plural, but rather to describe the voice of this species among the voices of all other species. It was said: according to this, the appropriate form for the voice of the donkey would be the singular for the attributed noun. It was answered that the purpose of the plural is generalisation and exaggeration in repulsion, for when the donkeys agree upon a voice, it becomes most hateful. It was objected that this implies that the hatefulness lies in agreement and not in singularity, which is not appropriate to the context. It was answered that one does not pay attention to such an imagined notion.

It was also said: the attributed voice was not made plural because it is a verbal noun (*maṣdar*), and this cannot be dualised, nor pluralised when the types are not intended, as in ﴿the most hateful of voices﴾. So reflect.

The apparent view is that the saying of Allah, Exalted is He, ﴿Indeed, the most hateful of voices is the braying of donkeys﴾ is part of the words of Luqman to his son, to deter him from raising his voice. It was also said that it is part of the words of Allah, Exalted is He. The counsel of Luqman ends with the words:

﴿And lower your voice﴾. By this, Glorified is He, responded to the polytheists who used to boast of loudness of voice and raising it, although that disturbs the listener and strikes the ear-canal forcefully, and may perhaps tear the membrane that is inside the ear. He, Mighty and Majestic, made clear that their likeness in raising their voices is the likeness of donkeys, and that the likeness of their voices which they raise is the likeness of their braying in intensity together with a dreadful ugliness. This is what is fitting to be taken as the point of comparison, not the absence of mention of Allah, Exalted is He, as is imagined on the basis of what Ibn Abi Hatim related from Sufyan al-Thawri, who said: "The cry of every thing is its glorification (*tasbīḥ*), except the donkey," because the point of comparison should be an apparent attribute, and the absence of mention in the donkey's voice is not such. Moreover, we do not accept the soundness of this report, for there is much in it. Similar to it is what has spread among the ignorant, that the braying of a donkey is a curse upon the Shiʿa, who continually bray by reviling the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them. Such things are among the superstitions which the hearing rejects, except the hearing of the long-eared one.

The apparent view is that what is meant by lowering the voice is lowering it during speech and conversation. It was said: lowering the voice is general, so it includes lowering it during sneezing, and one should not raise one's voice during it if it is possible to avoid raising it. This is what has been reported from Abu ʿAbd Allah, may Allah be pleased with him, which indicates it. Furthermore, lowering the voice is praiseworthy unless a legal reason calls for the opposite.

He followed the command to moderate the walk with the command to lower the voice, because one often reaches what is desired by the voice after being unable to reach it by walking. So it is said. Some have gone too far in discussing these two commands. They said: the first is an indication of moderation in actions, and the second is an indication of guarding against superfluous speech and moderation in words. And the saying of Allah, Exalted is He, ﴿If it be the weight of a mustard seed﴾ etc. was taken as an indication of the correction of the inner conscience. This is, as you see, far-fetched.

Ibn Abi ʿAbla read **"aṣwāt al-ḥamīr"** (the voices of the donkeys) in the plural, without the emphatic *lām*.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 31, verse 20:**

﴿Have you not seen that Allah has subjected to you whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth?﴾ This returns to the practices of those (who came) before the story of Luqman, in the address to the polytheists, and it is a rebuke for their persistence in what they were upon despite their witnessing the proofs of tawhid (the oneness of God). As for "taskhir" (subjection), al-Raghib said: it is driving a thing, by compulsion, toward the specific purpose proper to it. In Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim, the meaning of it is either: making the subjected thing such that it benefits the one to whom it is subjected, more general than being submissive to him, so that he disposes of it however he wills and uses it however he desires, like most things on earth that are subjected to humans and used by them, from the inanimate and the animals; or it is not like that, but rather it is a cause for the attainment of his purpose without his having any role in its use, like all the things in the heavens by which the interests of the servants are bound, in livelihood or in the hereafter. As for making it submissive to the command, made subservient, with the meaning of "lakum" (for you) being "for your sake":
صفحة 93
then indeed all that is in the heavens and the earth of created beings is subjected to Allah, the Exalted, bringing about the benefits of creation and what man uses as he wishes. And although it is subjected to him according to outward appearance, in reality it is subjected to Allah, Mighty and Majestic. ﴿And He has lavished﴾, i.e., completed and widened, ﴿upon you His blessings﴾. "Ni'am" is the plural of "ni'mah," and it originally means a pleasant state, for the pattern "fi'lah," like "jilsah" and "rukbah," denotes a form (of the action). Then it was used for what is agreeable among matters that cause that state, by way of attributing the effect to the cause. In the sense of this, they said: it is what is benefited from and enjoyed. Some of them added: "and whose outcome is praised." Others said: there is no need for this addition, because pleasure, according to the verifiers (muhaqqiqun), is a thing whose outcome is praised. On this basis, there is no blessing from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, upon a disbeliever. Al-Tibi reported from al-Imam that he said: a blessing is an expression for a benefit conferred by way of kindness to another. Some say: a good benefit conferred by way of kindness to another. They said: we added the qualifier "good" because a blessing merits gratitude, and if it is ugly it does not merit gratitude. The truth is that this qualifier is not valid, because it is possible for gratitude to be merited for kindness even if the act is forbidden, since the aspect of gratitude is that it is a kindness, and the aspect of meriting blame and punishment is the prohibition. So what is the impediment to the two being combined? Do you not see that the sinner merits gratitude for his benefaction and blame for his disobedience to Allah, the Exalted? So why should it not be the case here as well? As for our saying "benefit," it is because pure harm is not a blessing. As for our saying "conferred by way of kindness," it is because if it were a benefit, but the agent intended by it his own benefit and not the benefit of the one to whom it is done, it would not be a blessing; this is like one who is kind to his slave-girl in order to profit from her. End of quote. From this the ruling on the addition "and whose outcome is praised" is known. ﴿Outward and inward﴾, i.e., sensible and intelligible, known to you and unknown. It is narrated from Mujahid: the outward blessing is the manifestation of Islam and victory over the enemies, and the inward is the reinforcement from the angels, peace be upon them. It is narrated from al-Dahhak: the outward is beauty of form, the stature's height, and the balance of the limbs; the inward is knowledge. It has been said: the outward is sight, hearing, tongue and the rest of the limbs; the inward is the heart, intellect and understanding. It has been said: the outward is the blessings of this world, and the inward is the blessings of the hereafter. It has been said: the outward is such as the sending of messengers, the revelation of books, the granting of success in accepting Islam, adopting it, steadfastness upon the path of truthfulness, and adherence to servanthood; and the inward is what reached the spirits in the world of atoms (alam al-dharr) of the sprinkling of the light of the Light, and the first of the rain is a drop, then it pours forth.

Some of the Imamiyya (Twelver Shi'a) transmitted from al-Baqir, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: the outward is the Prophet, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him, and what he brought of knowledge of Allah, the Exalted, and His tawhid; and the inward is our wilayah (guardianship/allegiance) of the People of the House and the bond of our love. The generalization that we pointed to first is more appropriate. However, al-Bayhaqi narrated in Shu'ab al-Iman, from 'Ata', who said: "I asked Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, about His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and He has lavished upon you His blessings, outward and inward﴾. He said: this is among the treasures of my knowledge. I asked the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him, and he said: As for the outward, it is what He has fashioned of your creation; and as for the inward, it is what He has concealed of your nakedness (awrah). Had He revealed it, your family would have shunned you, and others besides them."

And in another narration, related by Ibn Mardawayh, al-Daylami, al-Bayhaqi and Ibn al-Najjar, from Ibn 'Abbas, that he said: "I asked the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him, about His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and He has lavished﴾ etc. He said: As for the outward, it is Islam, and what He has fashioned of your creation, and what He has lavished upon you of His provision; and as for the inward, it is what He has concealed of the faults of your deeds."

If what has been mentioned is authentic, then one should not turn away from it to generalization, unless it is said: the purpose of explaining the outward and inward by what we have explained is illustration (tamthil), and this is the apparent meaning, not restriction (takhsis); otherwise the two reports would contradict each other.

Furthermore, the apparent meaning of these two reports requires that sin, which is expressed in the first as "what He has concealed of the nakedness" and in the second as "what He has concealed of the faults of the deed," be a blessing. We have not found in their statements an explicit declaration of applying this term to it. It follows from this that whoever's sins are many, the blessings of Allah, Exalted is He, upon him are many,
صفحة 94
so the intended meaning is that the inward blessing is the concealment of what has been concealed of the nakedness and the faults of deeds. They did not state this, relying on the clarity of the matter. Some reports do indicate this. Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi related from Muqatil that he said regarding the verse: "outward" is Islam, and "inward" is His concealment of your sins from you. Indeed, in some narrations of the second report: "As for what is inward, it is the concealment of the faults of your deed."

It is also permissible that "ma" in "ma satara" in the two reports be a verbal particle (masdariyyah), and "min" be attached to "satara," not explanatory of "ma."

Yahya ibn 'Umarah read "wa-asbagha" with the sad (ص), and it is the dialect of the Banu Kalb, who replace the sin (س) with sad (ص) when it is combined with one of the emphatic letters, namely ghayn, kha', and qaf; so they say "salakha" for "salakha" (to skin), "saqara" for "saqara" (to scorch), and "sa'igh" for "sa'igh" (palatable). There is no difference in this whether a separator comes between them or not. The apparent statement of some of them is that there is also no difference whether the sin precedes one of those letters or follows it. Another stipulated that the sin must precede. Al-Khafaji mentioned that it is a regular substitution.

Some of the Seven Readers and Zayd ibn 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with both of them, read "ni'mah" (singular), and it was read "ni'matahu" (singular with a pronoun) and with the plural form. The justification for the singular is the intended genus, as was said regarding His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And if you count the blessings of Allah, you will not enumerate them﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: whoever reads "ni'mah" (singular) means what He has given them of tawhid; and whoever reads "ni'am" (plural) means all that He has bestowed upon them. The first is more appropriate. The accusative of ﴿outward and inward﴾ in the reading with the definite article is a circumstantial accusative (hal), and in the reading with indefiniteness it is an adjectival accusative (sifah).

﴿And among the people is one who disputes﴾, from "jidal," which is debate, namely mutual discourse by way of contention and overpowering. Its origin is from "jadaltu al-habl," meaning I tightened its twisting; as the two disputants each twists his companion away from his opinion. It has been said: the original meaning of jidal is wrestling and throwing one's companion onto the "jadalah," which is hard ground. It seems that the sentence is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun referring to Him, as it has been said. That is: Have you not seen that Allah, Glorified is He, did what He did of matters indicating His oneness, Glorified is He, and His power, Mighty and Majestic? And the situation of the people is that one who contends and disputes, like al-Nadr ibn al-Harith and Ubayy ibn Khalaf, who used to dispute with the Prophet ﷺ ﴿concerning Allah﴾, i.e., concerning His tawhid, Mighty and Majestic, and His attributes, exalted is His majesty, like the polytheists who deny His oneness, Glorified is He, and the generality of His power, exalted is His power, and its comprehensiveness for the resurrection. He did not say "fihi" (concerning it) as a substitute for "fi Allah" (concerning Allah), by returning the pronoun to the Glorious Name in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Have you not seen that Allah has subjected to you﴾, to magnify the matter of disputation. ﴿Without knowledge﴾, derived from a rational proof. ﴿Nor guidance﴾, referring to a messenger from whom it is taken. It is permissible to make "guidance" the very messenger as an intensification, but this is far-fetched. ﴿Nor a book﴾ sent down by Allah, the Exalted, ﴿illuminating﴾, i.e., possessing light; and what is meant by it is clear in its indication of the intended meaning. It has been said: a deliverer from the darkness of ignorance and error. Rather, they dispute merely by blind imitation (taqlid), as He, Glorified is He, said:

﴿And when it is said to them﴾, that is, to those who dispute, and the plural is in view of meaning, ﴿"Follow what Allah has sent down," they say, "Rather, we follow what we found our fathers upon."﴾ They mean the worship of what their fathers worshipped besides Allah, Mighty and Majestic. This is evident in prohibiting ((taqlid) (blind imitation)) in the fundamentals of religion (uṣūl al-dīn). The question is disputed. What the majority held, and what Imam al-Razi and al-Amidi preferred, is that taqlid is not permissible in the fundamentals, and that reflection (naẓar) is obligatory. What ʿUbayd Allah ibn al-Hasan al-ʿAnbari and a group held is that it is permissible. Some of them may have said that it is obligatory for the accountable person, and that reflection and independent effort (ijtihād) in it are forbidden. In any case, the beliefs of a sound (muḥiqq) imitator are valid, though he is sinful for abandoning reflection according to the first view. It is reported from al-Ashʿari that his faith is not valid. Ustadh Abu al-Qasim al-Qushayri said: "This is a lie attributed to him, because it entails declaring the common people to be disbelievers, and they are the majority of the believers." The verified position is that if taqlid is accepting the statement of another without proof, with the possibility of doubt and suspicion, such that the imitator does not hold it with certainty, then his faith is definitely not sufficient, because there is no faith with even the slightest hesitation in it. But if it is free of that, it becomes certainty, and it suffices according to al-Ashʿari and others. Abu Hashim disagreed, saying: "It does not suffice; rather, reflection is necessary for the validity of faith." Al-Khafaji mentioned that there is no disagreement about the impermissibility of imitating someone who is not known to be relying on a true proof. The apparent sense of the condemnation of those who dispute without knowledge, guidance, or a Book is that in reflection, a true transmitted proof suffices, just as a rational proof suffices.

﴿Even if the Shaytan was calling them﴾, that is, calling their fathers, not themselves, as has been said. The basis of the denial of following is that those who were followed were followers of the devils. This is supported by His, Exalted be He, saying: ﴿Even though their fathers did not understand anything and were not guided?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 170], after His saying: ﴿Rather, we follow what we found our fathers upon﴾ [al-Baqarah: 170]. From this it is known how the pronoun refers to the group, that is, those disputants and their fathers, ﴿to the punishment of the Blaze﴾, that is, to what it leads to, or what results from it, of associating partners with Allah, denying that His power extends to the resurrection, and similar misguidance. It is also permitted that "the punishment of the Blaze" be kept in its literal sense. The interrogative is for denial, and amazement is understood from the context, or it is for amazement, and denial is understood from the context. The waw is circumstantial (ḥāliyyah), and the meaning is: "Would they follow them while the Shaytan was calling them?" That is, in the state of the Shaytan calling them to the punishment. It is also permitted that the waw is coordinating (ʿāṭifah) upon an implied element, meaning: "Would they follow them if the Shaytan were not calling them to the punishment, and even if he were calling them to it?" These are two well-known views concerning the waw entering upon (law) of concession (lau al-waṣliyyah) and similar particles. Likewise, regarding whether it needs an answer (jawāb), there are two views: one holds that it needs it, and one holds that it does not, since it has come out of the meaning of conditional. Whoever holds the first view estimates it here as: "They would not follow them." This is unobjectionable if the waw is coordinating. As for if it is circumstantial, some claimed that this is not possible, but there is room for discussion. The discussion of this noble verse has already passed, so recall it.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 31, verse 22:

﴿And whoever submits his face to Allah﴾ — that is, who entrusts to Him, may He be exalted, all of his affairs, and turns to Him, glorified is He, with his heart and his body. Thus islam (submission) is like taslim (surrender), which is entrusting (tafwid). "Face" means the essence (dhat), and the expression is a metonymy (kinaya) for what we have indicated: the handing over of all affairs to Him, may He be exalted, and complete turning toward Him, mighty and majestic is He. Islam may also be construed with the particle lam, intentionally, to convey the meaning of sincerity (ikhlas).

ʿAli, may Allah ennoble his face, and al-Sulami, and ʿAbd Allah ibn Muslim ibn Yasar read ﴿yuslim﴾ with a doubled lam, from taslim. It is more famous in the sense of entrusting (tafwid) than islam. ﴿while he is a doer of good﴾ — that is, in his deeds. The clause is in the position of a circumstantial phrase (hal).

﴿Then he has grasped the most trustworthy handhold﴾ — he has held on in the most complete manner to the most reliable of the means one can hold on to. This is a compound allegorical comparison (tashbih tamthili), in which the state of one who relies upon Allah, may He be mighty and majestic, who entrusts to Him all his affairs while being a doer of good in his deeds, is likened to one who has climbed a towering mountain or let himself down from it and then grasped the most secure handhold of a strong rope whose severance is trusted to be impossible. It is also permitted that there is a metaphor in the singular term "the most trustworthy handhold", by likening beneficial reliance (tawakkul) whose outcome is praiseworthy to it, so that the term is borrowed for it. ﴿And to Allah is the outcome of affairs﴾ — that is, they all return to Him, mighty and majestic is He, not to anyone else, exalted is His majesty. Therefore no one other than Him, exalted and high is He, has any disposal over them by command and prohibition, or reward and punishment. So He, glorified is He, will recompense this one who relies upon Him with the best of recompense. It has been said: He will recompense each of this one who relies upon Him and that one who disputes with what befits them in accordance with wisdom. The (al) in "al-umur" (the affairs) is for comprehensiveness (istighraq). It has been said that it may bear the sense of a known reference (ahd), on the basis that the intended affairs are the matters mentioned of disputation and what follows them. The fronting of ﴿ila Allah﴾ (to Allah) is for restriction (hasr), as a refutation of the disbelievers in their assumption that their gods are a point of return for some affairs.

Page 96

Some scholars have chosen that it is for the glorification of the Divine Majesty (jalala) and for maintaining the rhyme (fasila), supposing that comprehensiveness is sufficient without restriction. This is not so.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 31, verse 23:

﴿And whoever disbelieves, let not his disbelief grieve you﴾. That is: let that not concern you (*yuhimmannaka*) ﴿to Us﴾, not to other than Us, ﴿is their return﴾, their return by resurrection on the Day of Judgment, ﴿and We will inform them of what they did﴾, that is, of their deeds, or of what they did in the world of disbelief and disobedience, by punishment and retribution. It was also said:

Their return to Us in both abodes (this world and the Hereafter), so We will requite them by destruction and punishment. The first is more apparent. In any case, the clause is in the position of a reason (*ta'lil*), as if it were said:

Let not the disbelief of the one who disbelieves concern you, because We will take vengeance on him and punish him for his deed, or for what he did. The plural in the three pronouns is according to the meaning of *man* (whoever), just as the singular in the first is according to its wording. It was read in the seven (canonical readings): ﴿wa-la yuḥzinka﴾ (with *yuḥzinka* from *aḥzana*), the imperfect of *aḥzana*, a derived form of *ḥazina*, the intransitive. Its intransitivity is assumed so that the transitive form has a purpose. *Ḥazina* and *aḥzana* are two dialects. Al-Yazidi said: *ḥazinahu* is the dialect of Quraysh and *aḥzanahu* is the dialect of Tamim, and both have been read. Al-Zamakhshari mentioned that what is most common in usage is the past tense of the verbs and the imperfect of the triliteral, and the responsibility for that rests on him. ﴿Indeed, Allah is Knower of what is within the breasts﴾. This is a reason for the "informing," which is expressed as recompense. That is, He (glorified is He) will requite them, because He, mighty and majestic, is Knower of hearts, so what then do you suppose about other than them?

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 31, verse 24:

﴿We give them enjoyment for a little﴾ — a little enjoyment, or for a little time, since what passes away is little in comparison with what endures. ﴿Then We will drive them to a harsh punishment﴾ — heavy upon them with the heaviness of huge, thick bodies. The meaning of "driving" (al-idtirar), i.e. compulsion (al-ilja'), is that We obligate them to that severe punishment in the manner of one who is compelled and cannot free himself from what he has been forced into. In al-Intisaf, the explanation of this compulsion is what is in the hadith, that because of the severity of what they endure from the Fire, they seek coolness, so zamharir (freezing cold) is sent upon them, and it becomes more painful for them than the blaze. So they wish for the return of the blaze out of compulsion; it is a choice born of compulsion. And with the hem of this eloquence al-Kindi clung when he said:

They see death before them and behind them, so they choose, and death is a compulsion.

It has also been said: the meaning is that We add to the burning the pressing and the constriction. So do not be heedless.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 31, verse 25:

﴿And if you asked them, "Who created the heavens and the earth?" they would surely say, "Allah."﴾ That is, Allah the Exalted created them. It is also permissible that the implied construction be "Allah created them," but the first (reading) is preferable, as has been explained in its proper place. Their saying this is due to the extreme clarity of the matter, to the point that they were compelled to acknowledge it. ﴿Say: "All praise is for Allah"﴾ over their being held to this and being forced to acknowledge what necessitates the invalidity of their associating others with Him, exalted is His majesty, in worship, which none deserves except the Creator and the true Bestower of blessings.

It is also permissible to take the thing praised as being the making of the proofs of monotheism such that even the obstinate cannot deny them. ﴿But most of them do not know﴾ that this binds them. It has been said: in it there is a fine intensification (iyghal hasan), as if He, glory be to Him, said: their ignorance has reached the point that they do not know what the praise of Allah is for in this context. The complete discussion of a parallel verse in Surat al-'Ankabut has already passed, so recall it.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 31, verse 26:

﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth﴾ in creation, dominion, and disposal, with no one besides Him, Mighty and Majestic, having independent authority or any partnership in them. Therefore none deserves worship in them other than Him, glorified and exalted, in any way whatsoever. This is a refutation of their belief from another angle, because what is owned cannot be a partner to its owner. How then could it deserve what is rightfully His, such as worship and other things? ﴿Indeed, Allah is the Self-Sufficient﴾ above everything, ﴿the Praiseworthy﴾, who deserves praise even if no one at all praises Him, Mighty and Exalted. Or He is the one praised in deed, whom every creature praises through the tongue of its condition. It seems that this sentence is an answer to what may come to some sick minds, namely: is the belonging of what is in the heavens and the earth to Him, Mighty and Majestic, due to His need of it, glorified be He?
Page 97
The answer is a denial of need in the most emphatic way. It would have sufficed in the answer to say: "Indeed Allah is Self-Sufficient," but the sentence was given in a form that includes exclusivity (restriction) for emphasis. "The Praiseworthy" was also brought as an affirmation of what it conveys of the denial of need, by indicating that He, exalted, is a benefactor to whatever is other than Him, glorified be He, or that He is characterized by all the attributes of perfection. So reflect deeply.

Al-Tibi said: the saying of the Exalted, (To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth), is a belittling of them and a showing that He, exalted, is independent of them, and of their praise and their worship. For this reason He, glorified be He, gave the reason with His saying:

﴿Indeed, Allah is the Self-Sufficient﴾, i.e., independent of the praise of those who praise, ﴿the Praiseworthy﴾, i.e., the one deserving praise, even if they do not praise Him, Mighty and Majestic.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 31, verse 27 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And if whatever is in the earth of trees were pens﴾ – meaning: if it were established that what is in the earth of trees were pens. Here "inna" (that) and what follows it is the subject (fa'il) of a verb "thabata" (was established) which is implied, by the evidence that "inna" indicates establishment and confirmation. This is the view of al-Mubarrad. Sibawayh said that this (dhalika) is a mubtada' (subject) which does not need a predicate (khabar), because the predicate and the subject that follow it are mentioned after it. It was also said: it is a mubtada' whose khabar is implied before it. Ibn 'Usfur said: it is after it. And "ma fi al-ard" (what is in the earth) is the ism of "inna", and "min shajarah" (of trees) is an explanation (bayan) for "ma", or for the pronoun returning to it in the adverbial phrase (zarf), so it is in the position of a circumstantial (hal) from it or from him, meaning: if it were established that what settled in the earth, being of a tree, [were pens]. "Aqlam" (pens) is the khabar of "inna". Abu Hayyan said: In this is evidence for the claim of al-Zamakhshari and some non-Arabs who support his view, that the khabar of "inna" which comes after "law" cannot be a solid noun (ism jamid) nor a derived noun (ism mushtaq), but must be a verb, and this is false, since the language of the Arabs is full of the contrary. The poet said:
"Had it been a sparrow, I would have thought it a marked one calling slaves and...."
And another said:
"How pleasant is life if only the man were a stone, against which the calamities turn aside while it remains unbroken."
And other examples besides these. It was objected that the condition that its khabar be a verb applies only when it is a derived noun, so "aqlam" here is not an objection, nor what is mentioned in the two verses. As for the saying of God Most High: ﴿Had they been in the desert [among the Bedouins]﴾ [al-Ahzab: 20], here "law" is for wishing, and the discussion concerns the khabar of "inna" which follows the conditional "law". The meaning of "shajarah" (a tree) is every tree. An indefinite noun may be general in an affirmative statement when the context requires it, as in the saying of God Most High: ﴿A soul will know what it has presented﴾ [al-Takwir: 14], and the saying of Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, to a man from the people of Syria, when he asked him about a muhrim who kills a locust, whether he should give a date in charity as a ransom for it? ("A date is better than a locust"), according to what a group has chosen. We do not accept that there is a contradiction between this generality and this singular "ta'" (the feminine marker). It is as if it was said: "Had every tree on the earth been pens," etc. The fact that every tree is pens is by consideration of its parts or its branches, so the meaning is interpreted as: had the parts or branches of every tree on the earth been pens, etc. What makes it good to intend generality in cases like this one is that the statement in which the indefinite noun occurs is a conditional with "law". For the conditional in general has a closeness to negation, so what do you think of it when it is conditional with this particle? Although here it does not have its famous meaning of the absence of the answer because the condition is absent, or the reverse; rather it indicates the establishment of the answer, or is a conditional particle for the future, as is detailed in al-Mughni. The choice of "shajarah" over "ashjar" or "shajar" is because speech on it is further from considering distribution, by which each tree among the trees or the tree would be a pen, which would undermine what the context requires of hyperbole through the abundance of His words, exalted is His majesty. In al-Bahr: this is among the cases where the singular is placed in the position of the plural and the indefinite in the position of the definite. Its parallels are: ﴿Whatever sign We abrogate﴾ [al-Baqarah: 106]; ﴿Whatever mercy Allah opens to people﴾ [Fatir: 2]; ﴿And to Allah prostrates whatever is in the heavens and whatever is in the earth of living creatures﴾ [al-Nahl: 49]; and the saying of the Arabs: "This is the first knight" and "This is the most excellent scholar," meaning the signs, the mercies, the creatures, and the first of the knights and the most excellent of the scholars. The indefinite singular is mentioned and by it is meant the meaning of the plural with the definite article, which is a well-known path in Arabic speech. Likewise it is estimated here: of the trees (shajarat), or of the trees (ashjar). End quote. So do not be heedless.

Al-Zamakhshari said: He, glorified is He, said "shajarah" in the singular, not the collective noun "shajar", because the intention is to detail the trees tree by tree, so that not one of the kind of trees remains, nor a single one, except that it has been made into pens. It was objected that the singular conveying detail without repetition is not a known usage; the known usage is conveying that detail by repetition, as in: "They came to me man by man." Reflect on this. The choice of the paucity plural "aqlam" (pens), though the plurality of abundance would be more fitting to the context, is because no plural other than it is known for "qalam", and "qilam" is not in common use, so its use is not good. "And the sea" (al-bahr): meaning the surrounding sea; the article is for specific reference (al-'ahd), because it is what comes first to mind, and because it is the singular representing the complete. It may be applied to its branches and to the great rivers such as the Tigris and the Euphrates. It is permitted to intend the genus. The first is perhaps more eloquent. ﴿Which is extended by it after it﴾, meaning: after its exhaustion. It was also said: from behind it. ﴿Seven seas﴾, supposed ones, each of which is like it in breadth, encompassing, and abundance of water. By "seven" is meant abundance, to the extent that it includes a hundred and a thousand, for example, not the specific known number, as in His saying, upon him be prayer and peace: "The believer eats in one stomach, and the disbeliever eats in seven intestines." It was chosen for this because it is a complete number, as you know from the discussion of His saying: ﴿Those are ten complete﴾. Many of the counted things that have importance, such as the heavens, the wandering planets, the true climes, and the days of the week, and so on, are limited to seven. So perhaps the mention of it here rather than seventy, which is used figuratively for abundance, is also a symbol of the greatness and importance of those seas. Since it was not originally laid down for this purpose, but for the known small number, its specification (abhur) came with the paucity form rather than "buhur", though it is intended only for abundance, in order to create correspondence between the two words. Just as "seven" is used figuratively for abundance, so "abhur" is used figuratively for it too. After making what is in the earth of trees into pens, the apparent expectation would be to say: "and the sea is ink." But what occurs in this sublime structure is that "yamudduhu" (extends it) dispenses with the mention of ink, for it derives from your saying: "madda al-dawah" and "amaddaha," meaning he made it possessed of ink and added to its ink. So there is an indication of ink along with what increases the hyperbole, namely depicting continuous replenishment, state after state, as the imperfect form indicates. Thus the sublime structure conveys making the surrounding sea like an inkwell, and making seven seas like it, filled with ink, which pours its ink into it continually without interruption. The nominative "al-bahr" according to what Abu Hayyan preferred is a mubtada', and the clause "yamudduhu" is its khabar, the waw is for the circumstantial, and the clause is a hal from the relative pronoun or the pronoun within its relative clause, meaning: had it been established that what is in the earth of trees were pens while the sea is extended by seven seas. The clause lacking a pronoun of the one in the state does no harm, for the waw provides a link which does not fall short of a pronoun, because it indicates concomitance. Al-Zamakhshari pointed out that this clause and similar ones, such as his saying:
"And I go out early while the birds are in their nests, with a swift, lean horse, bounding..."
and "I came while the army was lined up," are among the circumstantial phrases whose rule is the rule of adverbs, because they have the same meaning: "I came while the army was lined up," for instance, and "I came at the time of the army's lining up," are one. Since an adverb connects with what precedes it by its dependence on it, even when it has no pronoun in it, and when it becomes a hal it takes a pronoun, so what resembles it is as if it had a fixed pronoun. Abu Hayyan's objection cannot be raised against this, that when an adverb becomes a hal, the pronoun in the governing element shifts to the adverb, whereas a nominal clause as a hal with waw has no shifted pronoun, so how can it be said to be in the rule of an adverb? Indeed, the truth is that the connection by waw suffices in place of the pronoun, and there is no need with it for this burden. It is permitted that the clause be a hal from "al-ard" (the earth), the governing element being the sense of settling, and the connective being what you have heard, or the "al" in "al-bahr," according to the view of the Kufans, that "al" may be a substitute for the pronoun, as in His saying: ﴿Gardens of Eden, whose gates are opened for them﴾ [Sad: 50], meaning: had it been established that what settled in the earth, being of a tree, were pens while its sea is extended by seven seas.

Al-Kashshaf said: It is necessary to make "min shajarah" an explanation of the pronoun returning to "ma," lest there be a separation between the parts of the relative clause by a foreign element.

"Al-bahr," on the assumption that "al" in it is a substitute for the genitive pronoun referring to "al-ard," may be intended as the known one, or as other than it. Al-Tibi said: the sea on that basis encompasses all the seas by the evidence of the annexation, and it indicates that the seven are outside the sea of the earth. On the other reading, it may refer to the known portion familiar to the addressee. It was answered that there is no difference between them; rather, that its sea is the known is more apparent, because the known reference is the origin of the annexation, and this is not contradicted by the earth being inclusive of all regions, because the known sea is the surrounding ocean, which encompasses them all. Al-Zamakhshari permitted that its nominative be by coordination with the position of "anna" and what it governs, and the clause "yamudduhu" is a hal on the assumption: had it been established that what is in the earth of trees were pens, and the sea was established as extended by seven seas. It was objected that the verb implied is indicated by "anna" and its khabar, according to what was established in its chapter; thus it is not possible to reach the coordinated element without noticing an indicator, and in this coordination there is an exit from that noticing. It was answered that the follower may admit what the followed does not. Furthermore, it is not hidden that the coordination on this basis is coordination of a noun on a noun, not of a noun on a clause as was said, since the apparent coordinated element is the verbal noun which is the subject of "thabata," and it is a single noun, not a clause. It was permitted that the coordination be on that, based on the view of one who makes it a mubtada'. It was objected that this requires that "law" be directly followed by the explicit noun serving as a mubtada', since the assumed phrase becomes "and if the sea," and according to Abu Hayyan this is not permitted except in poetic necessity, such as the verse:
"Even if my throat choked on other than water, I would be like one who gasps for water in its absence."
It was answered that the follower may admit what the followed does not, as in: "Many a man and his brother say that." Some said: the coordination mentioned earlier requires that "law" be directly followed by the explicit noun, and this too is restricted to necessity; and the answer was the same, though in my view there is room for reflection. It was permitted that the nominative be a mubtada', with "yamudduhu" as its khabar, the waw being the waw of accompaniment, and the nominal clause, subject and predicate, in the position of an object with it (maf'ul ma'ahu), based on its being a clause, as transmitted from Ibn Hisham. Its remoteness is not hidden. It was permitted that the waw on this be for resumption, a resumption explanatory (bayani), as if it was said: "What then is the ink?" So it was said: "And the sea..." It was objected that the attachment of the answer with waw, even if the waw is resumptive, is not customary; and what was said, that it is attached with waw when it is an answer to a question by way of argument rather than seeking information, is not something to rely upon. Hence it was said: on the intention of resumption, the apparent thing is that it be grammatical. It was permitted in this construction other aspects of i'rab beyond what has been mentioned.

The two Basrans read "wal-bahra" with the accusative, on the basis that it is coordinated on the ism of "anna," with "yamudduhu" as its khabar, meaning: "and had the sea been extended by seven seas."

Ibn al-Hajib said in his Amali: It is not correct that "yamudduhu" be a hal, because that would also restrict a solid mubtada' by a hal, which is not permitted, since the hal explains the subject or the object, and the mubtada' is not like that; and it would lead to the mubtada' having no khabar; and it is not correct that "aqlam" be its khabar, because it is the khabar of the first. End quote. The possibility of assuming a khabar was not mentioned, as it is evidently contrary to the apparent sense.

It was permitted that it be in the accusative, as a conjunction of explanation (shari'at al-tafsir), coordinated on the implied verb, namely "thabata," and the entry of "law" on the imperfect is permitted; the clause "yamudduhu" etc. then has no place in grammatical analysis.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 31, verse 27 (part 2 of 2):

Ibn Mas'ud read: «wa-bahrun» (with indefinite *bahrun* and nominative *-un*). Ibn Jinni (Abu al-Fath Ibn Jinni) interpreted this as a *mubtada'* (subject of a nominal sentence, *mubtada'* = "grammatical subject"), whose predicate (*khabar*, "predicate") is omitted, meaning: "There is a sea that extends it, etc." The *waw* here is undoubtedly the *waw* of *hal* (the circumstantial *waw*, *waw al-hal*, "the *waw* introducing a circumstantial clause"). It is not permissible to coordinate it with *aqlam* ("pens"), because the sea and what is in it are not part of the discourse about the trees and the pens; rather, it is part of the discourse about the ink.

[p. 100]

In al-Bahr (*al-Bahr al-Muhit*, by Abu Hayyan): on this reading the *waw* is either a *waw al-hal* or a *waw* of coordination with what came before. If it is a *waw al-hal*, then *al-bahru* is a *mubtada'*. The beginning of the sentence with an indefinite noun (*nakirah*) is permitted by the fact that this *waw* precedes it, since this is counted among the justifications for beginning with an indefinite noun, as in the verse:

"We journeyed, and a star had shone, so when there appeared / Your face, every luminous one hid its light."

End of quotation. It is not hidden that if it is coordinated with the subject (*fa'il*) in *thabata*, then the clause *yamudduhu* is in the position of a descriptive clause (*sifah*) for it, not a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from it. Whoever permits a circumstantial clause from an indefinite noun has allowed that. The apparent reading, on the assumption that it is a *mubtada'*, is to make the clause its predicate, and there is no need to make its predicate omitted as Ibn Jinni did.

Ibn Mas'ud and Ubayy read «tamudduhu» with the feminine *ta'* from *madda*, like what is in the reading of the majority. Ibn Mas'ud also, al-Hasan, Ibn Musarrif, and Ibn Hurmuz read «yumiddu-hu» with a *dammah* on the *ya'* (*yumiddu*, from *al-imdad*, "supplying"). Ibn al-Shaykh said: *yamuddu* with a *fathah* then a *dammah*, and *yumiddu* with a *dammah* then a *kasrah*, are two dialectal forms with the same meaning.

Ja'far ibn Muhammad, may Allah be pleased with both of them, read: «wal-bahru midaduhu», meaning what is written with of ink. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: it is a verbal noun (*masdar*).

*Ma nafidat kalimatu Allah* ("the words of Allah would not be exhausted") is the answer (*jawab*) of *law* ("if"). There is an ellipsis in the speech called *hadhf ijaz* (ellipsis for conciseness), and the context indicates what is omitted. The estimated meaning is: "If whatever is on the earth of trees were pens, and the sea were extended by seven seas, and the words of Allah were written with those pens and with that ink, they would not be exhausted, because they are not finite, while those pens and that ink would be exhausted, because they are finite." A parallel of this in including ellipsis for conciseness is His, may He be exalted, saying: ﴿or whoever has an injury from his head, then a ransom﴾ [al-Baqarah: 196], meaning: "so he shaves his head to remove the injury he has, then a ransom."

By "His words" is meant the words of His knowledge and wisdom, glory be to Him, and this is what the occasion of revelation (*sabab al-nuzul*) requires, according to what Ibn Jarir reported from Ikrimah, who said: "The People of the Book asked the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, about the Spirit, so Allah, glory be to Him, revealed: ﴿They ask you about the Spirit. Say: The Spirit is of the command of my Lord, and you have not been given of knowledge except a little﴾ [al-Isra': 85]. They said: 'You claim that we have not been given of knowledge except a little, yet we have been given the Torah, which is wisdom, and whoever is given wisdom has been given much good.' So this was revealed: 'If...' etc."

The apparent meaning of this is that the Jews said that to him, peace be upon him, face to face, and this is apparent that the verse is Medinan. It was also said that they instructed a delegation of Quraysh to say that to him, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and this one who says that says it is Meccan. The summary of the answer is: although what you have been given is much good because it is wisdom, it is little in comparison with His wisdom, mighty and majestic.

In another narration: "There was revealed in Mecca His, may He be exalted, saying: ﴿They ask you...﴾ etc. When he, peace be upon him, emigrated, the rabbis of the Jews came to him and said: 'It has reached us that you say: ﴿You have not been given of knowledge except a little﴾. Do you mean us or your people?' The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: 'Not at all, I meant [you].' They said: 'Do you not recite in what came to you: "We have been given the Torah, and in it is the knowledge of everything"?' He, peace and salutations be upon him, said: 'It is, in the knowledge of Allah, little, and what has come to you, if you act upon it, you will be saved.' They said: 'O Muhammad, how do you claim this while you say: ﴿And whoever is given wisdom has been given much good﴾ [al-Baqarah: 269]? How can these come together?' The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: 'This is little knowledge and much good.' So Allah, exalted, revealed this verse."

This is an explicit text that the verse is Medinan.

It was also said: what is meant by it is His capabilities, may He be exalted, and His wonders, mighty and majestic, which when He, blessed and exalted, wills something of them, He says: ﴿Be, and it is﴾ [al-Baqarah: 117 and elsewhere]. Among that is His saying, exalted, concerning Jesus: ﴿and His word which He conveyed to Mary﴾ [an-Nisa': 171]. The application of "words" to what has been mentioned is the application of the cause to the effect (*itlaq al-sabab 'ala al-musabbab*). On this basis, the connection of the verse with what precedes it is clearer, as has been said, namely that when He, glory be to Him, said: ﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth﴾, and this might suggest that His dominion is finite, He followed that with what is clearly infinite. This is what the Imam chose regarding the meaning of His words, exalted, except that its fit with the occasion of revelation is obscure. From Abu Muslim: what is meant by it is what He promised, glory be to Him, to the people of His obedience of reward, and what He threatened, majestic is His glory, to the people of His disobedience of punishment. It seems that for him the verse is an explanation of the greater number of what has not yet appeared of His dominion, exalted, after the explanation of the abundance of what has appeared. It was also said: what is meant by it is what is most immediately understood from it, on the basis of what 'Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and others reported from Qatadah, who said: "The polytheists said: 'This is merely speech that will soon be exhausted.' So this was revealed: ﴿And if whatever is in the earth of trees were pens...﴾" etc. As for the connection of the verse with what is before it and after it on this view, it is very obscure, but it does not require that it be Medinan.

The choice of the sound feminine plural (*jam' al-mu'annath al-salim*), on the basis that it is like the sound masculine plural, is a plural of paucity (*jam' qillah*), because it suggests—even though it is joined with what may indicate totality and generality, such as the definite article *al-* or the construct (*idafah*)—its original form, which is paucity. That is, it does not suffice for little, so how much less for much.

Al-Hasan read «ma nafida» without a *ta'*, and «kalamu Allah» instead of «kalimati Allah». ﴿Indeed, Allah is Mighty﴾: nothing overcomes Him, glory be to Him. ﴿Wise﴾: nothing escapes His knowledge, exalted, and His wisdom, glory be to Him. The sentence is a reason (*ta'lil*) for the non-exhaustion of His words, blessed and exalted.

﴿Your creation and your resurrection are no more than that of a single soul.﴾ That is, [it is] no more than the creation and resurrection of one soul, in terms of the ease of accomplishment with respect to Him, exalted and majestic. For no matter occupies Him, exalted is He, from another matter, because the basis of the existence of all things is the connection of His necessary will (irada), or His saying, exalted and majestic, "Be" (kun), together with His essential power (qudra), glorified is He, and the possibility of the object of that connection. Such [existence] requires no instrument (alah) or direct contact that would entail succession, so that for Him, exalted is He, the one and the many would not differ as they differ for creatures. ﴿Indeed, Allah is All-Hearing﴾, who hears everything that is heard, ﴿All-Seeing﴾, who sees everything that is seen, in a single state, such that the perception of some of them does not preoccupy Him from the perception of others. So likewise [it is with] creation and resurrection. The summary of this is that, just as He, exalted is His majesty, perceives all visible things with a single sight, and hears all audible things with a single hearing, without any of that preoccupying Him from another, so too is it with respect to power and action. Thus this is an argument by what they themselves accept: it likens the objects of power, insofar as they are willed, to the objects of perception, insofar as they are perceived. So says al-Kashf.

The matter of this being accepted by them is objected to on the ground that some of them, when they reviled the religion, would say: "Keep your speech secret, lest the God of Muhammad (ﷺ) hear it." Then this was revealed: ﴿And keep your speech secret or declare it; indeed, He is Knowing of what is in the breasts﴾ [al-Mulk: 13].

It is answered that no account should be taken of such folly after He has refuted what they claimed and informed them of what they had concealed. It has also been said that the sentence is a justification for establishing complete power by means of wide knowledge, and that none of the objects of power preoccupies Him, glorified is He, from anything else, because of His knowledge, exalted is He, of their details and particulars, so that He disposes of them as He wills, just as one says: "So-and-so excels at doing such-and-such, because of his knowledge of its subtleties and completions." The purpose of mentioning the two attributes is to establish resurrection and gathering (al-hashr wa al-nashr), for these are the pillars of it. Do you not see how He followed that with what indicates the greatness of power and the comprehensiveness of knowledge?

Whichever of these is the case, the suspicion is dispelled that what is appropriate to what precedes would be to say: "Indeed, Allah is Strong, Powerful," or something of that sort, rather than what was mentioned, because creation and resurrection are not among the audible or visible things.

And from Muqatil: "The disbelievers of Quraysh said: 'Indeed Allah created us in stages: a drop, a clot, a lump of flesh. How then will He resurrect us as a new creation in a single hour?' So this was revealed." Al-Naqqash mentioned that it was revealed concerning Ubayy ibn Khalaf, Abu al-Aswad, and Nabih and Munabbih, the two sons of al-Hajjaj, and something similar to what was mentioned was related concerning the cause of its revelation regarding them. On the basis that the cause of revelation is that, it has been said that the meaning is: He is All-Hearing of their words that, and All-Seeing of what they conceal. And this, as you see, is far-fetched.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 31, verse 29:

﴿Have you not seen﴾ It has been said: this is an address to the master of those addressed, ﷺ. It has also been said: it is general, addressed to everyone who is fit to be addressed, and this is the most fitting in light of what precedes and what follows; that is, "Do you not know?"

Page 102

﴿that Allah causes the night to enter into the day and causes the day to enter into the night﴾ That is, He makes each of them enter into the other, and He attributes this to Himself, so that His state varies by it in increase and decrease. He turned away from saying "causes one of the two alternating periods to enter into the other," although that is more concise, to indicate the independence of each of them in showing the perfection of power. He placed the night before the day because of its suitability to the dark world of contingency (ʿalam al-imkan) in respect of its essential possibility. In some reports: "The world was in darkness; Allah, exalted is He, spread His light over them," and this entering occurs only in this world; "with your Lord there is no morning or evening." He placed the sun before the moon in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and He subjected the sun and the moon﴾, while placing the night, in which is the dominion of the moon, before the day, in which is the dominion of the sun, because the sun is like the origin for the moon, and because its subjection is, by reason of its greatness, more magnificent than the subjection of the moon; and also the effects of that subjection are greater than the effects of its subjection. Al-Imam said, in explaining the placement of each before what it was placed before: because souls seek the cause of what is first more than they seek the cause of what is later, and he explained that with what he explained. Perhaps what we have mentioned is more preferable, especially if it is established that the light of the moon is derived from the brightness of the sun. His saying, exalted is He, "subjected" (sakhkhara) is coordinated with His saying, exalted is He, "causes to enter" (yuliju). The difference between them is in form, because the entering of one of the two alternating periods into the other is renewed at every moment, whereas subjection is a matter with no multiplicity and no renewal; multiplicity and renewal are only in its effects, as His saying, exalted is He, indicates: ﴿Each﴾, that is, each one of the sun and the moon, ﴿runs﴾, proceeds with rapid, continuous motion, ﴿to a term﴾, that is, an end for the running, ﴿appointed﴾, which Allah, exalted is He, named and determined for that. It is, as al-Hasan said, the Day of Resurrection, for the running of the two luminaries does not cease and their motion is not nullified except on that day. The apparent meaning is that this running is this motion which every person of sight among the inhabitants of the inhabited world observes; according to the philosophers it is through the Greatest Sphere, for its motion is such, and through it is the motion of the rest of the spheres and of the stars within them. It is called the motion of the whole, the daily motion, the swift motion, the first motion, the motion against the order (of succession), the eastward motion; some call it the westward motion. It has also been said: it encompasses this motion and their particular motion proper to each of them, which is their motion through their own spheres in succession from west to east, and it is swifter for the moon than for the sun. Nothing in clear reason or sound transmission forbids affirming these two motions for each of the two luminaries, as is not hidden from the fair-minded knower. The end of this general running of both motions is also the Day of Resurrection. The clause, on the assumption that the address is general, is a parenthetical insertion between the two conjoined clauses, to explain the reality by way of digression; and on the assumption that it is specific to him, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, it is permissible for it to be a circumstantial clause (hal) concerning the sun and the moon, since their running until the Day of Resurrection is among what is within the scope of his vision, upon him be prayer and peace. It has been said that their running is an expression for their particular motion proper to each of them. The appointed term for the running of the sun is the end of the year called the true solar year, which is the time of the sun's return from any point assumed on the ecliptic back to it by its own motion. They took its beginning from the moment the sun arrives at the first point of Aries. Its duration according to some is three hundred and sixty-five days with a night, and a quarter of a day likewise. According to Ptolemy it is three hundred and sixty-five days with a night, and five hours, fifty-five minutes and twelve seconds. According to some later scholars it is three hundred and sixty-five days, five hours, forty-six minutes and twenty-four seconds. According to the sage Muhyi al-Din the excess fraction is five hours and one minute. By the new observation undertaken by al-Tusi at Maragha it is five hours and forty-nine minutes, and by the observation of Samarkand it was found to be a quarter of a minute more than this. As for the conventional (year), some, like the Romans and the earlier Persians, reckoned it as three hundred and sixty-five days with a night, and a quarter of a day likewise, and the fraction was taken as a complete quarter, except that the Romans make three years of three hundred and sixty-five days and intercalate a day in the fourth; the Persians used to intercalate a month every hundred and twenty years. Another group reckoned it, like the Copts and the modern users of the Persian calendar, as three hundred and sixty days with a night, and the fraction was dropped altogether. For the running of the moon, the appointed term is the end of the true lunar month, which is the time of the moon's separation, that is, the position it takes from the sun until its return to it; they took its beginning from the conjunction of the sun and the moon, and the time between two successive conjunctions is (kt la n) days and their minutes and seconds approximately. As for the non-true month, what is considered is the crescent, and the time between two crescents varies, as is known.

It has been said: according to this, the clause explains the manner of their subjection, or draws attention to the manner in which one of the two alternating periods enters into the other, and that this occurs according to the variation in the sun's running along its daily orbits: whenever its running is directed toward the zenith, the arc above the earth grows larger, so the day lengthens by some parts of the night being added to it, until it reaches the orbit nearest to the zenith, which occurs when it reaches the head of Cancer; then it returns, directed toward distance from the zenith, and the arcs above the earth continue to diminish, so the day shortens by some of its parts being added to the night, until it reaches the orbit farthest from the daily zenith, which occurs when it reaches the head of Capricorn.

You know that the running of the moon has no part in the entering, so mention of it in the noble verse weakens this view. Perhaps the more evident, on the assumption that their running is an expression for their particular motion proper to each of them, is to take the appointed term as an expression for the Day of Resurrection, or to take it as an expression for the end of the year and month known among the Arabs; so reflect. The verb jara (to run) is transitive with ila (to) at times and with li (for) at others; its construction with the first is by considering the object as an endpoint, and with the second by considering it as a purpose, so the lam is the lam of cause or of consequence. Al-Zamakhshari took it as the lam of specification, and each has its reasoning; it has not become clear to me why this context is specific to ila rather than other than lam. Al-Nisaburi said: the reason for this is that this verse begins with an expression of wonder, so lengthening is appropriate; and that, as you see, is far from sufficient, so consider it well.
