His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And that Allah is Aware of what you do﴾ is coordinated with His saying: ﴿that Allah causes the night to enter﴾, etc., and is included with it within the scope of the seeing, on both assumptions of the address being specific or general; for whoever witnesses such a splendid work and such fitting arrangement can hardly be unaware that its Maker, mighty and majestic is He, encompasses its grand and minute deeds. ʿAyyash related from Abu ʿAmr a reading "bi-ma ya'malun" with the third-person (ya') form.

**Page 104**

﴿That﴾ refers to what the verses contained and indicated of the vastness of knowledge, the perfection of power, and the exclusivity of the Creator, exalted is His station, in these attributes, ﴿because God is the Truth﴾, that is, because He, glory be to Him, alone is the One who is established and realized in His essence, meaning the Necessary Existent (*wajib al-wujud*).

﴿And that what they call upon besides Him﴾ as a god ﴿is the falsehood﴾, the non-existent in its own essence, which is the contingent (*mumkin*) that exists only through another, and that is the Necessary Existent, exalted is His station. ﴿And that God is the Most High﴾ over things ﴿the Great﴾, too great to have any partner, or to be described with any deficiency, with nothing higher than Him in station or greater in dominion, exalted is His station. The way the first (clause) is a cause for what was mentioned is that His being alone the Necessary Existent in His essence entails that He, glory be to Him alone, is the one who brings into existence all the marvelously wrought creatures. Thus it indicates the perfection of His power, mighty and majestic is He alone. Obligation by nature (*al-ijab*) has been refuted in the principles (*al-usul*) of theology. Whoever all those creatures issue from must be perfect in knowledge, as has been explained in the discussion. The way the third (clause) is a cause for that is that His being alone exalted over all things, dominating them, transcendent above having any partner or being described with any deficiency, mighty and majestic is He, entails **Page 105**

that He, exalted is He, alone is the Necessary Existent in His essence. You have already heard the discussion of this. As for the way that what they call upon besides Him as a god is a contingent falsehood in its essence, it is a cause for that: its contingency, despite the loftiness of its status in their view, entails the contingency of everything else that is other than God, mighty and majestic, because whatever in it indicates its contingency exists in the others exactly alike (*hadhw al-qadhdhah bil-qadhdhah*). And whenever what they call upon as a god besides God, exalted is He, and besides God, glory be to Him and exalted is He, is contingent, the necessity of existence becomes confined to God, exalted is He. Thus He, exalted and mighty, is alone the Necessary Existent in His essence. You already know how this yields the required conclusion. It seems that it was said "that what they call upon besides Him is the falsehood" rather than "that what is other than Him is falsehood," for example, like the saying of Labid:

*Surely everything other than God is vain*

as an explicit statement of the abhorrence of what they are upon. This entails that everything other than God, exalted is He, among existents, is contingent a fortiori, based on what the polytheists claim about their gods of lofty status. He did not suffice, in stating the cause, with His saying, glory be to Him, "because God is the Truth," but also conjoined to it what He conjoined, although it is among what returns to it. That clause hints at it, to show complete care for the required meaning, and by what the explicit content of the conjoined clause indicates of the nullity of a partner and of His, exalted is He, being the Most High, the Great.

It was also said: "That," i.e., that attribution to the wonders of power and wisdom contained in the verses, is due to the fact that God, exalted is He, is the god whose divinity is established, and that whoever is besides Him, glory be to Him, is vain in divinity, and that God, exalted is He, is the One of lofty status, great in dominion. The matter of causation turns on His, glory be to Him, being the one whose divinity is established. Al-Tibi explained this by saying: it has been established that whoever is a god is capable, a creator, knowing, and so on through the other attributes of perfection. Then he said: His saying, exalted is He, "that God is the Truth," is like a summation (*fadhlaka*) of what preceded from His saying, exalted is He, "Do you not see that God has subjected for you" up to this point, and His saying, exalted is He, "that God is the Most High, the Great," is like a summation of all those separate matters mentioned there.

Perhaps what we have put forward is more worthy of consideration. Al-'Allamah Abu al-Su'ud said in objection to this: You know that the truth of Him, exalted is He, and His loftiness and His majesty, although they are suitable as the causal basis for what has been mentioned of the attributes, yet the nullity of the divinity of the idols has no bearing on the causal basis at all, so there is no room to place it in the row of causes. Rather, it is a reversal of the matter, since the mentioned attributes are what necessitate their nullity, not that their nullity necessitates them. End of quotation. In this there is room for reflection. It is strange that he mentioned a similar objection to it regarding the parallel verse in Surat al-Hajj and did not follow it up with anything. It was also permitted that the meaning be: that which was recited of the noble verses, by way of explaining that God is the Truth in His divinity alone, and for the sake of them being explicit about the truth of monotheism, and for the sake of explaining the nullity of the divinity of what they claim besides Him, because they are a clear testimony in which there is no doubt, and for the sake of explaining that He, exalted is He, is the One elevated above everything and dominating it, for what is within the folds of those noble verses clearly explains the exclusivity of loftiness and majesty to Him. This is an interpretation with no artificiality in it, except for taking an omitted genitive (*mudaf*) into account, as is not hidden. It seems that here it was said, "and that what they call upon besides Him is the falsehood," without the separative pronoun (*damir al-fasl*), while in Surat al-Hajj it is: ﴿and that what they call upon besides Him, that is the falsehood﴾, with the separative pronoun inserted, because the disparagement of the polytheists and their gods in this surah is different from the disparagement of them in that surah.

Al-Nisaburi said regarding this: the verse of al-Hajj came among ten verses each of which is emphasized once or twice, so inserting the pronoun suited that, unlike here. It may be said: mention of Satan had preceded many times in that surah, so those emphases were mentioned for this reason, unlike this surah, in which the mention of Satan had not preceded in a manner similar to its mention there. Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir, and Abu Bakr read **"tad'una"** (you call) with the second-person taa.

Have you not seen that the ships sail on the sea by the favour of Allah? This is another testimony to His overwhelming power, the utmost of His wisdom, and the all-encompassing reach of His bounty, exalted and blessed is He. The meaning of "the favour of Allah" is His beneficence in preparing the causes of sailing, namely the wind, and making it subservient. So the bāʾ (bāʾ of transitivity, ba' al-ta'diyah) is as in "marartu bi-Zayd" (I passed by Zayd), or it is causal (sababiyyah) and attached to "tajri" (sails).

It is also permissible that by "His favour" is meant what He, exalted is His majesty, has bestowed through what the ships carry of food, goods and the like. In that case the bāʾ is of accompaniment and association (mulabasah wa-musahabah), attached to a omitted element that occurs as a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun of "al-fulk", meaning: they sail accompanied by the favour of Allah, exalted is He.

Mūsā ibn al-Zubayr read "al-fulk" (الفُلُكَ) with a ḍammah on the lām, and a similar form is well known in fuʿul patterns with a ḍammah on the first letter.

It is related from ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar that he said: "No form fuʿl with a ḍammah on the first letter and a sukūn on the middle letter has been heard except that the form fuʿul with a ḍammah on the middle letter has also been heard for it."

In al-Kashshāf: "Every fuʿl permits fuʿul, just as every faʿl permits faʿal. The ḍammah of the middle letter is for assimilation (ittibāʿ), and its sukūn is for lightness (takhfīf)."

Al-Aʿraj, al-Aʿmash and Ibn Yaʿmar read "bi-niʿmāti Allāh" (بِنِعْماتِ اللَّهِ) with a kasrah on the nūn and a sukūn on the ʿayn, as a plural with alif and tāʾ, being the plural of niʿmah with kasrah then sukūn. As several scholars said, in every plural of this type it is permissible to keep the ʿayn quiescent according to the original form, to vocalise it with kasrah for assimilation to the first letter, or to vocalise it with fatḥah for lightness.

Ibn Abī ʿAblah read "bi-naʿamāti Allāh" (بِنَعَماتِ اللَّهِ) with a fatḥah on the nūn and a kasrah on the ʿayn, as a plural of naʿmah with a fatḥah on the nūn, which is a noun for enjoying comfort (al-tanaʿʿum). It is said that it has the meaning of niʿmah with a kasrah.

"That He may show you of His signs" (لِيُرِيَكم مِن آياتِهِ), meaning some of the proofs of His divinity, His oneness, His power, exalted is His majesty, and His knowledge, mighty and majestic is He.

His saying, exalted is He: "Indeed in that are signs for every steadfast, grateful one" (إنَّ في ذَلِكَ لآياتٍ لِكُلِّ صَبّارٍ شَكُورٍ), is a causal explanation of what precedes it. That is, in what has been mentioned there are indeed signs, great in themselves and numerous in their number, for every one who is extremely patient in His trials, exalted is He, and extremely thankful for His blessings, exalted is His majesty.

"Steadfast, grateful" (صَبّارٍ شَكُورٍ) is a kināyah (allusive expression) for the believer, of the type: "a living thing, straight-statured, broad-nailed," for it is a kināyah for the human being. These two attributes are the pillars of faith, since faith and everything on which it depends is either the abandoning of what is generally habitual, which is by patience, or the performance of what brings one nearer to Allah, which is gratitude, owing to its generality: the action of the heart, the limbs and the tongue. For this reason it has been narrated: "Faith is two halves: half patience and half gratitude." Mentioning the two attributes after "the ships" is most appropriate, because the one who rides in them is never free of patience and gratitude.

It is also said that by "steadfast" is meant one who is very patient in the hardship of acquiring proofs from the self and the horizons. Otherwise the signs are not restricted to one who has endured hardship in general. Both attributes are built in the intensive pattern, and faʿʿāl according to what is in al-Baḥr is more intensive than faʿūl because of the added letters. It is said: the intensification in patience was chosen to hint that its little amount, because of its severe bitterness and its greater weight, equals much of something else.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 31, verse 32:

﴿And when a wave covers them like shadows﴾ meaning: it rises over them and covers them, from al-ghisha' (covering), in the sense of al-ghita' (a covering from above), which is the fitting meaning here. It was also said: meaning it reaches them, from al-ghashayan (coming), in the sense of al-ityan (arriving). If the pronoun in ﴿غَشِيَهُمْ﴾ [ghashiyahum, "covers them"] refers to the same group addressed before it, then there is a shift (iltifat) in the speech from address (khitab) to third person (ghaybah); otherwise there is no shift. Al-mawj is what rises from the crests of the water. It is a collective noun (ism jins) whose singular is mawjah, and its indefiniteness indicates magnitude and abundance. For this reason the comparison term is given in the singular while the thing compared to it is plural, in His words, exalted is He, ﴿كالظُّلَلِ﴾ [ka-l-zulal, "like shadows/canopies"], which is the plural of zullah, like ghurfah and ghuraf, and qurbah and qurab. What is meant by it is whatever overshadows, whether clouds, a mountain, or other things.

Al-Raghib said: al-zullah is a cloud that casts shade, and it is most often used of what is unpleasant and disliked. Qatadah explained al-zill here as clouds, and some explained it as mountains. Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyyah, may Allah be pleased with him, read ﴿كالظِّلالِ﴾ [ka-l-zilal], which is also the plural of zullah, like 'ulbah and 'ilab, and jufrah and jifar.

﴿وإذا﴾ [wa-idha, "and when"] is a temporal adverb (zarf) governing His words, ﴿دَعَوُا﴾ [da'awu, "they called"], meaning: they called upon ﴿اللَّهَ مُخْلِصِينَ لَهُ الدِّينَ﴾ [Allah, sincere to Him in religion] when a wave covers them like shadows. They did this at that time only because the desires and imitation that oppose the natural disposition (fitrah) had gone away, due to the severe fear that had overtaken them.

﴿فَلَمّا نَجّاهم إلى البَرِّ فَمِنهم مُقْتَصِدٌ﴾ [But when He brings them safely to land, some of them remain moderate]: the muqtasid is one who takes the middle course (qasd), i.e., the straight path, and does not deviate from it to anything else. Its original meaning is the straightness of the path, then it was applied to the one who follows it, as an intensification. The straight path here is metaphorically tawhid, so it is as if it was said: among them is one who adheres to tawhid. The statement of al-Hasan: "Every believer who recognizes Allah's right in this blessing returns to this," and it was said: muqtasid comes from al-iqtisad, meaning moderation and balance.

According to what has been said, what is meant then is: one who is moderate in his words and deeds, between fear and hope, fulfilling what he pledged to Allah in the sea. Interpreting it as "one who fulfils his covenant" is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them. In this sense, according to this meaning, 'Ikrimah ibn Abi Jahl is included among this group.

For al-Suddi narrated from Mus'ab ibn Sa'd, from his father, who said: "When the conquest of Makkah took place, the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, commanded the people to refrain from killing its inhabitants except for four men among them. He said: 'Kill them even if you find them clinging to the curtains of the Ka'bah: 'Ikrimah ibn Abi Jahl, 'Abdullah ibn Khatal, Qays ibn Subabah, and 'Abdullah ibn Abi Sarh.'

As for 'Ikrimah, he boarded a ship, and a violent wind struck them. The people of the ship said: 'Be sincere, for your gods will not avail you anything here.' 'Ikrimah said: 'If nothing but sincerity will save me at sea, then nothing else will save me on land. O Allah, indeed I make a covenant with You: if You grant me well-being from what I am in, I will come to Muhammad, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, until I place my hand in his, and I will certainly find him forgiving and generous.' He came and embraced Islam." It was also said: muqtasid means one who is intermediate in disbelief, since he was restrained by what he witnessed of some restraint.

It was also said: muqtasid means one who is intermediate in the sincerity that he had at sea, for the sincerity that arises at the time of fear rarely remains for anyone once the fear is gone. Whatever the case, the apparent meaning is that the counterpart to the division of the muqtasid is omitted, indicated by His words, ﴿وما يَجْحَدُ بِآياتِنا إلا كُلُّ خَتّارٍ﴾ [And none rejects Our signs except every treacherous ingrate]. This verse is the evidence of Ibn Malik and those who agree with him on the permissibility of the fa' entering the answer (jawab) of lamma. Whoever does not permit it says: the answer is omitted, meaning: "When He brought them safely to land, they divided into two groups: some of them are moderate, and some of them are deniers." Khattar is from al-khatr, which is the most severe treachery. From it comes their saying: "You do not extend to us a span of treachery except that we extend to you a fathom of treachery." Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, explained it in this manner to Ibn al-Azraq, and he recited the poet's verse:

"She certainly knew and was certain, the one within herself, that she would never fear, through all time, my severance or my treachery."

Similar to it is the saying of 'Amr ibn Ma'd Yakrib:

"Indeed, if you had seen Abu 'Umayr, you would have filled your hands with treachery and deceit."

In al-Raghib's Mufradat: al-khatr is treachery by which a person weakens (yakhtur), i.e., becomes weak, and it is pronounced with a kasra due to his striving in it. That is: "And none rejects Our signs and denies them except every treacherous one of the utmost treachery, because his disbelief is a breach of the natural covenant." It was also said: "because it is a breach of what he pledged to Allah at sea of sincerity toward Him, mighty and majestic." ﴿كَفُورٍ﴾ [kafur, "ungrateful"] is intensive in denying the favours of Allah. (And khattar) is the counterpart of sabbar (patient),

صفحة 107

because whoever betrays does not remain patient in the covenant, and kafur is the counterpart of shakur (grateful).

[Begins mid-commentary on 31:33]

﴿O mankind, fear your Lord and dread a Day when no father will avail anything for his son﴾. This is a command to God-consciousness (taqwa) in the manner of admonition and reminder, after the proofs of God's oneness, and by way of warning of a great Day. "Yajzi" here means "qada" (to discharge or settle), and from this it is said of the one who settles a debt, "mutaqadi" or "mutajazi": that no father will settle anything on behalf of his son.

Abu al-Simal, Amir ibn Abd Allah, and Abu al-Siwar read "لا يُجْزِئُ" (la yujzi'u), with a damma on the yaʾ and a kasra on the zayn, with a hamza. Its meaning is: no father will suffice for his son and will not benefit him in anything, from "ajza'tu 'anka majza fulan," meaning "I gave you enough in place of so-and-so."

Ikrima read "يُجْزى" (yujza), with a damma on the yaʾ and a fatha on the zayn, in the passive voice. On all these readings, the clause is a description (sifa) of "yawman" (a Day). The returning pronoun referring back to the described noun is elided, meaning "fihi" (in it). It may be omitted in its entirety, or in stages, by dropping the preposition so that the verb reaches the pronoun, and then the pronoun is elided as an object.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and no child who is born﴾ (wa la mawlud), is either a conjunction with "walid" (father), so that it is the subject of "yajzi," and His saying ﴿is himself one who will avail anything for his father﴾ (huwa jazin 'an walidihi shay'an) is in the position of a description of it. What is negated is the settling in the Hereafter, and what is affirmed for it is settling in this world. Alternatively, the meaning of "huwa jazin" is: it is within its nature to settle, because of the great right of the parent. Or the intended meaning of "la yajzi" is that what he is capable of settling will not be accepted. Or it is a subject (mubtada'), and what permits beginning with it despite its being indefinite is the prior negation. Al-Mahdawi overlooked this and so denied the validity of its being a subject, with the clause "huwa jazin" as its predicate, and "shay'an" as the object, or as an accusative of the verbal noun (masdar), since it is a description of an elided verbal noun. On both views it is said that the two verbs "yajzi" and "jazin" contend for it (tanazu', the grammatical contention in which two governing words compete for the same complement).

The choice of an unemphasized negation in the first clause and an emphasized one in the second is because most of the Muslims and their notables at the time of the address had fathers who had died in unbelief and upon the pre-Islamic religion. When the unbeliever's benefit to the Muslim was remote, its negation did not need emphasis. But when the Muslim's benefit to the unbeliever was something that might occur to the imagination, its negation was emphasized. So said al-Zamakhshari.

Ibn al-Munir criticized this, saying that its validity depends on the address being specific to those present at that time, whereas the correct view is that it is general to them and to everyone to whom the name "mankind" applies. Al-Kashshaf rejected this, saying that the two premises are both faulty. As for the second, it is established in the principles of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh) that "O mankind" encompasses those present, and for others it does so by informing them, or by way of that informing. The Malikis agree. As for the first, on the assumption of acceptance, there is no doubt that the great believers and their elders until the end of the world are the Prophet (ﷺ) and his Companions (may God be pleased with them), and it is known that most of their fathers died in unbelief. So from where does the restriction come? End of quotation.

Ibn al-Munir chose, as the explanation of this, that God, when He emphasized the injunction regarding parents and linked the obligation of gratitude to them with the obligation of gratitude to Himself, and obliged the child to spare his parent whatever harms him to the utmost of his ability, cut off here the parent's delusion that the child on the Day of Resurrection would repay him his right and suffice him against what he meets of the terrors of that Day, just as God obliged him in this world to do so for the parent's sake. Since the child's repaying on behalf of the parent was a likely occurrence, because God urged it in this world, it was fitting for the negation to be emphasized to remove this delusion. The reverse is not the case.

Close to this is what al-Imam (al-Razi) said: the child by his nature is one who repays his parent, because of the rights the parent has over him, while the child's benefit to the parent is the provision of maintenance, and this is not obligatory upon him. Therefore God said regarding the child "la yajzi" (will not avail), and regarding the child who is born "wa la mawlud huwa jazin 'an walidihi" (nor a child who is born, he will avail for his father). Do you not see that one says of someone who weaves, when weaving is not his profession, "huwa yahik" (he weaves), and of one who weaves, when it is his profession, "huwa haik" (he is a weaver)?

It was also said: the emphasis in the second clause is to indicate that the child who is born is more fitting for this ruling not to avail, because he is less than the parent in tenderness and compassion. Since he is more deserving of this ruling, he deserves emphasis. [Page 108] There is something in the heart about this. It may be said that the Arabs used to store up children for their benefit, for the repelling of harm from them, and for the fulfilment of what concerns them, and most people probably are like that. So it was intended to cut off the delusion of their benefit to them and their repelling of harm, and the fulfilment of what is important on behalf of their fathers on the Day of Resurrection. Therefore the clause which states the negation of that from them was emphasized.

Among the emphatic devices is counted the expression "al-mawlud" (the one who is born), because it refers to one born without an intermediary, unlike "al-walad" (the child), which is general and includes the child's child. So when the clause states that the nearest child does not avail for his parent, it is known that whoever is other than him among the children does not avail for his grandfather, by way of a fortiori reasoning.

It is objected that this distinction between "walad" and "mawlud" was not established by the lexicographers. It is answered that al-Zamakhshari and al-Mutarrizi mentioned it, and they suffice as proof. Furthermore, there is also a question regarding the generality of "walad" to include the child's child, for a group held that it is specific in its true sense to the direct (sulbi) child.

The author of al-Mughrib said: "mawlud" is said of the young child, even if the older one is also "mawlud," because of the nearness of his time of birth, just as one says "laban halib" (fresh milk) and "rutab janiy" (fresh dates) for the freshest of them. The purpose of the emphasis on it is that if the young child does not avail in that state, because he is not occupied with himself since he was not charged with obligation in this world, then the older one who is occupied with himself is more deserving of this. This is as you see. Some of them restricted the generality to other than the children of the Muslims, because of the established reports about their intercession for their parents.

This is objected to on the grounds that intercession is not a judgment, and even if it were granted, since it depends on acceptance, the judgment would be from Him, exalted and mighty, in reality. So reflect.

﴿Indeed, the promise of God﴾. It is said: it refers to reward and punishment, by giving precedence to the promise over the threat. Or it is in its linguistic sense: ﴿is true﴾ (haqq), established and certain, not to be broken. That the promise of reward is not broken is not a matter of dispute. As for the promise of punishment not being broken, there is a discussion about it, and the truth is that it is also not broken. The non-punishment of those among the disobedient who are threatened and who are forgiven is not a breaking of the threat at all, because the threat regarding them was conditional upon a condition that was not mentioned, as a means of intimidation and warning. According to this, the sentence is a justification for the negation of the settlement. It was also said: the meaning is that God's promise concerning that Day is true. The sentence is then a resumptive explanatory apposition (istinaf bayani, a new clause answering an unstated question), as if, when it was said "O mankind, fear a Day..." etc., someone asked whether that Day would really come. It was then said: indeed, God's promise is true, that is, yes, it will certainly happen, because of the promise regarding it. This is an answer in the most eloquent manner, and the words of al-Imam point to it.

﴿So let not the present life deceive you﴾, by its pleasures diverting you from acts of obedience, ﴿and let not the Deceiver deceive you concerning God﴾, that is, Satan, as narrated from Ibn Abbas, Ikrima, Qatada, Mujahid, and al-Dahhak. He deceives you by leading you into sins through making them attractive to you, and by holding out to you the hope of repentance and forgiveness from Him, exalted is He. Or he tells you that they will not harm the one whose death upon faith was foreordained in God's knowledge, and that leaving them will not benefit the one whose death upon unbelief was foreordained in knowledge. From Abu Ubayda: every thing that deceives you until you disobey God and abandon what He, glorified is He, has commanded you, is a deception, whether it is Satan or something else. Al-Raghib went to this view and said: deception (ghuroor) is everything that deceives a person, such as wealth, rank, desire, or Satan.

It has been explained as Satan, since he is the most wicked of deceivers. It has also been explained as the world, because of what is said: the world deceives, harms, and passes away. The root of "ghuroor" is from "gharra fulanan," when one strikes his heedlessness (ghirrah), that is his carelessness, and attains from him what he desires. What is meant by it is deception. The apparent reading is that "bi-Allah" (concerning God) is connected to "yaghurrannakum," meaning: let him not deceive you by mentioning some of God's attributes which embolden you to disobey Him, glorified is He.

It is permitted that it be an oath, but this is remote. Ibn Abi Ishaq, Ibn Abi Abla, and Yaʿqub read "تَغُرَّنَّكُمْ" (taghurrannakum) with the light nun (nun khafifa). [Page 109] Simal ibn Harb and Abu Haywa read "الغُرُورُ" (al-ghuroor) with a damma on the ghayn, and it is a verbal noun (masdar). The expression is of the type of "jadda jiddahu" (he strove with his striving), and it can be explained as Satan, making him the very essence of deception, as an intensification.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 31, verse 34 (part 1 of 3):

﴿Indeed, Allah has knowledge of the Hour﴾ etc.

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ikrimah: "A man called al-Harith ibn Amr came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: 'O Muhammad, when will the Hour come? Our lands have become barren, so when will they become fertile? I have left my wife pregnant, so what will she bear? I know what I have earned today, so what will I earn tomorrow? And I know in what land I was born, so in what land will I die?' Then this verse was revealed." Al-Baghawi, al-Wahidi and al-Tha'labi, the Muhyi al-Sunnah, mentioned something similar. So, considering the occasion of revelation, it is an answer to a real question; and considering the verses preceding it, it is an answer to an implied question, as if someone were saying: "When is this day whose affairs have been described?" So it was said: "Indeed Allah," and it did not say "Knowledge of the Hour is with Allah," even though that is shorter, because the name of Allah, glorified is He, is more deserving of being placed first. Also, placing it first and building the predicate upon it conveys restriction (hasr), as al-Tibi established, together with the merit of repeating the attribution. And placing the adverbial phrase also conveys exclusivity; indeed the word "ʿinda" (with Him) is likewise, for it conveys its preservation in a way that it cannot be reached. Thus the sentence conveys, from several aspects, that knowledge of the time of the Resurrection belongs exclusively to Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

As for His saying, ﴿and He sends down the rain﴾, meaning at its proper time, without advance or delay, in a land it does not pass beyond, and in a quantity that wisdom requires: the apparent reading is that it is conjoined to the nominal-adverbial clause built upon the Glorious Name, contrary to His saying: ﴿We give you to drink from what is in their bellies, and for you in them are benefits﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 21]. So it would be a predicate built upon the Glorious Name, like the thing it is conjoined to, and the sentence conveys exclusivity too. The intended meaning is the restrictions of sending down the rain that relate to knowledge, not mere power to send it down, since there is no doubt about that. So the exclusivity returns to knowledge of its time, its place and its quantity, as the statement of al-Kashshaf indicates. The Allamah al-Tibi said in his commentary on the Kashshaf: the indication of this sentence upon knowledge of the unseen is from the aspect that a decreed thing that is firm and perfected indicates comprehensive knowledge.

As for His saying, ﴿and He knows what is in the wombs﴾, meaning: is it male or female? Is it complete or deficient? And likewise whatever other states, it is conjoined to the adverbial clause too, like the preceding one. And a difference was made between ﴿with Him is knowledge of the Hour﴾ and this, so that the first would indicate greater exclusivity, out of concern for the matter of the Hour and indication of the intensity of its concealment; and in this, indication of the continual renewal of the connections according to the renewal of the objects, together with exclusivity. This style was not observed in what came before it, by saying "and He knows the rain," for example, since the attribution of sending down to the Glorious Name explicitly points to the greatness of its matter, because of the abundance of its benefits for the kinds of creatures, and the wide use of the evidence from what results from it, the revival of the earth, for the truth of the resurrection indicated by the Hour in the Mighty Book. He, Exalted, said: ﴿And even though they were, before it was sent down to them, certainly despairing﴾ ﴿So look at the traces of the mercy of Allah, how He gives life to the earth after its death; indeed that is the Giver of life to the dead﴾ [al-Rum: 49, 50], and He, glorified is He, said: ﴿He brings the earth to life after its death, and thus you will be brought forth﴾ [al-Rum: 19], and other than that. It may be said that the sending down of rain, even if it is not the well-known rain, has a role in the resurrection, based on what came in the hadith: "The rain of the sky after the first blast will be a rain like the semen of men."

It was also said: the exclusivity returns to the sending down, and what its restrictions return to that the context requires of knowledge. In this there is a refutation of those who say, "We were given rain by such-and-such a star (nawʾ)." And for the sake of refuting that, because it contains shirk in lordship, it was turned away from "He knows" to "He sends down." But it is as you see.

As for His saying, ﴿and no soul knows﴾, meaning every soul, whether righteous or wicked, as indicated by the occurrence of the indefinite noun in the context of negation: ﴿what it will earn tomorrow﴾, meaning in the future time, of good or evil. And His saying, glorified is He, ﴿and no soul knows in what land it will die﴾ is conjoined to what the author of al-Kashshaf inferred regarding His saying, ﴿Indeed Allah has knowledge of the Hour﴾. He pointed out that since the discourse is directed toward exclusivity, not toward affirming the basic knowledge for Allah, Exalted, for that is not denied, the negation in the sense of comprehensiveness necessarily entails His exclusive possession of it, Mighty and Majestic, by way of metonymy in the most eloquent manner. And in the shift from the word "ʿilm" (knowledge) to the word "dirayah" (knowing), there is that in it of the meaning of deception and stratagem, because the origin of "daraa" is to throw at the "dariyyah," which is the ring that archers aim to hit, and what is used for practising spear-thrusting, and the she-camel that the hunter lets loose so that the game becomes accustomed to it, then he hides behind it and shoots. In each there is a stratagem. And since it is a kind of knowledge with a form of deception and stratagem, it is not attributed to Him, Mighty and Majestic, except when it is interpreted as absolute knowledge, as in the report: "Five things none knows except Allah, Exalted."

It was also said: it may be said that what is prohibited is attributing it to Him alone, Exalted; but with others, may His name be blessed, by way of generalization, there is no prohibition. And it is understood from the statements of some of them that attributing it to Him, Majestic and Exalted, is valid by way of mushakalah (parallelism of expression), as in the saying:

"O Allah, I do not know, and You are the Knower."

So there is no need for what was said: that it is the speech of an uncouth Bedouin who does not know what may be applied to Allah, Exalted, and what is forbidden. The meaning would then be: no soul knows, even if it deploys its stratagems, what clings to it and is specific to it, and does not go beyond it; and nothing is more specific to a human than his earning and his end. So if there is no way for him to know these two, then his knowledge of what lies beyond them is further and further away. In this style the aforementioned embedding (idmaj) has been observed; for this reason it did not say: "and He knows what each soul will earn, and He knows that each soul will die in what land." 

It was also permitted that the basis of "﴿and He sends down the rain﴾" be "that He sends down the rain," so "an" was elided and the verb was put in the nominative, as in His saying:

"O you who restrains me from entering the battle."

Likewise His saying, glorified is He: ﴿and He knows what is in the wombs﴾, and the conjunction is upon "the knowledge of the Hour," so it is as if it were said: "Indeed Allah has knowledge of the Hour, and the sending down of the rain, and the knowledge of what is in the wombs." The indication of this upon the exclusivity of the knowledge of sending down the rain to Him, glorified is He, is clear, since it is evident that what is meant by "with Him is the sending down of the rain" is "with Him is the knowledge of its sending down." And if "He sends down" is conjoined to "the Hour," the exclusivity is more apparent, because the knowledge of what is attributed to the Hour then extends to the sending down. So it is as if it were said: "Indeed Allah has knowledge of the Hour and knowledge of the sending down of the rain." This conjunction hardly holds for "He knows," since the estimate would be: "and with Him is the knowledge of the knowledge of what is in the wombs," and that is not intended at all.

Al-Tibi made "and no soul knows" etc. conjoined to the predicate of "inna" in meaning, by making the negated into an affirmed, so that it says: "and He knows what each soul will earn tomorrow, and He knows that each soul will die in what land." He said that such a thing is permissible in speech when its subtle purposes are observed, as in His saying, Exalted: ﴿Recite what your Lord has forbidden you: that you associate nothing with Him, and to parents, good treatment﴾ [al-An'am: 151], for the conjunction there is according to the return of the prohibition to the opposite of good treatment, which is harm. He mentioned, in explaining the subtle reason for shifting from the affirmative to the negative, something like what we mentioned just now. The author of al-Kashshaf criticized this, saying that there is an alternative to it, namely by what he mentioned of conjoining it to the sentence: ﴿Indeed Allah has knowledge of the Hour﴾.

Al-Imam said regarding the arrangement of the sentences: the truth is that when He, Exalted, said: ﴿and fear a Day﴾ etc., and mentioned, glorified is He, that it is coming by His saying, Mighty and Majestic, "Indeed the promise of Allah is true," it is as if a speaker were to say: "So when is this Day?" Then it was answered that this knowledge is something not attained by anyone other than Him, Exalted, and that is His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Indeed Allah has knowledge of the Hour﴾. Then He, Exalted and Majestic, mentioned the two proofs that had been mentioned repeatedly for the resurrection. One of them is the revival of the earth after its death, indicated by His saying, Exalted: ﴿and He sends down the rain﴾; and the second is creation from the beginning, indicated by His saying, glorified is He: ﴿and He knows what is in the wombs﴾. So it is as if He, Mighty and Majestic, said: "O questioner, indeed you do not know its time, but it is coming, and Allah, Exalted, is able over it, just as He, glorified is He, is able to revive the earth, and to create in the wombs." Then after that, He, Majestic and Exalted, mentioned that He is the one who knows that, by His saying, Mighty and Majestic: "And no soul knows" etc. So it is as if He, Exalted, said: "O questioner, you ask about the Hour, when it will anchor; and indeed there are matters more important than it. You do not know your livelihood and your return, nor do you know what you will earn tomorrow, though it is your action and your time; and you do not know where you will die, though it is your concern and your place. So how will you know the establishment of the Hour, when it will be?" Allah, Exalted, did not teach you what you will earn tomorrow, nor did He teach you where you will die, though there are many benefits for you in that. He did not inform you of it only so that at every time, because of livelihood, you would be returning, relying upon Him, glorified is He; and so that you would not feel secure from death, if you are in a land other than the one in which He, glorified is He, informed you that you would die. Since He did not inform you of what you need, how would He inform you of what you have no need for, which is the time of the Resurrection? The need is only for knowledge that it will occur, and Allah, Exalted, has informed you of that through the tongues of His prophets, peace and blessings be upon them. End of quote.

It is not hidden that the apparent reading according to what he mentioned would be to say "and by the creation of what is in the wombs," just as He, glorified is He, said: "and He sends down the rain." The reason for turning away from that to what is in the noble arrangement is not clear; moreover, his words afterwards are not free of something. That the intended meaning is the exclusivity of the knowledge of these five to Him, Mighty and Majestic, is what the hadiths and reports indicate. Al-Shaykhan and others transmitted from Abu Hurayrah, in a long hadith, that the Prophet (ﷺ) was asked, "When is the Hour?" He said to the questioner: "The one asked about it is no more knowledgeable than the questioner. But I will inform you of its signs: when a slave-woman gives birth to her mistress, and when barefoot herdsmen compete in building tall buildings, in five things none knows except Allah, Exalted." Then the Prophet (ﷺ) recited: ﴿Indeed Allah has knowledge of the Hour, and He sends down the rain﴾, the verse...

That is, to the end of the surah, as in some of the narrations. What occurs in al-Bukhari's Tafsir, "to the wombs," is an abbreviation by some narrator. They both, and others, also transmitted from Ibn Umar who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The keys (in another narration, keys) of the Unseen are five, none knows them except Allah, Exalted: no one knows what will happen tomorrow; no one knows what is in the wombs; no soul knows what it will earn tomorrow; no soul knows in what land it will die; and no one knows when the rain will come."

Ahmad, al-Bazzar, Ibn Mardawayh, al-Ruwayani and al-Diya' transmitted, with a sound chain, from Buraydah who said: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: 'Five things none knows except Allah: indeed with Him is knowledge of the Hour,' the verse..."

The apparent meaning of these reports requires that other unseen matters besides these five may be known to others besides Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and some have gone to this view.

Humayd ibn Zanjawayh transmitted from some of the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, that he mentioned knowledge of the time of an eclipse before it appeared, and was denounced for it. He said: "The unseen is only five," and recited this verse. Whatever is beyond that is unseen which some people know and others do not. Some reports indicate that knowledge of these five was not given to the Prophet (ﷺ), and this necessarily implies that it was not given to anyone else, peace and blessings be upon him, all the more so.

Ahmad and al-Tabarani narrated, on the authority of Ibn 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with them both), that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "I have been given the keys of everything except these five: ﴿Indeed, Allah has knowledge of the Hour﴾ ..., the verse."

Ahmad, Abu Ya'la, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Mardawayh narrated, on the authority of Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "Your Prophet (ﷺ) was given the keys of everything except five: ﴿Indeed, Allah has knowledge of the Hour﴾ ... the verse."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated, on the authority of 'Ali (may Allah ennoble his face), who said: "Nothing was concealed from your Prophet (ﷺ) except five of the secrets of the unseen. This verse at the end of Luqman: ﴿Indeed, Allah has knowledge of the Hour﴾, up to the end of the surah."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ahmad and al-Bukhari in al-Adab narrated, on the authority of Ribi' ibn Hirash, who said: "A man of the Banu 'Amir told me that he said: 'O Messenger of Allah, is there any knowledge that you do not know?' He (peace be upon him) said: 'Allah the Exalted has taught me what is good. Indeed, among knowledge is that which no one knows except Allah the Exalted: the five, ﴿Indeed, Allah has knowledge of the Hour﴾, the verse.'"

Some scholars explicitly stated that Allah the Exalted alone holds these five. Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated, on the authority of Qatadah, that he said concerning the verse: "Five of the unseen which Allah the Exalted has reserved for Himself. He has not informed of them any angel brought near, nor any prophet sent: ﴿Indeed, Allah has knowledge of the Hour﴾,
[Page 112]
and no one among people knows when the Hour will establish, in which year or in which month, by night or by day. He sends down the rain, and no one knows when the rain will descend, by night or by day. He knows what is in the wombs, and no one knows what is in the wombs: male or female, red or black. No soul knows what it will earn tomorrow, good or evil. And no one knows in what land it will die. No one among people knows where his resting place on the earth will be: in a sea or on land, in a plain or on a mountain."

What should be understood is that every unseen matter is known only to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. The unseen matters are not restricted to these five; they were singled out for mention because questions were asked about them, or because souls often yearn to know them. Al-Qastallani said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) mentioned five, although the unseen is not limited, because the number does not negate what exceeds it, and because these five are those whose knowledge people used to claim." End of quotation. Yet in this last reason there is an obvious issue. It is permissible that Allah the Exalted informs some of His chosen servants about one of these five, and grants them knowledge of it in general terms. Their particular knowledge, which belongs to Him alone, is that which encompasses each of them comprehensively and in full detail in the most complete manner. In al-Munawi's large commentary on al-Jami' al-Saghir, in discussing the earlier hadith of Buraydah: "Five which none knows except Allah," [it is stated that this refers to] knowledge in the sense of comprehensive and total encompassment, both in its general and particular aspects. Thus it does not contradict Allah informing some of His special servants about some of the unseen matters among these five, because they are countable particulars. The denial of this by the Mu'tazilah (a rationalist theological school) is mere obstinacy. End of quotation.

From what we have mentioned, the way of reconciling the reports indicating that Allah alone holds knowledge of these matters with what indicates otherwise becomes clear, such as some of the Prophet's (peace be upon him) reports of unseen matters belonging to this category. Whoever consults works such as al-Shifa and al-Mawahib al-Laduniyyah, which mention the miracles of the Prophet (ﷺ) and his reports of unseen matters, will know this.

Al-Qastallani also mentioned that when Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, commands the rain and drives it to whatever places He wills, the angels entrusted with it know it, along with whomever of His creation He, glorified is He, wills. Likewise, when Allah, Blessed and Exalted, wills to create a person in a womb, He, glorified is He, informs the angel entrusted with the womb of what He, Exalted and Majestic, intends. This is shown by what al-Bukhari narrated on the authority of Anas ibn Malik, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Indeed, Allah the Exalted has entrusted an angel with the womb who says: 'O Lord, a drop! O Lord, a clot! O Lord, a lump!' When Allah the Exalted wills to complete its creation, He says: 'Male or female? Wretched or blessed? What is the provision and the term?' Then it is written in its mother's belly. At that point the angel knows of it, and so does whomever of His creation Allah the Exalted wills, Mighty and Majestic."

This does not contradict the exclusivity and sole possession of knowledge of the matters mentioned, based on what you have heard from us: that what Allah, glorified is He, has reserved for Himself is complete knowledge of the state of each in full detail. What the angel knows and what some special servants become aware of may be less than that knowledge; indeed, it is so in reality, without doubt. It may be said that what the saints (awliya') attain of knowledge of any of the matters mentioned is not certain knowledge. 'Ali al-Qari said in his commentary on al-Shifa: "The saints, although some things may be revealed to them, their knowledge is not certain, and their inspiration yields only a conjectural matter. In my view, the like of this, or rather what is far below it, is the knowledge of the astrologer and the like, through signs they possess regarding the descent of rain, whether the pregnancy is male or female, or similar matters. I do not consider the one who claims such knowledge to be an unbeliever, since it is a conjecture about an ordinary matter." Al-'Asqalani also related in Fath al-Bari from al-Qurtubi that he said: "Whoever claims knowledge of any of the five, not traced back to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), is lying in his claim. As for conjecture about the unseen, it may be permissible for the astrologer and others if it is based on an ordinary matter, and that is not knowledge." Accordingly, al-Qastallani's statement, "Whoever claims knowledge of any of them has disbelieved in the Mighty Qur'an," should be understood as referring to the kind of knowledge that Allah has reserved for Himself, not to absolute knowledge, which includes conjecture and what resembles it.

After all this, the matter of the Hour is the most hidden of the matters mentioned, and what Allah has informed His Prophet (ﷺ) of concerning its time is in the utmost generality, although it is more complete than the knowledge of any other human, (ﷺ).

His statement (peace be upon him): "I and the Hour have been sent like these two," [pointing with his two fingers]

indicates no more than general knowledge of its time. I do not think that the noble angels, the elite among them, know more of this than the Prophet (may Allah the Exalted bless him and grant him peace).

What supports my view is what al-Humaydi narrated in his Nawadir with an isnad from al-Sha'bi, who said: "'Isa ibn Maryam asked Jibril (peace be upon them both) about the Hour, and he shook his wings and said: 'The one asked is no more knowledgeable than the one asking.'" The intended meaning is equality in knowledge, in that Allah the Exalted has reserved its knowledge in the most perfect manner. The mention of its signs guides one to general knowledge of it, as is not hidden. It is also possible that Allah the Exalted informed His beloved (peace be upon him) of its time in a complete manner, but not in a way that resembles His own knowledge of it. Allah, glorified is He, obliged him (may Allah the Exalted bless him and grant him peace) to conceal it for a wisdom, and this would be among his special distinctions (peace be upon him). I do not have anything that establishes this with certainty.

Furthermore, in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And no soul knows in what land it will die﴾, He specified the place so that the time would be understood by a fortiori reasoning, since knowing the first is within a soul's capacity in general, unlike the second.

Ahmad and a group narrated on the authority of Abu Ghurrah al-Hudhali, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'When Allah wills to take the soul of a servant in a land, He makes for him a need therein, and he does not stop until he arrives there.' Then he (peace be upon him) recited: ﴿And no soul knows in what land it will die﴾."

Ibn Abi Shaybah narrated in al-Musannaf, on the authority of Khaythamah, that the Angel of Death passed by Sulayman (peace be upon him), and began looking at a man among his companions, gazing at him for a long time. The man said: "Who is this?" He said: "The Angel of Death." The man said: "It seems he wants me. Command the wind to carry me and drop me in India." He did so. The angel said: "My prolonged gaze at him was out of wonder, for I was commanded to take his soul in India, and he is with you."

(*Tadri*) in both places is suspended (in grammar), so the clause ﴿what it will earn﴾ is in the position of the object. It is also possible that the whole of "mādha" is a relative pronoun in the accusative position, governed by *tadri*, as if it were said: "And no soul knows the thing it will earn tomorrow." (*Bi-ayyi*) is connected to (*tamūtu*), the *bā'* being adverbial of place, and the clause is in the accusative position governed by (*tadri*).

Many of the Seven Readers recited *yunzilu* (he sends down) from *al-inzal*. Musa al-Aswari and Ibn Abi 'Abla recited *bi-ayyati ardin* with the feminine *tā'*, because it is in apposition to a feminine noun. This is a rare dialect form, just as *kull* when annexed to a feminine noun may occasionally take the feminine, as in *kullatuhunna fa'alna dhalika*. Let this be noted. And Allah, Mighty and Majestic, knows best.

﴿Indeed, Allah is All-Knowing﴾ (*'Alim*), intensive in knowledge, so nothing among things escapes His knowledge, glorified is He; ﴿All-Aware﴾ (*Khabir*), who knows their inner aspects as He knows their outer aspects. The combination of the two descriptions points to the equality of knowledge of the outward and the inward with Him, Mighty and Majestic. The clause, according to what has been said, is in the position of a justification for His knowledge of what has been mentioned. It has also been said that it is a response to a question arising from the negation of the souls' awareness of what they will earn tomorrow and in what land they will die, as if it were said: "Then who knows that?" So it is said: "Indeed, Allah is All-Knowing, All-Aware," and this is an answer that Allah the Exalted knows that and more. It is clear that if this clause is a continuation of the two preceding clauses, the meaning of the speech indicates the restriction of knowledge of the two matters, of which knowledge is denied to every soul, which is very evident. So reflect on this, and may Allah, Mighty and Majestic, guide you.

* * *

(From the gate of allusion in the noble surah): ﴿Alif Lam Mim﴾ is an allusion to His blessings, His kindness, His majesty, Exalted is His dignity and Mighty and Majestic is His glory. ﴿Those who establish prayer﴾ with presence of heart and turning away from all else. This is the prayer of the elite of the elite. As for the prayer of the elite, it is by negating evil thoughts and worldly desires, and seeking Paradise or the like does not harm it. As for the prayer of the common people, it is what most people do. There is no power nor strength except by Allah, the Exalted, the Mighty. ﴿And give zakah﴾ by giving up existence to the King who is worshipped, in order to attain the sought goal. This is the zakah of the most select. The zakah of the special ones is by giving all one's wealth to purify their hearts from the rust of love of this world. The zakah of the general people is by giving the known measure of wealth in the legally prescribed and well-known manner, to purify their souls from the impurity of stinginess. ﴿And among people is one who buys idle talk﴾: it is that which distracts from Allah, the remembrance of Whom it prevents, and which hinders hearing Him, Mighty and Majestic. As for singing, according to many of them, it has categories, some of which are part of idle talk. Some have reported from al-Junayd, may his secret be sanctified, that he said: "Listening (*sama'*) is forbidden for the people of the carnal soul, because their souls remain; it is permissible for the people of the hearts, because of the abundance of their knowledge and the purity of their hearts; and it is obligatory for our companions, because their portions have perished." And from Abu Bakr al-Kinani: "The listening of the common people is following nature; the listening of the seekers is desire and fear; the listening of the saints is seeing the blessings and favors; the listening of the knowers is by witnessing; and the listening of the people of truth is by unveiling and direct vision. Each of these has a source and a station." They also mentioned that among the people there is one who hears in Allah, for Allah, and through Allah, and from Allah, Exalted is He, and does not hear with human hearing but with the lordly hearing, as in the sacred hadith: "I was his hearing with which he hears."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 31, verse 34 (part 3 of 3):

They say: Wine is forbidden only because it is intoxicating (lahw). So whoever is not intoxicated by it is not forbidden it, since the effective cause (ʿillah) of the prohibition is absent in his case, and a ruling revolves around its cause in both existence and non-existence. They are also committed to permitting the drinking of an intoxicant for one who is not intoxicated by it, especially for one whom it increases in energy for worship. Among the heretical Qalandariyya (a wandering antinomian Sufi order) is one who holds that wine, hashish and similar prohibited intoxicants are permitted without any dispute, claiming that using them opens for them the doors of unveilings (kashf). Some of the ignorant, whom Satan has played with, seek aid from them in that state. May God fight them; how are they deluded!

﴿And We had certainly given Luqman wisdom.﴾ It has been said: wisdom is the perception of the address of the Truth in the manner of inspiration (ilham). They mention that wisdom is a gift of the saints (awliya’), just as revelation is a gift of the prophets, peace be upon them. Each of them is not acquired by effort, except that effort has some role in wisdom.

It has been transmitted: "Whoever sincerely devotes himself to God, the Exalted, for forty mornings, springs of wisdom will gush forth from his heart."

The wisdom which the philosophers claim to be wisdom is not wisdom, since it is among the products of reflection (fikr). It is attained by believer and unbeliever alike, and it rarely escapes the taints of the afflictions of illusion (wahm). For this reason, great disagreement has arisen among its people. Some of the Sufis counted it among "idle talk" (lahw al-hadith), and this is not far from the truth. The story of Luqman points to tawhid (the oneness of God), the station of the gathering of the gathering (jamʿ al-jamʿ), the essence of the gathering (ʿayn al-jamʿ), following the path of the perfected ones, turning away from all other than God, perfecting others, patience in hardships, humility toward people, good conduct in companionship, dealings and manner of life, avoiding swagger in walking, and avoiding raising the voice. It has been said that "the donkeys" (al-ḥamīr) in God's words, ﴿Indeed, the most hateful of voices is the voice of donkeys﴾, are the Sufis who speak the language of gnosis (maʿrifa) before permission is given to them. Some have applied everything in the story to what is within the souls.

﴿And He has completed His favours upon you, both outward and inward.﴾ Al-Junayd said: the outward favours are good character, and the inward favours are kinds of gnosis. It has been said: according to the reading "favour" (niʿmah) in the singular, the outward favour is following the outward knowledge (ʿilm), and the inward is seeking the reality (ḥaqiqah) in following. It has also been said: the outward favour is without slip, and the inward is a heart without heedlessness.

﴿And among the people is one who disputes about God without knowledge, guidance or an illuminating Book.﴾ This refers to the people of disputation among the philosophers, for they dispute about the essence of God, the Exalted, and His attributes, in the same manner upon close examination, because they do not regard the words of the messengers, peace be upon them, nor the books sent down from heaven. Most of their sciences are tainted with the affliction of illusion. Yet, the affairs of God, the Exalted, lie beyond the realm which reason can reach:

Far is it that the phoenix of eternity could hunt, with their saliva, the spiders of thoughts.

More remote than the convex sphere of the ninth heaven is the attainment of knowledge of God, the Exalted, and of His attributes, glorified be He, that is worthy of account, without a divine light by which reason may be illuminated. Their intellects are in darknesses, one above another. The doors of arrival have been closed except to the one who follows the Messenger ﷺ. One of them addressed the presence of the Bearer of the Message, peace be upon him, saying:

You are the gate of God; whoever comes to it other than through you will not enter.

[Page 115]

﴿That is because God, He is the Truth﴾ up to His words, glorified be He: ﴿and that God, He is the Most High, the Great﴾. In this there is an indication that He, glorified be He, is perfection and beyond perfection. By the first is meant one for whom everything that is permissible for him has been attained, and to this the words of God, the Exalted, "He is the Truth," point. By the second is meant one for whom that has been attained, and for whom everything else has attained what is permissible for it, and to this the words of God, the Exalted, "He is the Most High, the Great," point. Beyond these two matters lies the deficient, which is one who does not have what befits him, such as the child, the sick, and the blind, and the one who is self-sufficient (mukتafin), who is one given what meets his need at its time, like the human who has such instruments that his need is met at its time, but they are on the verge of dissolution and decay.

﴿Indeed, God has with Him the knowledge of the Hour﴾ and the verse. More than one has related accounts of the saints containing God, the Exalted's, informing them of what is beyond the knowledge of the Hour among the five. You have already known the discussion of this matter. The most remarkable thing I have seen is what al-Sha'rani mentioned from one of them, that he used to sell rain, and it would rain upon the land of whoever bought it from him whenever he wished. Whoever has a sound intellect does not accept such a story, and how many such narrations are there in the mouths of storytellers! We ask God, the Exalted, to protect us and you from believing in superstitions that have no basis. He, glorified be He, is the Guardian of protection and success.
